en: In the *Vasantatilakā*: Oṃ, homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!

You who abide in the nature of phenomena situated within the thirty-seven factors of great awakening and the equal and unequal great bliss; you whose primary [form] consists of the four wheels of the channels of one’s own body, adorned with the five vowels and the thirty-four consonants along with the twelve measures (*mātrā*); you who are the Lord of the ten levels beginning with the *pīṭhas*, which abide as the divisions of body, speech, and mind; you who are all-pervading, present in the center of the hearts of all living beings, having the form of space, supreme, and profoundly peaceful. ||1||

The Commentary *Rahasyadīpikā*: Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Vajraḍāka! Having prostrated before the Lord Heruka, whose intrinsic nature is non-different from the thirty-six consciousnesses (*saṃvid*), I shall explain the *Vasantatilaka* in due order.

The fourth [master], who had attained the siddhi of Mahāmudrā and was firmly committed to accomplishing the welfare of himself and others, captivated those to be trained by demonstrating extraordinary and wondrous conduct taught in the Yoginī-tantras. Among the twenty-four [masters]—the primary ones adorned with the fourteen vowels (*mā-kā*... *cha-ja*) and the consonants (*bhedasaṃsthī-bho-nāṃ*), ten of whom are situated in the middle—he [is the one].
Ṅa. Cha. Ca. Ja carita-ka

In this *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, the great master named Śrī Kṛṣṇapāda—who possesses various instructions appearing to his own intellect, who is as visible as the second Śrī Heruka himself, and who has exerted himself with the intention of revealing the specific oral tradition manifesting within him to those seeking it—desiring to undertake this manual for the means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāyikā*) of the Blessed Śrī Heruka according to the sequence of inner yoga (*adhyātmakrama*), composes this prologue to the manual for the sake of recollecting his own nature, in order to pay homage to that very reality which is inseparable from his own nature and endowed with its innate character, by means of the verse beginning with "sama-viṣama... and so forth.
In this regard, first of all, the title and so forth are stated:

"Vasantatilaka" is the title; the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*); the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakalakṣaṇa*); the purpose (*prayojana*) is easy comprehension by way of general characteristics;

and the ultimate aim (*tatprayojana*) is the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world, preceded by the attainment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) based on perfect knowledge—this is the summary.

The connection is as follows: "Having bowed to that which is designated as Śrī Heruka, I shall explain the Vasantatilaka. Of what nature is it? It is that whose nature consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*)—beginning with the application of mindfulness of the body and ending with right concentration—which are subsumed within the five paths; these are "even" (*sama*), being of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*), and "uneven" (*viṣama*), being of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). They are "great bliss" (*mahāsaukhya*), being of the form of their non-duality. It is that which abides in that very form. Thus is the connection.
In this context, twenty-two factors are "even" because they are comprised within the mundane path;
fifteen factors are "uneven" because they are comprised within the supramundane path.
Alternatively, the "even" cognitions are those arising from the right channel, while the "uneven" are those arising from the left channel.

For each of the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, there are twenty-four types of bliss (*ānanda*) distinguished by joy (*ānanda*) and the rest; within the four wheels (*cakra*), there are twelve types of bliss through the threefold division of bliss and so forth according to the sequence of the three stages beginning with entry; and there is one [bliss] from the dissolution of all limbs.

Thus, the Blessed One, established in the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), has a single innate form (*sahajaikamūrti*), and externally he is likewise joined with that many *ḍākinīs*.
In order to demonstrate that very state of being the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvaratva*), he says: "One's own channels" (*svāṅganāḍī*) and so forth.

These channels located within one's own eight limbs—the gates of the body—which have the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, and which take the forms of Kākāsyā and the others; likewise, the four wheels beginning with the Emanation (*nirmāṇa*) wheel, situated respectively at the navel, heart, throat, and crown, whose natures are the Emanation, Dharma, Enjoyment, and Essential Body (*svabhāvakāya*); in these [wheels] consisting of the wheels of Wisdom, Mind, Speech, and Body, [the central deity] is the sovereign, existing as the nature of the Heart (*hṛdaya*)—the form of Awakening (*bodhi*) in which the conventional and ultimate truths are non-different.
He also describes its nature as being the embodiment of mantra: "The consonant adorned with the five vowels, the twelve mātrās, and the thirty-four [consonants].
Because of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation of the term "five-vowel-word," ten [vowels] are obtained.

Therein, in the center of the Dharma-chakra and on the four cardinal petals, the first instruction is the purification of the aggregates (*skandha-viśuddhi*) through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas—marked by the vowels *hūṃ*, *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hrīṃ*, and *khaṃ*. Likewise, in the Saṃbhoga-chakra, the purification of the five elements (*pañca-dhātu-viśuddhi*) occurs through the placement of the five seed-syllables *auṃ*, *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, and *ai*. Similarly, the twelve vowels—excluding the four neuter ones—are downward-facing in the left channel (*vāmā*), while those same vowels are upward-facing in the right channel; these are surrounded by the twenty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, which are both upward and downward facing and colored by the anusvāra, the nature of *ma*.
Likewise, those same sixteen vowels, doubled and including the neuter [vowels], are situated in the *mahāsukhacakra*, excluding the syllables at the top and bottom;
and the thirty-two consonants beginning with *ka*, doubled, are in the *nirmāṇacakra*.

According to the system of assigning twenty-four channels, the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are in the corners of the *dharmacakra*, while the aspirates (*ya-ra-la-vā*) are situated outside of that as the vessel-form.

In the center of all four wheels, it is adorned with the syllables beginning with the vowels, *meghanāda*, *brahman*, and the *anāhata*; with the letter *ra* at *ajālaṃdhara* and the letter *kṣa* at the lower gate— thus it has the form of a mantra-line.

In order to demonstrate his sovereignty over the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), he says: "Having prostrated to the Lord of the ten stages—namely the *pīṭha* and so forth, which abide as the divisions of body, speech, and mind—and what else? To whom else?—I shall speak the *Vasantatilakā*. He is the sovereign, the master, of those ten Bodhisattva stages whose nature is the *Pramuditā* and so forth, which abide in the wheels (*cakra*) of the body and so on through their reverse-order divisions as the *pīṭha* and so forth; that is, the channels (*nāḍī*) in the locations such as the head, whose forms are indivisible and so on."

In this context, there are ten bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*), upon which the bodhisattva, having incinerated the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, perceives reality through the direct realization of the non-conceptual realm (*avikalpadhātu*) and attains perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*) within three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*). As it is stated in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*: "This [generation of the mind] is considered to be the generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*); it is the stage of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), another is that of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayika*), then that of maturation (*vaipākya*) on the stages, and likewise that which is free from obscurations."

In this context, however, the distinction from the vision of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is that the direct realization of the state of Śrī Heruka—which is synonymous with the glorious Great Bliss (*Mahāsukha*), which is self-cognizable, and which consists primarily in the attainment of the Svābhāvikakāya (the body of intrinsic nature) characterized by the dissolution (*laya*) and so forth accomplished through the traversal of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) symbolized by Pullīra and the other sites—is achieved more swiftly, even in this very life.

Therefore, because the innate (*sahaja*) itself holds sovereignty over the stages of the *pīṭhas* and so forth in the form of the Dharmakāya and the others, the Lord’s status as the master of the ten stages is established.
The etymological derivation (*nirukti*) and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the *pīṭhas* and the *bhūmis* will be explained later.
[The reading] *gaṃgṛhī* is found in manuscripts *ga*, *ṅa*, and *cha*; [the reading] *catuṣpathe* is found in manuscripts *kha*, *gha*, and *cha*.
It is indeed empty—what is its intrinsic nature? These two are [present]. O Bho, this is the external space of the fourfold manifestation.
The grains are said to be: ka, ya, tra,
te, ga,
cha, hī, ta, kā, ṅa, ca.
‘Tam’ does not exist— ṅa, cha,
yāvatī— kha, gha;
you have attained it— bho.
The five consonants [are]: gha, cha,
in the wheel— ka, jāṃ, ka, jīṃ, ca.
Having known the seed-syllables *e*, *gha*, *ca*, *mā*, *trā*, *n*, *kha*, *gha*, *cha* as twenty, and *i*, *ca*, *tyā*— these are the twenty locations (*viṃśatisthāna*). *Bho*.
By those colored—what?
The *repha*s consisting of both the upward and downward directions—Ka. Bho! Re! Ka.
The letter *ka* [is the first of] the series of mantras adorned with *kha*, *gha*, and *cha*;
*bho* [is followed by] *nya* and *tī*.
‘This’ does not exist—ka, kha;
by way of division—kha, gha; tenfold—kha, gha; element—cha.
sampa-ka. ga. ṅa; kārābhatri-kha. gha. ca. cha;
kalpo-ka.
khyeyaṃ – kra. kha. ga. ṅa;
khyāśa – cha; vipākṣo – kha.; kṣyo – gha. ca. cha.

- *caraṇa* (foot), *ka kha ga gha ṅa* (the five gutturals), *yādhi* (disease), *ca sigamapra* (the letters *ca*, *si*, *ga*, *ma*, *pra*), *ka*, *gamapradhyāna* (meditation on *ga*, *ma*, *pra*), *gha*.
*bhūmī* (earth) – *dharma-kha*; *bhūmidharma* (the nature of the earth) – *cha*, together with *yasyai* – *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *cha*; and *nāṃ ca bhū-* – *kha*, *cha*.
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "Śrī Heruka, whose nature is the reality of supreme bliss, shines with the radiant splendor of the radiating *Vasantatilakā*.

And what else is he like? He is all-pervading (*sarvaga*), because the aggregates (*skandha*) and all other phenomena abide therein as their true nature (*dharmatā*); thus, he is the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."

"Residing in the center of the hearts of all living beings" means: "all living beings" refers to animals, birds, reptiles, humans, and so forth; "residing in the center of their own hearts" means situated within the pericarp of the lotus-cavity of the heart. Its nature consists of the four elements beginning with earth. It resides in the center of the solar and lunar mandalas, being of a nature that is the most subtle *dharmadhātu*, subtler than even a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair. It exists in a form distinct from all the *cakras*, *ḍākinīs*, heroes (*vīras*), and so on. And it has been said: "The single *bindu*, the imperishable syllable, eternally abides in the heart."

"And for those men who cultivate that, supreme knowledge arises. Thus it is said. Regarding the "enveloping" (*saṃpuṭa*), when there is the state of being enveloped, the single *bindu* shines forth—according to the statement: "Having become un-enveloped by an envelope, the *bindu* shall proceed to the state of being *nirbindu*. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has the form of space (*vyomarūpa*) because it is the *dharmakāya*.
Alternatively, it has the form of the five voids because it is accessible through the touch of the channels such as *trivṛtā* and so forth;
and it is said: "The space in the center of the *bhaga*, adorned with the five voids, joined with the pericarp and filaments, and embellished by eight petals," and so forth.
"Supremely peaceful," and so forth:
it is supreme because its nature is ultimate bodhicitta, and it is peaceful because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

With the words beginning "Śrī Heruka," he speaks in order to correctly demonstrate the nature of bodhicitta as both the ultimate (*vivṛti*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*): "Śrī Heruka" refers to the reality of supreme bliss (*paramanirvṛti-tattva*), which consists of the four liberations taught in the tantra; it is the *sahaja* (innate) single *dharmakāya*. He is of that form—that is, identical with it.

Likewise, this Vārāhī—who arises from emanation, who emerges as the very nature of the coming spring through the conjunction with the blossoming of the flowers of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth—is united with Heruka. Like a *tilaka* mark, she is the flame of the fire of gnosis (*jñāna*), consisting of light, which consumes the fuel of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Her radiation (*spharaṇa*) is the upward movement through the three wheels (*cakra*) by way of the central channel (*madhyamārga*); by that she is radiant, and her splendor (*bhā*)—the light shimmering with its shadow—is [present] in every limb.
And there is no "ja" in "sphuraṇo," nor "cha" [in the manuscript]; "sphura" is in "ña" and "ḍa."
In these [manuscripts], the phrase "hanmadhyaga" is absent in manuscript cha; in manuscript gha it is "dhyage," and in manuscript ca it is "dhyage."
And in the Puḍhe-ca-dhyagaṃ-cha manuscript, it is stated that they exist in the form of a *tilaka* (mark), O [Lord]. (kha. gha)
śante—kha; śanaḥ—gha; puṭayuto—ca; śrī—kha gha ca cha; divivṛ—kha gha cha.
Gha. Ca. Cha. "Sphuraṇam" — Cha. ||
The state below is the state—kha. gha.
supreme—ka. kha. cha.

Likewise, form or mind... [suitable] by means of... Having bowed to the Lord of the channel-wheels (*nāḍicakra*), who is the accumulation of the expansion of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*) and the source of happiness for the welfare of oneself and others in the world—[to him whose]... *Note: The text provided contains fragments and abbreviations (e.g., *vā citta-kha. yogyena -kha.*). The translation reflects the available Sanskrit terms while acknowledging the lacunae.*

Likewise, I bow to you, Sahaja-Ātma-Heruka—the non-dual *tilaka* of the *dharmadhātu*—who abide within the five voids of the Great Sky, situated inside the pericarp of the secret *kokanada* lotus of Anantavīrīṇī; [I bow to you] who are reckoned by that accumulation of the flow of the three channels, Rasanā and the others, which take the form of the three families of body, speech, and mind, and whose flow in the places such as Pullīra and the Nirmāṇa [chakras] consists of twenty-four, one hundred and twenty, twenty-one thousand, and seventy-two thousand in number, thereby defining this wheel of channels.

I bow to you, Herukī, Mother of the World, whose brilliance exceeds the fierce mass of lightning flashing from within a bank of dark clouds, and who simultaneously consumes both sentient beings and their environments.

"I bow to you, who are born from the union of the thunderbolt and the lotus at the navel-cakra within the ocean of the void, who are skilled in drinking the essence of the finest nectar, and who possess the brilliance of the submarine fire.

Having thus prostrated to the nature of the *dharmakāya*, he speaks with the other two [limbs] in order to pay homage: "The bliss of the world" refers to the bliss of the three realms that is to be personally realized; this is one's own bliss (*svasukham*). From the opening of the thunderbolt, during the state of non-emission, is the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
In that which is other than this, there is the bliss for the sake of others, the nature of which is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
This very arising of the world is the arising of the Tathāgata, because the world has that as its nature.
And it is said in the *Saṃpuṭatilaka*: "Heruka, Mahāsaṃvara, the form of light, the form of reality, known as Vasantatilaka."
"Having prostrated before the Lord of the Wheel of Channels, for the sake of the happiness of the self and others in the world"—this is the reading in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary.
"I shall describe the *Vasantatilakā*, which has emerged from the Seat of Yoga (*yogapīṭha*), in the form of both the external and the internal, [explaining] the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara* in due order. (3)
Consisting entirely of ḍākinīs, he is red and arises from all vajras;
he is known as Padmanarteśvara through his yoga with the manifestation of the lotus.
He is further renowned as Vajrasūrya, possessing a radiant, upward-shining light. It is also stated in the *Śrīvajraḍāka*: "It shines."
That which blazes is the Sage Mahāvairocana;

at the end of cessation (*viramānta*), he is the supreme horse (*paramāśva*) because of the universal arising of the winds. For this very reason, his body is embraced by Vārāhī—this is the completion of the sentence according to the previously stated principle. [Regarding the phrase "named Śrī Heruka":
although the Blessed One is nameless, he is established through the conventional designation "Śrī Heruka."]
[The verse] beginning with *hūṃ* is delightful and captivating because of its resonance, which is like an echo;

that very resonance is the *vasantatilakā*. By means of that sound (*dhvani*), the Lord *bindu* is revealed. Therefore, the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of *nāda* and *bindu* is their *samāpatti*, which is their "arising" (*utpatti*). Because it transcends sequence, it has the nature of the *utpannakrama*; having prostrated [to this], the connection is with what precedes. (2) What kind of *vasantatilakā* shall I describe?—that which has emerged from the *yogapīṭha*.

There are four yoga-seats (*yogapīṭha*), known as the seats of self, other, mantra, and reality (*tattva*). These are, respectively, the navel, heart, throat, and head. From these [seats], that which has issued forth and proceeds by way of coming and going—being the means for the practice of speech—is also called the *Vasantatilaka*. Just as in the epic poem *Sītāharaṇa*, he asks: "From where was this extracted? He replies: "The tantra named *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*. Within that, I shall explain the sequence (*krama*)—the path characterized as both external and internal, known as the arisen and the unarisen—in its true nature (*svarūpa*). This is the connection with what precedes.

For instance, in the stage of generation (utpattikrama), there is the mandala-circle consisting of thirty-seven [deities], whereas in the stage of completion (niṣpannakrama), within great bliss, there is the channel-wheel (nāḍīcakra) numbering the same; in this manner, other [correspondences] should also be inferred. || 3 ||

The first instruction: The glorious Vajraḍākinī is established within one's own body; this is for the sake of clear understanding by those who have very little inclination [for extensive teachings]. (4)
Having abandoned the artificial mandala, the artificial fire-offering ritual, the artificial meditative cultivation, and even the artificial recitation; ||5||
"All is artificial," and so forth; "all," and so forth, refers to the nature of the application of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
He states the purpose for the external artificial practice in order to realize one's own true nature, beginning with "Śrīvajraḍākinī," and so forth.

This Blessed Lady Vajraḍākinī—*vajra* being *saṃvara*, the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) situated at the gateway, the unstruck nectar flowing from the hand held in the *khagamukha* gesture, emitting waves and ripples from the milk-ocean—she is called *Vajraḍākinī* because she flies or moves; the Blessed Lady whose limbs are illuminated like thousands of flashes of lightning, the radiance of the fire of primordial wisdom (*jñānāgni*), is Vārāhī. She is perfected (*siddhā*) because her nature is the form of *dharmatā*, being spontaneously accomplished by her very nature (*prakṛtyā*), and because she is to be known by all.

Is she situated outside? No, he says: she is "established" (*vyavasthitā*), meaning she dwells within one's own body, the physical form composed of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, because she is perceived precisely through that [body] in the manner previously described.

Therefore, for the sake of those individuals who are unable to penetrate the extensive tantra and who have very little interest, I shall explain it so that there may be a clear understanding—that is, a realization—of her; the meaning is: for the sake of realizing the complete *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion) by means of a concise text. || 4 ||

In this context, what should the lord of yogins who has ascended to the stage of the perfected process (*niṣpannakrama*) perform—such as the maṇḍala, fire-offerings (*homa*), meditations, or recitations? He says "no," beginning with the words "in the artificial" (*kṛtrime*) and so forth.

All these things, such as images and the like, which exist externally in the generation process (*utpattikrama*), are artificial and fabricated because they are conceptual constructs and because they must be accomplished through external implements. Like a jar or similar objects, they possess the nature of perishing due to the destruction of their constituent parts.
Therefore, the sense is: what is the use of performing or meditating upon those things which are merely causes of distraction?

If this is so, why [is it said]...? [The reading] "saṃvaram" does not exist in manuscripts *bho*, *ka*, *ṅa*, and *ca*; [the reading] "bāhyāṃ" appears in *ka*, *ṅa*, and *ca*, while "hyaṃ" appears in *ga* and *ja*. In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, regarding the realization of one's own nature (*svarūpapratipatti*), the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*) is certainly not the cause; just as a raft is employed by certain seekers of the further shore.
Just so, that very process is abandoned upon reaching the further shore.
Fearing that this might be suspected as having been taught by the Blessed One [as something ultimately real], he says: "The ritual procedure is artificial," and so forth.

This ritual procedure of the mandala and so on, which was previously mentioned, although it is artificial, was taught for the sake of realizing—that is, understanding—the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the mandala and other such things, which are established by their own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). It is not that very [artificial] procedure itself which constitutes the fruit.
Therefore, relying on the union with that mandala and so forth—which will be described as being of the nature of the innate (*sahajasiddha*)—everything external is indeed merely artificial.
The intended meaning is that one should meditate upon the mandala within the body.

Let those who are devoted to the external mandala and so forth first engage in the meditation on its causes; subsequently, by means of that very path, they will realize that these [mandalas] are established by their own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). Thus, having caused them to abandon attachment to the external, they are introduced to the internal; therefore, even the teaching of those [external mandalas] is purposeful. (5–6)
He provides an illustration with the words "Just as by those seeking the further shore," and so forth:

just as those desiring to reach the far shore of the ocean and such first diligently rely upon a boat or raft as a means of crossing, but having reached the shore, they discard it like a blade of grass—even so, having attained the external mandala and subsequently attaining that which is internal, they discard the external; for there is the saying: "When the goal has been reached, those who are to be abandoned are called 'means'."

Those jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) who have previously practiced artificial mandalas and the like attain, by means of a mere sudden resolve toward the non-artificial mandala, the non-artificial [mandala] itself; this is the distinction.
Such a spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is extremely rare.

In the stage of the perfected process (*niṣpannakrama*), that lineage is recognized through the door of difficult-to-grasp [signs], such as sandalwood and other specific signs (*nimitta-viśeṣa*); for fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane.
For it is said: "The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by means of signs" (Tattvārthapaṭala, p. 230). (7)
The first exposition: whatever rites of the maṇḍala and so forth those with artificial intentions perform, all of it is good and not bad; even when applied [by them], it is clearly effective.

Just as the Victors have taught that the continuum of the activity of karma exists for the sake of the cognition of real entities, so too do the Sages compose their treatises for the sake of verbal knowledge. || 9 ||
In this context, the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is itself enlightenment (*bodhi*).

Since even that which is being cultivated becomes manifest despite being unreal, there may be the doubt that both the manifest and the unmanifest serve as causes for enlightenment. Anticipating this, he says: "That which is the mandala... and so forth.

Those yogins who are conceptualizers with artificial intentions perform the previously mentioned mandalas and other rites either by drawing them or mentally; whether all that be good or bad, when it is being cultivated, it first becomes manifest. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "that is the reality" (*tattvam*).
Even a frog, when repeatedly meditated upon here by the ignorant, appears as one radiant with a mass of matted hair,
grey with ashes, wearing a white sacred thread, and carrying a water-pot and a staff upon his shoulder.
(Ādi-mahākāvya 1.18) Whatever is repeatedly contemplated here by fools, that very thing comes to be perceived.
For it is stated [in the Āgama-māhātmya, verse 57]: "That very thing appears before one. || 8 ||

Fearing that the expansion of ritual activity (*karmaprasara*) might not be the reality (*tattva*) itself—just like the mandala and other such elements—the author says, "the expansion of ritual activity," and so forth.

Even though the Blessed One taught a tantra associated with the expansion of ritual activity that must be accomplished through various efforts, that was not intended as the ultimate reality (*tattva*), but rather as the [means for attaining] the true entity (*sad-vastu*).

For the sake of the experience and realization of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), since those who engage in meditative cultivation for the purpose of accomplishing the expansion of karma enter the co-emergent—which is of the nature of the self-existent reality (*dharmatā*) and the form of the supreme space—precisely by means of that [cultivation] through the removal of its habitual tendencies (*saṃskāra*), the teaching of those various tantras is intended in this sense; it is not, however, devoid of purpose.
To illustrate this, he says: "for the sake of verbal knowledge."

Just as sages compose that treatise on grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) for the thorough understanding of external sounds alone, yet no realization of ultimate reality (*tattvāvagati*) arises from its composition; in the very same way, according to their karma, they perform their functions—like actors or singers—in accordance with the processes suited to their respective castes and physical forms, based on the accumulation of merit from former friends and kin.

For, having roused the afflictions with effort, they indeed cause their own minds to run away.
Therefore, in every respect, the ritual procedures for the mandala and so forth lead to liberation and are by no means a cause of supreme exertion.

Due to the absence of correct aspirational prayers (*samyak-praṇidhāna*), they do not become attainers of the state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). However, those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and other such factors would indeed be direct realizers of that state, as it has been said: "Through hearing the sublime Dharma, through attending upon virtuous friends, and by virtue of their spiritual lineage, there shall be eligibility for this [attainment] for those who have previously performed meritorious deeds" (Ārya-mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa).

Not only do they fail to attain reality, but even that which is cultivated as artificial fails them due to mental distraction caused by physical exhaustion; thus, having fallen from both, those deluded in their practice fall into confusion. For it is said [in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*]: "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated, and one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
Furthermore, in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*: "Through the application of the mantra-form, there is neither awakening nor cultivation."

Having reflected, it was said: "In brief, one should meditate upon the characteristics of body, speech, and mind as the union with awakening, the samādhi fashioned by mantra," and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By exerting effort, having aroused the afflictions," and so on;
this is easy to understand.

The first instruction is: Buddhahood does not arise from the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), nor likewise from the conceptual (*savikalpa*);
it arises for the wise only from perfectly pure thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*)."
Some say: Buddhahood is attained by resorting to non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), just like the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*);
for in that state, there is an absence of conceptualizations regarding both the defiled and the purified, and Buddhahood consists precisely of that.
It is said: "Buddhahood does not arise from the non-conceptual.
For emptiness is of such a nature that it entails the annihilation of the form consisting of appearance;
yet Buddhahood is that which abandons both positions—thus there is a contradiction.

Now, [the author] speaks in order to refute the notion that the deity’s form arising through the sequence beginning with Candravajrā, when accompanied by the pride (*ahaṅkāra*) of a Tathāgata, will become the cause for attaining Buddhahood due to its specific conceptualization: "It would not arise from that which is conceptual.

Even from such a specific form when cultivated, Buddhahood does not result; for there is no difference between a specific and a non-specific conceptualization, as both are causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
And it has been said: "What indeed is the difference in a conceptualization, whether it be pure or impure?"
"There is no difference in the burning capacity of fire due to a difference in its substratum" (*Ārya-mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa*), and so forth.
From what, then, would that [distinction] arise? He says: "By means of the *suviśuddha*," and so on.
That [distinction] arises from the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the rest.

Since these aggregates and so forth are by their very nature primordially pure as the co-emergent (*sahaja*), which is a synonym for great bliss, therefore it is impossible for them to be separated from or joined with any phenomenon,
just as space cannot be [affected] by smoke and the like.
It is stated that the primary cause for this is simply the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and nothing else; furthermore,
that [knowledge] depends upon a teacher who provides instruction,
while anything else is merely a conventional rule (*samaya*).

First Chapter: The Second Indication. Now, another [explanation] concerning the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which constitute the essence of the Tantra beginning with Form (rūpa): Vairocana is the Buddha; Vajrasūrya is Feeling (vedanā); Padmanarteśvara is Perception (saṃjñā); and likewise, Vajrarāja is Mental Formations (saṃskāra). ||2||

These formations (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth, which produce the diverse emanations of sentient beings through the impelling of two manifestations—he is the King of Vajras (*vajrarāj*) among the Tathāgatas because he rules over them. At the end of the *virama* [joy], he is the Supreme Horse (*paramāśva*), whose intrinsic nature is the gnosis of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and not [the deity] Śyāma. || 1–2 ||
Furthermore, this is the reading of this verse in the *Mātṛkā*: "Form is the Buddha Vairocana; feeling is Ratnasaṃbhava; perception is Amitābha; and mental formations are Amoghavajra."

In the *Mātṛkā*, there is this additional reading: "Form is the Buddha Vairocana; sensation is Ratnasaṃbhava; perception is Amitābha; mental formations are Amoghasiddhi; and consciousness is Vajrasattva. Furthermore, all form is Heruka. Thus, within the bodies of living beings, the aggregates (*skandha*) have the Tathāgatas as their essence. One should know the five colors to be white, yellow, red, dark green, and fair, as well as deep black. The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is held to be white, holding a wheel weapon in the right hand and joined with a bell in the left; it stands proudly upon the tip of the nose. The second aggregate is considered to be yellow, holding a jewel weapon in the right hand and joined with a bell in the left; its left hand rests at the heart. The third aggregate is measured as red, holding a lotus weapon in the right hand and accompanied by a bell in the left; its left hand rests at the heart. The fourth aggregate is remembered as dark green, holding a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) weapon in the hand and beautifully adorned with a bell in the left; its left hand rests at the heart. The fifth is deep black and possesses sovereignty; its right hand is placed at the heart, and one knows its left hand, joined with a bell, to be situated at the hip region."
The second explanation: Consciousness is Vajrasattva; all forms are Heruka. The eye is called Mohavajra, and the ear is designated as Dveṣavajra. (3)

"That which is this consciousness (*vijñāna*) which discerns objects is itself the indestructible being (*sattva*) like a vajra; he who possesses that is Vajrasattva. He is Akṣobhya, the Vajra of Mind, whose nature is the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu-jñāna*, characterized by the state of essential identity (*samarasīkaraṇa*) of the two—*sattva* and *rajas*. He is not an external blue-colored form. Likewise, because he possesses the form of all those five previously mentioned [elements] as his innate nature (*sahajātmaka*), he is Sarvarūpī, the pervasive one. He is the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, the sixth Mahāvajradhara; it should be understood that his nature is *dharmatā*. This is the remainder [of the explanation]."
It is stated in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas" (*Guhyasamāja* 17.50).

Also in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*: "The aggregates themselves are indeed the Perfectly Awakened Ones, arising from conditions for the sake of enlightenment; they are known as Tathāgatas because of their union with non-dual suchness. Furthermore, in the *Guhyendutilaka*: "Let this entire world, whose nature consists of the five Buddhas, behold the wondrous divine drama, wherein the one named Great Bliss dances with manifold moods."

Also in the *Vajrapañjara*: "Akṣobhya himself is called Amitāyus; ten million [times that] is proclaimed as Vajraṅga by the Vajrin. Amita is declared by Amitāyus," and likewise in the *Saṃpuṭa*: "The three born of the mother are the measures, entirely free from passion, as far as the lord of the seven horses [the sun] reaches the sky," and so forth.
And also: "The three born of the father, this aggregate of six thousand [parts], is the form of the six Tathāgatas," and so forth.
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "Jealousy-vajra is the nose, and passion-vajra is known as the mouth; the body is stinginess-vajra—these five are the gross deities. (4)
Mātsaryavajra is all the sense-bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), while Heruka is the Supreme Lord.
The earth element is Pātanī, and the water element is known as Māraṇī. (5)

In order to direct the sense bases (*āyatana*) toward the heroes, he says: "The two eyes are called Mohavajra," and so forth. The pair of eyes is Mohavajra; because of its lack of attachment to the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), it brings about other objects, and thus its activity is delusion (*moha*). It is *prabhāsvara* (luminosity), and therein the *vajra* is the indivisible one, possessing great power from the body wheel (*kāyacakra*). The faculty of hearing (*śruti*) is the ear organ; it is Dveṣavajra from the mind wheel (*cittacakra*), being Khaṇḍakapālin. This is because, through the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in grasping sound, there is an aversion to other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). || 3 ||
The olfactory faculty is Marṣyāvatra; Virūpākṣa [arises] from the wheel of speech.
"I alone am the enjoyer of all odors through my entire self; there is no other whatsoever, because of my pervasiveness.
The mouth is that which resides in the mouth, the gustatory faculty; Rāgavajra is the primordial Aṅkurika from the wheel of speech.
"Touch" refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Mātsaryavajra is Vajrasattva, the Hero, who pervades the end of the body-cakra because of his all-pervasiveness.
"Miserliness" (*mātsarya*) is the thought: "The bliss of touching the lotus of all mudrās has been experienced by me alone, and not by anyone else. (4)
The mind-faculty (*manas*) is the sense-base of all [faculties].
Heruka, from the end of the mind-wheel, should be known as the vajra-body that pervades all the sense-faculties.

Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, Viṣkambhin, and the illustrious Samantabhadra—these are designated as the eyes and so forth. Pātanī is fair-complexioned; Māraṇī is black-complexioned; Ākarṣaṇī is red-complexioned; and Narteśvarī is dark-green. Cakradharī is Kati; she is Pātanī, holding [the discus] with two arms, and in her two left hands she holds a skull-cup (kapāla) and a staff with a skull at the top (khaṭvāṅga) as weapons. Vajradharī is Kati; she is Māraṇī, holding [the vajra] with two arms, and in her two left hands she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga as weapons. Padmadharī is Kati; she is the goddess Ākarṣaṇī standing there, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in her two left hands as weapons. Khaṅgadharī is Kati; she is Īśvarī, holding [the sword] with two arms, and in her two left hands she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga as weapons. And Jvālinī is the Great Goddess, three-faced and holding six arms. She is red-complexioned and resides in the element of space (ākāśadhātu). With her arms she firmly holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga, while with her left hands she holds a noose (pāśa), a hook (aṅkuśa), a severed head (chinnamuṇḍa), and a skull-cup (kati). With her right hands she holds [the remaining implements].
The second explanation: the fire element is considered Ākarṣaṇī, while the wind element is Vāyu-narteśvarī; the space element is said to be Padmajvālinī-anākulā.
Because of this statement.

Primarily, however, these receive the designation of "heroes" (*vīra*) because they are permeated by great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and not because they hold the vajra and vajra-bell, since those are merely conceptualized.
Also in the *Śrīsamāja*: "The supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas is indeed the sense-bases (*āyatana*) of the vajras," as stated in verse 17.50.
He speaks of the reality of the elements (*dhātutattva*), beginning with "the one who causes falling" (*pātanī*) and so forth.

This earth element—whether it be the wheel that constructs bone, flesh, and so on, or the hardness-tactile sensation during meditative absorption (*samāpatti*)—is to be known as *Pātanī* the *Ḍākinī*, whose nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), bliss (*ānanda*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and skillful means (*upāya*), and who crushes the conceptualizations of attachment to those [elements].

This water element—whether it be the wheel of movement (*lāsaga*) and so on, or the wheel of phenomena (*dharmacakra*), or the fluidity-tactile sensation during meditative absorption—is to be known as *Māraṇī* the *Lāmā*, who brings about the destruction of attachment to those [elements], and whose nature is the signless (*animitta*), supreme compassion (*paramakaruṇā*), and aspiration (*praṇidhi*).

This element of fire (*tejodhātu*) which exists as warmth within the limbs, or as the *saṃbhogacakra* during meditative absorption, or as the touch of lightness, or as the blazing flame of the fire of gnosis—this should be known as Ākarṣaṇī, who destroys attachment to that [fire]; she is Khaṇḍarohā, whose nature consists of the power of wishlessness, cessation, and sympathetic joy.

Likewise, this element of wind (*vāyudhātu*), characterized by going and coming, contracting and expanding, or the radiation and entry [of light] into the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) during meditative absorption; or the entering and exiting, the arising and emerging [from it]; or the movement of the sixteen hundred and twenty breaths day and night—this is to be known as Narteśvarī, the mistress of the dance, which is the action to be accomplished through all its limbs; she is embodied, consisting of the nature of the bliss of volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*), innate joy (*sahajānanda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and gnosis (*jñāna*).
These very ones—the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the doctrine-seal (*dharmamudrā*), and the commitment-seal (*samayamudrā*)—are to be understood by me as having been designated as such.
And it is said: "Earth is called Locanā; Water is remembered as Māraṇī; Fire is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; Wind is proclaimed as Tārā. Also, in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*:
"The letter E is to be known as Earth, while the Action-Seal is Locanā," and so forth. (Guhyasamāja 17.51).
Through the union of bola and kakkola, the earth element is born there; the space element is said to be the unagitated Padmajvālinī. (1110138) 6.
Thus, in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, it is said: "In this way, the body of embodied beings consists of the deities of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth;

having indeed encountered pleasure, pain, karma, afflictions (*kleśas*), and the like, and by resorting to arising and destruction, one attains both worldly existence (*bhava*) and liberation (*nirvāṇa*). (7)

Thus, from the *Śrīhevajra* [tantra], following the second chapter of the *Śrīvasantatilakā*, which is the instruction on the description of the forms of the deities such as Vairocana as they truly abide within the body of the Tathāgata consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*): "That which is this space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is all the channels (*nāḍī*); whether it be the dissolution of the doors of the sense-faculties or the space of the pores of the skin, she is named Padmajvālinī, that is, Vārāhī. She is the mistress of the network of channels within the lotus; unsmeared by the mud of defilement (*uparāga*), she is to be known as pervading the four aforementioned elements, having transcended the conceptualization of subject and object."
And it is said: "Abiding in the form of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), that very [state] is remembered as Khecarī.

Also, in the *Vajrapañjara*, because of the statement, "By means of the interior of all elements," and from the words of the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*: "In this [reality] whose sole intrinsic nature is space, the Great Sage dwelt. (5–6)
He states the conclusion: "In this way," and so forth.

By this reasoning, the body of all embodied beings dwelling within the three realms—the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the rest—should be understood as being of the nature of the deity; it is not an external [form] endowed with a face, arms, and so on.

Therefore, all these things contained within the basket of the aggregates—such as pleasure, pain, afflictions (*kleśas*), karma, arising, and cessation—are themselves of the nature of the deity, because they are non-different from that [deity].
Therefore, that which is saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa; there is no distinction whatsoever between the two. || 7 ||
Thus ends the detailed commentary on the second instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a manual for the means of accomplishment in the *Vasantatilakā*. 2.

Now, I shall explain the division of the gates according to the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior [states] pertaining to the body, speech, and mind of whichever Tathāgata-body [is concerned]. || 1 ||
It has one pillar, nine gates, and is gross; it possesses five presiding deities.
With its gates situated within the nine streams, it is proclaimed as "nine-gated. ||2||

Having established in the second chapter that the body of all embodied beings is of the nature of the Tathāgata, [the author] introduces the following section with the words "Now," etc., in order to explain the doors—distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior—through which their entry and exit occur;
the meaning of this is easy to understand. ||1||
He states the detailed explanation with the words beginning "a single pillar," and so forth.

This body, which contains all the deities, is called the "Skeleton" (*kaṅkāla*); it has a single pillar that extends from the middle of the hips and shoulders at the back as far as the soles of the feet, consisting primarily of a structural column. On its left and right sides, there exist twenty-four heroes who are essentially the *pārśvasthitakaṇikāvīra-yoginīs*, subsumed within the three wheels (*tricakra*). Standing in their midst is the supporting staff (*daṇḍa*), the foundation of the worlds *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, which bears the designation of the Great Skeleton (*Mahākaṅkāla*) in the form of Śrī Heruka.

He has a single pillar of that kind; as it is also stated in the *Saṃpuṭa*: "Having become twelvefold and doubled, [the pillar stands] on both sides between two wings, surrounded on all sides by the host of Vīras and Yoginīs."
This skeleton, in the form of a staff, is Heruka, the supreme support;
he is designated as the stūpa of the Buddhas of the aggregates, elements, and so forth. Thus it is said.

Then, for him—*ña*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*. To the one who has gone to Tripura—*na*, *ḍha*. By the division of the inferior (*adhama*) mind—*ja*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*. And by *dena*—*ga*. The door-pillars—*ga*. The single-pillar, nine-doored, throbbing five-fold—*ka*. *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*. The five also—*ḍha*. The gross five—*kha*. The deities of the petals and so forth—*ga*. The single-pillar, nine-doored body of Śrī Heruka and others—*ja*. Gone to the ear—*ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *cha*. Gone—*ga*, *gha*. Gone to the ear—*ja*. Ninefold—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*. Ninefold form—*bho*. Described—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*. For that purpose, the excellent—*kha*, *cha*. The deities—*kha*, *gha*, *cha*. In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "The inferior bodily door is the gross one, fashioned by the deity."
Furthermore, the fourfold door of speech is known as the middle one. ||3||
In the *Śrīvajraḍāka* it is also said: "Just as a house is supported effortlessly by a great pillar, so too this body is supported by the skeletons alone.

Alternatively: "The *avadhūtī* is like a single pillar in the support of the entire network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*); because it is joined with this [support], it is 'single-pillared' (*ekastambha*)."
In the center of the navel is the great wheel, woven with sixteen threads and joined with the letter *A* through the yoga of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*).
"Established there in the center as the support of all, in the form of a pillar, she is celebrated as the Great Queen Sāvadhūtī.
Thus ends the enumeration beginning with "the nine gates."
He provides the explanation: "Furthermore, what is the nature of the nine streams? and so forth.
The nine streams are the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the secret organ, and that which is called the anus; that [body] in which these exist is thus described.
Furthermore, each individual gateway is proclaimed to be ninefold.
For instance, because the eye faculty is associated with earth, water, fire, air, space, consciousness, and both wholesome and unwholesome mental factors, there are nine divisions;
the same applies elsewhere as well.
And these are of the nature of the five Buddhas and four Yoginīs.
Thus, it should be understood that each door is joined with a ninefold maṇḍala-cakra.

In this way, although the body has ninety-nine doors, it arises as having eighty-one doors; and those [deities] who are the outpourings from these [doors] should also be understood as being Tathāgatas themselves. ||2||

To that end, he says: "The inferior bodily door, gross and fashioned by the deity"—this very bodily door, which is ninefold along with its adjuncts, is called *adharma* because it consists of forms appearing as reflections (*pratibhāva-pratibhāsa-rūpa*). Furthermore, it is *adharma* because it manifests externally; yet, it is not [inferior] because it is the vehicle of its own natural vibration (*sva-niṣpanda-vāhana*), but rather because of its lowness (*hīnatva*).

Therefore, [they speak of] the one who dwells in the gross deities (sthūladevanivāsinam)—[variants: *sthūladevatāni* (ja), *caturviṃśa* (ga), *cikaṃ ca pracakṣate* (gha), *lekha* (kha, ṅa, cha), *dyuktādeka* (kha, cha), *śata* (bho), *rājñāṃ* (ka), *ta eva* (kha, cha), *sthāpyam* (kha, gha, cha), *vāraṃ* (kha, gha, cha), *vāraṃ* (kha, cha), *nāsti* (gha), *cakram iti* (bho), *tivāraṃ* (kha, cha), *adharma* (kha, gha, cha), *sphū* (kha), *sphu* (gha), *vāraṃ* (kha, gha, cha), *chedaṃ* (ka, kha, gha), *apratibhāva* is absent (ka, kha, ca, cha), *bhoḥ*, third instruction: "The Āgneya, the Vāyavya, the Māhendra, and likewise the Vāruṇa."
By means of the movement of the mind, he [placed it] above, on the sides, and below. || 4 ||
Thus, in comparison with the other doors, this is "gross" and possesses form;
because it has the nature of the aforementioned nine goddesses of the Tathāgatas, it is "created by a deity.
He speaks of the door of speech as follows: "Another," and so forth, is the brief statement (*uddeśa*).
Because it exists between body and mind, the fourfold door of speech should be known as being in the middle. ||3||
He states the explanation, beginning with "belonging to Agni," and so forth.

In this body, there exist four channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) known as those of Agni, Vāyu, Mahendra, and Varuṇa, situated respectively in the throat, the navel, the secret place, and the heart. They have the forms of Padmanarteśvara, Ratnasambhava, Paramāśva, and Akṣobhya; their intrinsic natures are those of Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī, Lāmā, and Ḍākinī. They move slowly through the right, left, both, and the central [channels], and are red, green, yellow, and white in color according to the distinction of the primary qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, they are mutually numbered as the fourth [set]; by means of twenty-four entries of movement day and night, they carry two thousand one hundred and sixty breaths, and are directly perceptible to all embodied beings.
Those very channels through which the movement, activity, and coming and going of consciousness, which has the wind as its vehicle, are experienced at every moment, are the gateways of speech;
from those very openings of the left, right, and middle channels, the Blessed Lady, the Mother of Syllables, arises.
Because there is no difference between cause and effect, that [cause] is the very place of manifestation for the [result];
and as for how those [processes] such as entry and so forth belong to fire and the other elements, he says: "Upward," and so on.

Respectively, the fire-maṇḍala proceeds upwards; because the devourers of oblations (the fires) blaze upwards, the wind-maṇḍala flows through the gateway from the sides; because the wind moves in a curved path, the Māhendra [wind] flows straight and clearly, owing to its evenness.
The wind carries the water-element; thus, the downward movement of the waters has been described. And it is said: "The ray that has emerged from the south is the orb of the fire-eater (the sun);
this is clearly red in color, and Padmanātha is the deity here."
In the Āgneya, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and Vāruṇa [spheres], the letters *ña*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ḍa* are remembered; [the letters] *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa* are established [therein]. [Variants:
*vyavasthitaḥ* (ga.), *sthitāḥ* (gha.), *sthitam* (ja.).

And it gives happiness;
there is also its manifestation. Thus, [the reading] "pravekha" [is found in] manuscripts gha and cha.

In the Vasantatilakā with its commentary, the third mental door, distinguished by the moon and the sun.
Through both entry and exit, the door indeed becomes supreme. || 5 ||
The primary and supreme gateway is proclaimed to be both below and above;
through the lower gateway comes discernment, and through the upper gateway, the elements.
"Stable, with slow movement, resembling a white kunda flower or the moon—this is indeed the mandala of Varuṇa, and Vajranātha is the deity here. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the fourfold *ālī* as well—as in the *sampuṭa*: there are four movements: upward (*ūrdhva*), sideways (*pārśva*), straight (*ṛju*), and downward (*adhas*).

"In the Āgneya, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and likewise the Vāruṇa [cakras], through the movement of the mind, there is upward, lateral, and downward motion. Thus it is said. Also in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*: "In the Āgneya, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and likewise the Vāruṇa..."
By means of the movement of the mind, one effects upward, lateral, and downward motion.
Among them, the fourth yoga is their mutual deity. Thus [ends verse 4].
He states the door of the mind: it is the third, in relation to the doors of body and speech.
"Mental" means accessible by the mind alone.
How so?
Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinction between moon and sun":
the moon and sun flow through the two channels, the left and the right, by means of these two divisions.

Above, they flow according to the sequence of wind; below, according to the sequence of substance, as the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and in-breath (*apāna*), due to the carrying of semen and blood respectively.
Therefore, precisely because it is accessible through subtle yoga, it is the supreme gateway. Thus he says: "By entry and by exit.
This refers to the upward entry and exit of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and the downward entry and exit of the two substances (*dravya*).
Alternatively, "down" refers to entry, and "up" refers to exit.
This is the supreme door.
To explain by which door the activity of whom occurs, he says: "by the lower door," and so forth.

[it is] the movement of the mind of the wheel (cakracittasaṃcāra). O! [it is] the fourfold.

The third instruction: "The Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, reside moving within the upper gate.
Their establishment is below, while their emanation occurs through the upper [gate]. (7)

Through the lower door, by way of the *lalanā*, distinguished gnosis (*jñāna*) and higher cognition (*vijñāna*), known as Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), proceeds; for when the two manifestations proceed downward, there is the arising of the innate (*sahaja*) through the manifestation of the spring season.

Through the upper door called the *rasanā*, the constituents (*dhātu*)—the elements whose nature is earth and so forth, and the impurities such as the eyes—manifest, because they have the form of the cremation grounds characterized by the smell of moisture and so on.

Alternatively, through the lower door, the pentad of aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with consciousness manifests within the bodies of embodied beings, because the pentad of aggregates is inward-facing.
Through the upper gateway, the elements—the five great elements beginning with earth—are produced, because of their outward-facing nature. (5–6)

Likewise, these six groups of active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, which have the nature of the Buddhas Vairocana and the others, move and proceed through the upper opening in order to grasp the six objects such as form. The deities of those objects enter them; for those whose desire is not yet fulfilled, their abiding and entry are experienced. Once they have entered within, they are again emitted through the upper opening for the sake of the enjoyment of their own respective deities—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Alternatively, it means that one is endowed with consciousness, which is distinguished gnosis (*vijñāna-viśiṣṭajñāna*), from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).

By the power of yoga, it reaches the lotus-bud through the lower gate via the path of the *lalanā* and other channels; when drawn upward by that same [power], it becomes the nourisher of the twenty-four elements and arises in the seats (*pīṭhas*) of the four [classes of] practitioners. And it is said: "It is marked by the rays of the nine-fold full moon, shining brilliantly from the peak of its rising crest, like the beautiful, radiant, and sun-expanded [lotus] with its powerful filaments gathered into a central core."

Though the flute is skilled in the essences of various flower-liquors and sounds out in fast, slow, and medium tempos, the bee approaches during the great festival of midnight and drinks from it; that his mind is thus captivated by it is truly a marvel.
The moon rises and again goes to its setting, and from there returns once more to the crest of the mountain of sunrise;
yet, when one observes the two ends of its orbit, neither the moon nor the sun truly shines.
The sun rises within the petals of the lotus; the moon dissolves even from its mountain peak.
The fire of universal destruction ascends upward, while Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun from below.

In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, the perfectly awakened *ḍākinīs*, who are the mothers of yoga, are [described] by means of coming and going in the form of invocation and so forth. (8)
In both engagement and withdrawal, by virtue of their inherent nature as qualities and defects,
pleasure and pain are established as having the nature of co-emergence.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Differentiation of the Doors of the Tathāgata’s Activity Consisting of the Aggregates, Elements, and Bases," in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*. 3.
The third explanation: the Sahajayoginīs are established.
Alternatively, it shows the distinction that these are established as "naturally accomplished" (sahajasiddhāḥ), meaning they are established by their very nature and are not merely imagined.
How so?

Engagement and withdrawal, arising and dissolution, emergence and entry, concentration and non-concentration, virtues and faults, the auspicious and inauspicious, affliction and purification, and pleasure and pain—which consists of the nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) such as the agreeable and disagreeable—all this, occurring through the three gateways, should be known as the innate, spontaneously accomplished nature of the Hero and Yoginī. (8–6)

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the third instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 3.
The closing of the eyes, which are like lotuses upon a bed of water-lilies, comes first;
then follows the closing of this pair of thunderbolt-like lotuses, the two hands.
Instantly, through the friction of the seed-syllable of the practitioner, the triad reaches the fourth sky;
it is endowed with the series of digits of the imperishable abode, innate, and repeatedly licking as it dissolves time.

If one has attained the realization through the oral instruction of a well-trained Guru of Vajravilāsinī, then he becomes a knower of reality who reaches the definitive certainty regarding the superior, middling, and inferior [levels]. Thus [it is said]. (7)
Therefore, he says "invocation," and so forth.

By means of this distinction between the upper and lower gates, there are the sending forth (*visarjana*) and summoning (*āhvāna*) in the form of going and coming. In that manner, all the Buddhas of the three times, residing in the three wheels, are of the nature of the *dhātu*; the twenty-four heroes (*vīra*), with Śrī Heruka as the twenty-fifth; likewise, the twenty-eight Ḍākinīs residing in the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body; the Yoginīs within the indestructible central channel (*nāḍī*); and the Siddhas and Heroes who, by way of the eyes and other gates, are of the nature of the channels—these are [to be understood] through the sequence of invocation and dismissal, such as *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *kā*, *saṃgha*, *kā*, *ja*.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is *gha*; the essential form (*svarūpa*) is *ja* (according to Nāsti Ka, Kha, Gha, Ṅa, Ca, Cha, Ja, and Tilaka), while in the *Vasantatattva* it is *na*; [the syllable] of the body is not *ḍha*.

vilāyana (ka. kha. gha.);

Now, I shall demonstrate the ten stages, beginning with Pīṭha, of the body of a certain Tathāgata. 1.
The channels that carry the nine streams are situated at the nine gates; the tenth, however, is in the center of the bhaga, and it is the most excellent among them.
Beginning from the location of the forehead, the determination of the wheel of the syllable *haṃ* [is made]; thirty-two streams of bodhicitta flow there day and night. (3)

Having established the circle of deities residing in the three gates, he says "atha" and so forth in order to show their abiding according to the sequence of the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭhas*.
The meaning of "after the indication of the gates" has been stated.
"Of any one" (*anyatamasya*) means of whichever [Tathāgata body] it may be—the common [body] of all sentient beings, and not merely my own.
The connection [of the verse] is: "I shall show the locations such as the pīṭhas. || 1 ||
Regarding this, he says: "The nine streams," and so forth.

Those channels (*nāḍī*) situated within the nine streams (*srotas*), which are the previously mentioned gateways of the body, are the nine deities. Likewise, beginning from the head and ending with the *avadhūtī* located in the center of the *bhaga*, these ten are called the stages (*bhūmi*) of the ten Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

When their experience is perceived within oneself through the vision of truth (*satyadarśana*) and so forth, then what is the point of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the rest, which must be accomplished through great effort? This is the intended meaning. || 2 ||
Having described the grounds (*bhūmi*), he speaks of those situated on the grounds, beginning with "the forehead" (*lalāṭa*) and so forth.

Here, in this body, starting from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) located at the forehead, the determination—that is, the definitive ascertainment—of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) is to be known.
For indeed, that which pertains to it is set forth as the tenth [chapter] in the *Mātṛkā*.

Now I shall describe another set of ten, beginning with the *pīṭhas*: "ja" refers to the ten *pīṭhas* and so forth of a certain Tathāgata; "bho śivasya kāyasya" (of the body of Śiva) refers to the ten *pīṭhas* and so forth beginning with "ña" and "ḍha.
"Bho" [is used] for the ten beginning with the *pīṭhas*.

In manuscript ṅa, the passage beginning with *deśa yi ṭa ṭha ḍa navasrotāśayaḥ ka. kha. gha. cha*, *srotāśayā* - ga., *śayo* - ḍa., *bhagavandhe* - gha., *saṃkhye (jñe)* - ṭa., and *śreṣṭhottamā matā* - ja, and ending with *bhūcaryo 'pi tathāparāḥ*, is absent. In manuscript ja, [the text] begins from the word *sthāna*.
Huṃkāra—ña. The determination of Kārañja—kha. ña. bho. The definitive conclusion (vinirṇaya)—ghaṃ.
All—kha. ca. cha. The deity—kha. gha. ca. cha.

And those [beings] have gone to that essence; they are remembered as being situated both externally and internally in the form of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth. These eight Yoginīs, beginning with Khecarī, as well as others who are Earth-walkers (*bhūcarī*), are likewise present. (4)
And all those who dwell in the netherworlds (pātāla) are likewise situated within them, according to the distinctions of their various locations in the wheels of body, speech, and mind.

The ten stages, beginning with the *pīṭhas*, which abide as the innate (*sahaja*), are differentiated according to their respective locations and essential natures by way of twenty-four divisions. (6)

These thirty-two indeed extend from the *saṃbhoga* [cakra] and so forth, because the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra is the root of the body-tree; for this very reason, the body-tree has its branches below. Furthermore, there are twenty channels with downward-facing openings in the four limbs of the hands and feet; three on the sides and the back; six in the heart-cakra; and three chains of binding channels for the stupa of the four cakras.
Thus, the determination of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) is made precisely at the forehead and other locations. Those thirty-two yoginīs flow with as many drops of bodhicitta;
they themselves are the heroes (*vīra*), such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others, the great heroes (*mahāvīra*) such as Vajracaṇḍa and others, and Śrī Heruka, who is the Vajramaṇḍala.
To that end, he says: "The rivers," and so forth. || 3 ||

These [energies] reside in the external gateways of the body and in the locations such as Jālandhara and others—which are situated within the twenty-four *pīṭhas* starting from the head—corresponding to the internal states of foul odors and the like, as well as the fierce and terrible [sentient beings].

He explains their division with the words "the sky-farers" (*khecaryaḥ*) and so forth: the channels (*nāḍīs*) beginning from Pullīra and ending at Mālava are the sky-farers; those beginning from Kāmarūpa and ending at the Himalayas are the earth-farers (*bhūcaryaḥ*); and those beginning from Pretapurī and ending at Kulatā are the dwellers of the underworld (*pātālavāsinyaḥ*).
Due to the division between the upper, middle, and lower parts of the body, these twenty-four, beginning with the sky-farers, are established upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
In its constituent parts and in the gates, channels (nāḍīs) having the nature of the Crow-Face (Kākāsyā) and others are established. (4-43)
