These very stages, beginning with Muditā (Joy), have been fully explained; they are the abode of those who are not yet bodhisattvas, whose nature consists of the faculties and so forth. //7//
It is the support for all Buddhas, especially for the aggregates and so forth; it is the supreme bringer of Buddhahood for both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (8)
This is what it says: "Body, speech, and mind," and so forth.
The ellipsis of the sentence is that they abide by depending upon the various divisions of locations, such as the head and so on.

Therefore, these twenty-four *pīṭhas* and so forth, which are the channels (*nāḍīs*) in the form of the supported (*ādheya*), are the *ḍākinīs*; likewise, those ten channels which serve as their support and are of the nature of the ground (*bhūmi*).

"According to the nature of their respective locations" means not exceeding their proper place (*yathāsthānam*). For whichever yoginī has whichever location, her innate state (*sahaja*) abides in that very place; it is not imagined (*kalpitā*). (5–6)
"These very ten stages, beginning with Pramuditā, have been taught by me.

In that context, the head, the crown-lock (*śikhā*), the right ear, and the back constitute the *pīṭha*; it is the seat of the *bodhicitta*, and that itself is *Pramuditā*, because it generates the three types of bliss through the sequence of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth.
The left ear, the space between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the base of the arms constitute the *upapīṭha*, which is near to the *pīṭha*.

That very [ground] is Vimalā, because the stains of conceptual construction are burned away by the fire of gnosis; it is Kakṣa and Stanau, because the bodhicitta is sprinkled there under the guise of sweat and milk;
that very [ground] is Prabhākarī, because from beholding that, the light of bliss arises in the mind.
The *upakṣetra* is at the tip of the navel and nose, because it carries the *bindu* and *siṅghāṇa*;
that itself is *arciṣmatī*, because it illuminates the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*).
The mouth and throat are the *chandoha*, [symbolized by] *haḥ*, because the function of the *chanda* (meter/impulse) occurs during the enjoyment of flavors.
That very [state] is *sudurjayā* (the "very difficult to conquer"), because it is impossible to turn back from the *rasa* (flavor/essence).

The *upachandoha* (subsidiary junction) is in the heart and the *meḍhra* (genitals), because there is an aversion to that [flavor] when the meaning is understood— that is, when the "cooking" (*pāka*) of what is to be enjoyed has occurred—
and because there is a turning toward it at the limit of that [aversion], during the cooking.
The secret *guḍī* is the meeting place (*melāpaka*) of wisdom and means through their meditative union (*samāpatti*);
because of that merging and the unification of the channels (*nāḍī*), it is indeed the "Far-reaching" (*dūraṅgamā*).
Because of the distance of the channel-essence (*nāḍīsoshīya*), the meeting place is at the thighs and shanks, due to the merging of even those previously mentioned.
That very [place] is Acalā, because its union is unavoidable;
it is Śmaśāna on the back of the fingers and feet, because it is the essence of all seats (pīṭha) and because of the experience of the state beyond conceptual construction;
and that same [place] is Sādhumatī, because the "sage" (sādhu), namely selflessness (nairātmya), exists therein.
Of the Sadāśivas—ña; of those possessing form—ka, kha, ga, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, bho;
"of those who have taken form"—gha; and likewise of the Samayas—ja;
of all the Śivas—ña, ḍha; "of all the Buddhas and especially of Brahmā and the others"—ja.
Of the gods of gods—[omitted] from Śiva [to the end]. The supreme [form]—ka. kha. gha. ṅa. ṭa. ḍha. The internal division—ca.
The support when deposited—ka.
*kathitā*—kha, gha, cha; *karṇe*—ka, kha, gha; *'bhrū'* is not present—kha, gha, cha.
From the production—kha. ca. cha. The mind, [which is] all-bliss—bho; produced—kha.
Gandha-bho mokṣapāke-kha cha,
having abandoned the last of the pīṭhas-ca.
When the thirty-two bodhicittas reach fullness here, then Buddhahood becomes near for the Buddhas together with their sons. || 9 ||
Buddhahood resides in one's own body alone and nowhere else; it is held that Buddhahood exists elsewhere than in the body for those whose [vision] is obscured by ignorance. (10)

The thumbs and knees are the cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*). As before, that same [state] is the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). Because it is the support of the Dharma, the marrow of the stable [body], through the upward stream of the higher [element], rains like a cloud; or rather, it is the end of the application of rain, free from disease.
Thus are the twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*) comprised within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Those very ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are increased through the successive progression of knowledge in the order of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth.
To the question of whose these ten stages are, he says: "The *ālaya*, etc.

Those Bodhisattvas who have the nature of the six sense-faculties, such as the eye, and likewise those Buddhas previously explained who consist of the aggregates (*skandha*) of form and so forth—for them, those are the stages; they exist by their very nature within these, and thus they are called "stages" (*bhūmi*).

For this very reason, they bring about Buddhahood not only for the Noble Ones, but even for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); for those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-faculties (*indriya*) as their intrinsic nature also bring about Buddhahood, because in reality there is no difference between the Tathāgata and an ordinary being. (7–8)

Now, one might object: "Since enlightenment is attained only after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), how can the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth be fully awakened to? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The thirty-two," and so on.

When the fullness of the thirty-two states of bodhicitta is experienced either at the tip of the thunderbolt (*dambholi-mukha*) or within the lap of the lotus (*payoja-kroḍa*), then Buddhahood exists for them nearby or in close proximity;
the distinction is that it does not depend upon time. 2 || 6 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "While we exist in the human state, the Buddhas reside in Buddha-fields such as Abhirati in the form of the mandala of gnosis; how then can awakening be near? To dispel this doubt, he says "in one's own body" and so forth.
Awakening (*buddha*) is the realization of one's own nature; the state of that is Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). That resides and is established in one's very own body;
for this very reason, that itself is the Buddha-field, because the naturally accomplished, innate Buddha abides right here.
"Not elsewhere"—meaning not in delight (*abhirati*) and so forth;

therefore, Buddhahood does not exist elsewhere than in this body, nor in external places. Those who arise from nature (*prakṛti*) are "natural" (*prākṛta*). As stated in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "The sacred seat (*pīṭha*) and the secondary seat (*upapīṭha*), the field (*kṣetra*) and the secondary field (*upakṣetra*), as well as the grove (*chandoha*) and the other, the secondary grove (*upacchandoha*). (11)
Likewise, the melāpaka and the upamelāpaka, as well as the śmaśāna and upaśmaśāna—these are the ten stages beginning with the pīṭhas. || 12 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Description of the Nature of the Ten Seats and Other Stages, [Situated] within the Central Channel amidst the Nine Streams of the Tathāgata’s Body," in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*. 4.

Just as they were born, so too do they remain; however, those of developed intelligence do not hold such a view. But for those who know the realization of the *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage), Buddhahood is accepted as being established by its very nature (*svabhāvasiddha*), because of the statement: "This entire world has the five Buddhas as its essence. Furthermore, [the Buddha] remains a Tathāgata after death; thus, those who speculate on the undeclared questions (*avyākṛta*) are refuted. For there is the *Hevajra* statement: "There is not a single sentient being who is not a Buddha; rather, everyone is a perfectly awakened one. (2.4.73)
Ācārya Vajrapāṇi also stated: "Men are the forms of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣits.
Furthermore, in the *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra* it is said: "The activities of body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings are the secret of the three families.

And by Jñānapāda it was likewise declared: "Whatever actions of body, speech, and mind of such a kind exist in the mind, they are described as having the form of mudrās and mantras by all the Buddhas. (10)
He states the names of the ten bhūmis previously mentioned: "pīṭhopapīṭha," and so forth; their etymological explanations have been stated previously. || 11-12 ||

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the fourth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, the commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 4.

The Tenth Chapter: The Fifth Instruction. Now, I shall explain the distinction of the ten regions according to the differentiation of other locations, which reside within the channel situated in the center of the nine-streams of the body of a certain Tathāgata, and which consist of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), perfections (*pāramitā*), and the wheels (*cakra*) of body, speech, and mind, beginning with the primary seats (*pīṭha*). || 1 ||
The head is the land of Malaya, while the crest-lock is Jālandhara; likewise, Oḍiyāna is said to be the right ear.

Now, with the words "Then of another," and so forth, he states—in the order of brief mention (*uddeśa*) and detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*)—the names of the previously mentioned twenty-four seats (*pīṭhas*) through their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the head and other parts [of the body], as well as the nature of the channels (*nāḍīs*) situated therein as being *khecarī* and so on.
The portion from "Now" up to "I shall explain" is easy to understand. || 1 ||
He provides the explanation beginning with "The head is the Malaya region," and so forth.

In this context, "Malaya" refers to that in which the bodhicitta—whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and which is indivisible from the conventional and ultimate truths—is dissolved; thus, such a place is the Malaya region. The "head" (*śiras*) is the Malaya region because it is precisely there that [the bodhicitta] exists.
It is the root of the network of channels (*nāḍījāla*), and its support (*dhāraṇa*) is Jālandhara, the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

By the path of the left ear, the movement (*yāna*) of Caṇḍālī through the *uḍḍiyāna* known as Oḍḍiyāna occurs via the *khecarī* mode; "there" refers to the right ear. Through these two messengers, the vowels and consonants, by means of the union with the three *mudrās*, one experiences non-conceptual bliss (*avikalpa-sukhānubhava*) due to the piercing of the staff of the Lord of the Karmic Wind (*karmamāruteśvara-daṇḍabheda*). This is called *arbuda*. [The word] *pṛṣṭha* [is derived from] the back of the head; according to the rule for *pṛṣodarādi* compounds, the *h* is replaced by *ḍ*.
● *ja.* lacks "pāramitā" — *bho* 6. *bhedenabhedaṃ* — *ga*, *gha*. *oḍyāna* — *ka*, *ca*, *cha*; *oḍyāyana* — *kha*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ja*; *vaḍiyāna* — *ṭa*, *ṭha*.
10. caiva – ka. kha. ga. ṅa. ca. cha. ja. 11. dakṣiṇaṃ – gha.; karṇasu – ga. gha. 12. uddeśaṃ – ka.; taddeśa – cha.
Intrinsic nature—ka. 14. [The reading] *vaḍrākhya*—kha. gha.; *vaḍrākhye*—cha.; "going" (*yānam*) means exiting externally; that very thing by way of its function—ka.
15. *oḍriyānam*—ka.; *vuḍiyāna*—kha. gha.; *vaḍiyānam*—cha.
Arbuda: "The four regions of the back are known as the seats (pīṭhas). Likewise, Godāvarī should be understood as having the nature of the left ear. (3)
Rāmeśvara is likewise renowned as being between the eyebrows; Devīkoṭṭa is another, located at the eyes; and Mālava is at the base of the arms. ||4||
Thus, these secondary seats (upapīṭhas) are established within the wheel of the mind; they are declared to be the specific locations of the sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs). ||5||

By the logic previously stated, these four should be known as the *pīṭhas*. Furthermore, they are the spheres (*gocara*), that is, the objects, of the four channels located therein which are called *khecarīs* by names such as *Pracaṇḍā* and so forth; they have the nature of the *ādhāras* due to their similarity with the *ūṣmas* and other [elements], and are of four types through the experience of conceptual bliss. Because it is a state of joy (*muditā*) characterized by the experience of a distinguished delight, it is the earth (*bhūmi*). Thus, "Godā" refers to the *avadhūtī*, which is the *nirmāṇacakra* by nature, as it is the "best cow" (*go-vara*). It is called *godāvarī* because it is "covered" (*vriyate*) or concealed by that [channel], namely the left ear, due to its pervasion thereof.

The two *rāme*s are the eyebrows, which possess the nature of the aesthetic sentiment of love (*lalanā-rasa*) and are the locus of sovereignty for the flame of knowledge; that space between them is the "tuft of hair" (*ūrṇākoṣa*).
Here, the "fortress of the Goddess" (*devīkoṭṭa*) refers to the fortress of that very Goddess; the two eyes are situated there as their support, because they are attained [through that path].
Likewise, the "Mālava" region is located at the two roots of the arms—that is, the two shoulders—situated within the forearms.
Because of the "mowing" (lavana), that is, the cutting off (chedana) of the "garlands" (mālā), which are the heterogeneous conceptual constructions (vikalpa), they are called *mālava*.

From such experience, these secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) should be known as the spheres (*gocara*), that is, the objects of the sky-farers (*khecarī*) who reside there—namely Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā.
This is the wheel of the mind (*cittacakra*). 3–5.
Rāmeśvarī is thus proclaimed—O! Your [letters] ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa;
koṭis—ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha; the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) of Devīkoṭa—ja. But the root [text] is—ka.
In the root text, however, it is *gha*.
The seats (*pīṭhas*) are: *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*.
Their essential forms (*svarūpiṇaḥ*) are [as follows]: *ka*.
kha. gha. ca, piṇī-ṭha, śeṣacārikā - ja. 9.
tatrasthānāṃ - kha.
| 10. nāsti - kha ca
11. 'pra' is not present—ka.
12. bhrūrapī—ca.
13. śāstavambha—kha, cha; śāstavabhū—gha.
14. *vara* — kha. gha. cha; 15. *stajjñairmadhya* — kha. cha; 16. *koṭaye* — kha. cha.; *koṭayeti koṭa* — gha.
• • • • Fifth Instruction: Kāmarūpa is considered [the first]; Kakṣī is proclaimed to be [at] the two breasts; these are designated as the Field (kṣetra); the Navel is considered Triśakuni. ||6||
Kośala is said to be the tip of the nose, while Kaliṅga is declared to be the mouth; Lampāka is located in the middle of the throat.
The place known as Chandoha is the heart; Kāñcī is called my Meḍhra, and Himālaya is likewise the Upachandoha. ||8||

The two armpits and the two breasts are, respectively, *kāmarūpa*—that which possesses desirable form (*rūpa*) and appearance (*darśana*) according to one's desire—and *oḍra*. *Oḍra* refers to the two breasts because the *caṇḍālī* takes them as her own by ascending upward (*ūrdhvagamanena*). These two constitute the field (*kṣetra*) according to the previously stated principle. The navel and the tip of the nose are the two sites of the *triśakuni*. The *triśakuni* consists of three birds (*tri-śakuni*); like birds (*khaga*), the channels of body, speech, and mind have the shape of bird-beaks. Because it has the nature of a vajra-knot, the navel region is the *triśakuni*.
Likewise, because it nourishes and sustains the perfected ones (*siddha*), that "Kośala" is the tip of the nose.
These should be understood as the secondary fields (*upakṣetra*) according to the sequence previously mentioned. (6.63)

The face and throat are Kaliṅga and Lampāka. It is called *kaliṅga* because it marks (*liṅgayati*) or conveys (*gamayati*) bliss (*kaṃ*); for at the time of service, bliss arises simply from the sight of it.
Likewise, the tongue is *lampikā* because it is greedy (*lampaṭā*) for tasting the nectar of the lower lip (*lambikā*); due to that connection, the throat is *lampāka*.
By the previously mentioned explanation, these are called the *cchandohas*. The heart and the genitals are considered the *rūpa*—ka, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja; *mata*—kha.
The breasts are Oḍra—ka, kha, ga, ṅa, cha.
Below the breast are *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, and the two *ja*s; *ddiṣṭau* is *gha*; in the field indicated is *ṭa*; in the belly is *ga*, *gha*; the armpit is *ja*.
Oḍukī—ja; titāḥ—ga;
ṭa and ṭha—these two are proclaimed as kṣetra—ka, kha, gha, ṅa, ca, cha; kṣetrau—gha... that which marks with the liṅga—ka; ṭha—ja.

But the letter *ṅ* is known as the group beginning with *ka, kha, ga, gha*; *ja* [is the group] beginning with *ca*; *dhyage* is proclaimed as *ṭa, ṭha, ha* (according to *ga*); *khyātī* is *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa*.
On the lips—*bho*—in dissolution—*gha*—and *cha*; and *ya* is said to be *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa* (according to *ja*).
*vaḍyo*—*gha*; *uḍyo*—*ca*;
*vajraṃ*—*kha gha cha*, *uḍū*—*ca*; "two" (*dve*) is not present in *kha gha cha*; *samalati*—*kha gha cha*.
The face— *ka*, *kha*. Lampikā— *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *cha* is said— *ka*, *kha*.
The secondary field (upakṣetrī) of *grasta* is *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, and *ja*; [the secondary field] of *grastu* is *ṅa* at the mouth of *cha* and *ja*.

Madhyaka says: "Ga, ha"—Ja says: "The two hands are ṭa and ṭha. According to the Vasantatilakā with its commentary, all these [letters] are thus established in the wheel of speech (vākcakra) as the specific locations of the Bhūcarīs. 9.
The Pretādhivāsinī resides in the linga, while the Gṛhadevatā is in the anus; these two are declared to be the Melāpaka, and the thighs are said to be Saurāṣṭra. || 10 ||

The *kācī* is the Himālaya. For instance: that which attains (*añcati*), goes to, or flows toward bliss (*ka*)—namely, the bodhicitta, which is snow-white because it is accompanied by the tube of the maiden of Māra, which resembles a plantain flower (*kadalīpuṣpa*) in its form of hanging down with its face turned downward and dripping drops of nectar—and because it is the abode (*ālaya*) of that [bodhicitta], the male organ (*meḍhra*) is called the Himālaya.
The *upachandoha* is as before.

By the words "in this way" and so forth, these locations of the channels (*nāḍī*) situated there—namely Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmā, Devī, Subhadrā, Hathakargā, and Khagānanā—are to be known as the stations of the *bhūcarīs*.
They are called *bhūcarīs* because they reside within the body. || 76 ||
Likewise, the *liṅga* is twofold: feminine and masculine. It is the same for the anus as well;
therefore, they should be known respectively as the deities of the City of the Dead (*pretapurī*) and the House (*gṛhadevatā*).

To explain: the "city of the hungry ghosts" (*pretapurī*) is like a city belonging to the five spaces of the hungry ghosts. The pair of banners (*dhvajayugalī*) is the deity of the house—that is, of the body—and Vairocana is the deity of the house because he is its presiding architect; thus, the anus is the "house-deity" as it is the support for that [deity]. These two should be known respectively by the name *melāpaka*, due to their union at the time of *samāpatti* (meditative absorption) between the two banners and the path of excretion (*apānamārga*).
Likewise, the two thighs and the two shanks are to be understood as Saurāṣṭra and Suvarṇadvīpa.
For instance: the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) of bliss (*saukhya*), and because they manifest at distinct times, the two thighs are mutually [so designated];
likewise, the two shanks are like an island (*dvīpa*) for the mind that has the brilliant luster of gold (*suvarṇa*). This should be understood as a prior conjunction (*upamelāpaka*).
Likewise, the eight toes and the back of the foot are to be known as the "city" (*nagara*) and the "river" (*sindhu*).
Because they do not move, the toes are called "non-movers" (*naga*); hence, due to their lack of further extension, it is the city.
From the back of the foot to the big toe, because of the vibration of the *bodhicitta*, it is the river; thus, it is the back of the foot.
These two, according to the previously stated principle, are the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
The fifth instruction: the two shanks are renowned as Suvarṇadvīpa; Upamelāpaka is indeed [located] there, and the city is said to be in the fingers. (11)
Sindhu is indeed the top of the foot, and the cremation ground (śmaśāna) is declared to be [the sole];
the thumb is called Maru, and Kulūtā is said to be the knee. || 12 ||
This cremation ground (śmaśāna) is indeed the ten stages beginning with the sacred seats (pīṭha);
all these are born from one's own body and are differentiated according to the distinction of their locations. || 13 ||
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Buddhas, situated both externally and internally, exist within the wheels of body, speech, and mind through twenty-four divisions. (14)
The big toe and the knee are to be known as *maru* and *kulatā*.
Because of the roaring (*ravaṇa*) of the great bliss located in the head, it is *maru*;
because of the cutting away (*lavana*) of false conceptualizations, it is *kulatā*.
These two are called "upaśmaśāna" (near-cemetery) respectively, as previously described.
These ten stages, beginning with the *pīṭha*, are thus designated by the terms *pīṭha* and so forth. (10–123)

"Born in one's own body" (*svadehajāḥ*) means those born together with one's own body through the sequence of the ten months; they are not, however, to be attained through the sequence of the path of vision (*dṛṅmārga*).
Furthermore, these [stages] are differentiated according to their locations, as has been largely stated.
For this very reason, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are spoken of by combining the nine external gates with the one internal [gate].
To whom do those stages belong?
They belong to the Buddhas—those whose nature is solely gnosis, though appearing in the form of the aggregate of form and so forth.
Alternatively, the Buddhas are the heroes (*vīra*) who take the form of the twenty-four elements (*dhātu*).

The Buddhas and the twenty-four channels, such as Abhedya and the rest—when reduced by the rule of single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), these ten are the innate (*sahaja*) stages of the heroes and yoginīs; the sense is that they are not imagined or something to be accomplished. || 13-133 ||
To show that these are not only the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), but also those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), he says: "In the wheels of mind, speech, and body," and so forth.

According to the previously mentioned sequence, within the wheels of the mind and so on situated in the body, there are twenty-four distinct locations; the *upapīṭhas* are *ja*, *ru*, *pi*, *ṇī*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *cha*; and the *cārikās* are *jaṃ*.
And the two meeting points (melāpakau) are *ja*.

The thighs (*urū*) are said to be *ka*, *kha*, and *gha*; the knees (*ga*) are said to be [the same]. The armpits (*kakṣau*) and thighs (*ūrū*) are *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ḍa*. The face (*mukha*) is *ka* and *kha*.
The object of knowledge is Kha and Cha because of their equality— Kha and Cha are the city— Ka and Kha.

In the *Vasantatilakā* together with its commentary, the locations of all the channels (*nāḍī*) have been fully explained in their entirety.
In these locations, the ḍākinīs abide in the form of the channels (nāḍīs). || 15 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the "Instruction on the Ten Stages beginning with the Pīṭhas and the Distinctions of the Localities," in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*. 5.

Even among all embodied beings—whether they be footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—these ten stages exist in the form of channels (nāḍīs), because in reality all sentient beings possess mastery over these stages. || 14-15 ||

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the fifth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 5.
1. *nāḍi*—ka. kha. gha. ṅa. ca. cha. ja.
| And the Lord of all the *ḍākinīs* is the illustrious Herukreśvara.
3. The word "illustrious" (*śrī*) is not present in ka. kha. gha. ṅa. ca. cha. ja.
O! 4. The classification of the expansion of the stages—O! the exposition of the ten stages:
Ja. 5. By way of division: Ṭa, Ṭha, Ḍa.
6. Ninth Chapter: *Jaḥ*. 7. [This is] not present in manuscripts Kha, Gha, and Cha.
Sixth Instruction: Now, I shall indicate in brief the body of any one of the Tathāgatas. || 1 ||
The wheel of channels situated in their respective places is located in the center of one's own heart as an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
In its center is the channel, whose nature is that of a blazing fire. (2)
Resembling a plantain flower, hanging down with its face turned downward—in the center of that stands the Hero, about the size of a mustard seed. ||3||
In order to establish the identity with the mantra whose nature is established by its own-being (*svabhāva-siddha*), and to introduce the sixth instruction, he says "atha" and so forth.
"Of one or another" means belonging to the realm of all sentient beings.
"Of the Tathāgata-body" is as explained previously.
Or else, it consists of ninety deities whose nature is the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
situated in their respective places without transgressing their proper locations,
the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) itself is the assembly of Yoginīs.
"We shall indicate" means "we shall explain"; this is the general outline (uddeśa). || 1 ||
Regarding that, he describes the abiding of the presiding deity in the form of the mantra with the words "situated in the center of *hun*" and so forth.

Here, in the hearts of all embodied beings, there exists a channel-wheel (*nāḍī-cakra*) at the pericarp of the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*), endowed with filaments and eight petals, which has as its intrinsic nature the purification of the eight watches of the day.

In its center is that which is named *trivṛtā*, having the nature of an oil-fed flame, facing downwards, and resembling a plantain flower. In the middle of that, emitting drops resembling morning dew-drops falling from the mass of the sun’s rays, is the *hūṃ* syllable, the size of a minute mustard seed. Because it cannot be articulated, it is the "unstruck" (*anāhata*); because it has emerged from all conceptual constructions and fears, it is the "hero" (*vīra*). That very [syllable]... [Note: The commentary fragments provided indicate that this refers to the *ḍākinī-cakra*, the nature of the channels located in their respective places, which I am pointing out.]
4. *hṛnmadhyamataṃ*—not [in] Na; *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha bho*, *saṃgataṃ*—Ja.
5. *madhye gatā*—Gha, Na, Ḍha. 6. *pitā*—Kha.
7. mānāmadho – ka. kha. ga. ṅa. ca. cha.; mānamadho – gha.; mānā adho – ja bho. | 8. sthitaṃ vīraṃ – ja. | 9. paṃtrakam – ka kha ga gha ṅa. ca. cha. ja. |
10. "Ninety," O sir, does not exist. 11. "I am pervading," O sir. 12. "Above the vajra," O sir. (kha. gha. cha.)
13. *paterdharma*mantra—kha. cha. | 14. by name— | 15. calculated—ka. kha. |
17. Due to fearlessness—[as found in] the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "The syllable *HŪṂ* is the unstruck (*anāhata*) seed-syllable, resembling falling snow;
it is renowned as 'Spring' (*vasanta*), the delighter of the hearts of embodied beings. (4)
Vārāhī, in the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), is known as the Tilakā;
fanned by the wind of karma, she blazes within the circle of the navel.
Having attained the spring and being satisfied, she remains established in meditative absorption;
this hero Śrīruka is known as Vasantatilakā.
Because he generates joy in the hearts of all embodied beings, the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka should be known as "Vasanta" (Spring), like the season of spring;
he is not, however, four-faced and twelve-armed. (2–4)

This fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*), which resembles the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*), is awakened by the wind of action characterized by the union of the churning stick and the churning base; blazing forth from the region of the navel, it ascends through the upper path and touches that Hero situated in the heart with a torrential downpour of the stream of its nectar, which has likewise been liquefied. Precisely because of this non-dual union and absorption (*samāpatti*), it is called the *vasantatilakā*. || 5.53 ||
Therefore he says: "This Śrī," and so forth.
This *hūṃ* syllable, which has been described with the characteristics previously mentioned, is indeed Śrī Heruka.
Furthermore, the flame of gnosis (*jñānajvālā*) is called the *tilaka* of Vajravārāhī.
She herself, assuming the previously mentioned form of the Yoginī of red color, remains within the world consisting of the moving and the non-moving—that is, the animate and the inanimate.

Likewise, that very Blessed Lady, having divided herself through the three doors of inferior, middling, and superior according to the distinctions of body and so forth, performs the acts of going, coming, and staying in fifteen ways.
And it is not only she who does so; rather, the meaning is that she is established within every body.
In order to demonstrate the pervasion of the four wheels (*cakra*) by the Lord of the Maṇḍala, he says [the passage] ending with "he sports here according to his pleasure.
Therein, in the *nirmāṇacakra* at the navel, that very [Lord] is the spring season, the letter *A* in its short form.
In the heart, in the *dharmacakra*, he is the letter *Ā* in the form of a vowel, joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
In the enjoyment wheel at the throat, that very [syllable] is three-mora and protracted— thus [ends the section], marked as ṭha in the Ka and Kha recensions.

The sixth exposition: "Having assumed the form of a Yoginī, she abides within the moving and the unmoving. Through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, there is a threefold exit through the gates."
Established within all bodies, this [breath] performs the coming and going;
it is proclaimed as short (hrasva) by way of its form as the letter *na*.

Indeed, in the heart, the syllable *huṃ* is remembered as having two long morae (*dīrghamātrā*); in the throat, in the form of the syllable *oṃ*, it is called "protracted" (*pluta*) with three morae. It has the nature of the *praṇava*. Because of the curvature of the channels (*nāḍī*), it undergoes three revolutions due to the entry and exit through the *Aṇḍālī*.
In the forehead, at the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), is the syllable *haṃ*, the unstruck sound (*anāhatākṣara*), adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
That very [system] in reverse order constitutes the head, throat, heart, and navel of Śrī Heruka, whose form is the mantra.
He describes their support: those four wheels (*cakras*) which have the nature of earth and the other elements constitute his buddha-field.

The four junctions (*sandhyā*) of day and night—characterized by midday, evening, midnight, and dawn—are the channel-flows (*cakravāhinī*) numbering one hundred and fifty-four breaths; these alone are the four faces of him who has Prajñā as his consort.
These four, beginning with Vicitra, serve as the indicators of bliss.
That seed is the source of all worlds, both the moving and the stationary;
it exists through the multitude of seeds born from it, in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Therefore, the body of all embodied beings arises from that;
it is established as the form of flowing nectar, great and imperishable.

By that very [means], desire is born, which is the cause of the creation of the world. As stated in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "On the forehead and the palate, this syllable *Haṃ* is the unstruck sound (*anāhata-nāda*) and the point (*bindu*)."
In the great elements, beginning with earth, according to the fourfold division of the wheels.
Presiding over the four junctions (sandhyās), arising from the four moments (kṣaṇas),
having the nature of the four joys (ānandas), and being devoted to the four yogas through the form of supreme bliss.
Through the relationship of action and agent, he sports here at ease in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
Furthermore, the four elemental channels situated in the four directions at the four petals are established in the position of the armor of the mind.

The four moments (*kṣaṇa*), beginning with bliss (*ānanda*), and the four yogas—namely *tvaritabāṣpa*, *vibandhaka*, *viśvasita*, and *kāścat*—are those very [moments] renounced; they are his twelve arms, and likewise, when directed upward, they are the twelve eyes. They themselves, situated in the center, are the twelve weapons. Therefore, through the state of *sāmarasya* (essential identity) between the agent and the action, or between the nourisher and the one being nourished, he is Śrītilakā; Vajrasattva is the spring (*vasanta*), and his form is that. By means of that, resorting to the nature of the four joys (*caturānanda*) as he pleases, he plays; the meaning is that he delights in the bodies of all embodied beings.

Having thus revealed the central deity together with his consort—including their faces, arms, colors, postures, attributes, and inner forms—he speaks in order to present the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*), the ḍākinīs, the offerings, and the four vases, beginning with the passage "the four petals" and ending with "the five channels are established."

There, situated in the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions of the *dharmacakra*, are the four [energies] characterized by holding (*dhāraṇa*), flowing (*srāvaṇa*), sharpening (*tejana*), and impelling (*preraṇa*); these are also those of the *cittavajra*, appearing in the form of the syllable *ha* together with the *bindu*. However, it is the syllable *huṃ*, not *ḍha*. Arising from the navel, they are established during the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) and the four moments (*kṣaṇa*).

And from the forms (rūpa) comes *gha*; with form (*rūpeṇa*)—the forms, however, are the enjoyer (*bhāvaka*) by way of the nature of Space-Vajra (*khavajrasvarūpeṇa*), [bestowing] great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Having bestowed [it] upon each of the four petals, and having bestowed that upon the four known as the gates, and also upon the four petals situated there—having become the channels (*nāḍī*), he remains; the four [deities] are thus described, meaning they are described individually.

Thus, above [the head], the twelve-fold meditation on the body; one who delights in the body is a progenitor as previously described. This is the sixth instruction concerning the latter part of Śrāvaṇa: "And likewise Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī—the four channels situated in the intermediate directions are also contained therein."
Those [channels] carrying the five nectars have attained the nature of its worship;
they are renowned as the "fourfold worship," for they are indeed of that very form through meditative realization.
Thus, within the center of the heart of the body, five channels are established;
they are declared to be twenty-four within the wheels of body, speech, and mind.
Those who reside in the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) at the feet of Śrīrūka are to be understood as the Ḍākinīs and so forth—namely Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
Among them, she is called Ḍākinī because of her movement (ḍayana) in the space of the earth element;
she is called Lāmā because of her shining (lasanāt) in the space of the water element.
The transposition of letters is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

[The term] *teja* [is used for *tejas*]. That which breaks (*khaṇḍayati*) and moves (*gacchati*) is a "fragment" (*khaṇḍa*); because she ascends (*rohati*) right there through the purification of that fragment, she is *Khaṇḍarohā*.
Thus, it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).
She is called "the embodied one" (*rūpiṇī*) because she gives form to and purifies the wind and space.
Having spoken of the *Ḍākinīs* of the cardinal directions, he speaks of the offering jars situated in the intermediate directions with the words "situated in the intermediate directions.

In that very context, within the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) at the heart, those channels (*nāḍī*) located in the corners which carry the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are themselves the jars; they should be understood as the fourfold offering consisting of the essence of nectar (*sudhātmānaḥ*), situated upon a garland of skulls formed by the cavities of those elements.
He states the conclusion: "Thus, of the body," and so forth.
By the reasoning thus stated, within the body, the five channels beginning with Trivṛt, as well as the Jñānapadma and the Ḍākinīs, are to be known together with the fourfold worship;
however, they are not external or imagined, because they consist of the nature of direct experience.
The Yoginī, whose form consists of the three wheels and the channels, is Rāhukāyavākcitta;
although it should be stated as "cittavākkāya," the reverse order is for the purpose of concealing it from those who are unworthy.

And thus, within the wheel of consciousness (*cittacakra*) and so forth—which consists of the twenty-four sacred seats (*pīṭha*) beginning with the head and takes the form of the twenty-four channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with Pracaṇḍā—they are established in their respective locations, from the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and so on, down to the cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) and ending at the two knees, as naturally perfected. As it is said in the Root Tantra (*Mūlatantra*): "The Yoginīs [are] in the Root Tantra—[the Yoginīs] Tuka, Kha, Ga, Ṅa, Ca, Ja; Khaṇḍārohā [is] Tu-tu-ka, Kha, Ga, Ṅa, Ca, Cha, Ña, Hācaiva; bearing five goads (*pañcāṅkuśa*); [they are] indeed of such a form; situated in the directions; the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) carrying nectar; supreme (*parāḥ*); among those to be worshipped; 'to be worshipped' (*pūjyeṣu*); in the wheel (*cakre*) by way of twenty divisions; Viśadudā, Khāṇḍa, Kākapālāvalī, Ḍāka, Tāka. The reading taken [from the commentary] is: "In the Root Tantra, they are remembered as being born from the head" (*mūlatantre śirasijāḥ smṛtāḥ*). This portion does not exist [in the original].
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, the channels (*nāḍīs*) situated here and there according to the various divisions of the seats (*pīṭhas*) and so forth,
which have emerged from the head, are known as "head-born" (*śirasija*).
Among them, the leaders are of the nature of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
in Pullīra, the one named Pracaṇḍā is known as the bearer of nails and teeth.
In Jālandhara is Caṇḍākṣī, and likewise Keśaromā;
in the great seat (pīṭha) of Oḍiyāna, Prabhāvatī is established.
Residing at the right ear, wearing skin and filth, the flesh-eating Dākinī Mahānāsā is located in Arbuda.
Four ḍākinīs are proclaimed as the leaders of the pīṭhas; the channel which is situated in Mahoru is established in Godāvarī.
She who is renowned as Va-ramati remains in a state of firm form;
that channel which is well-known at Rāmeśvara is called Kharvarī.
Because of the statement, "They are innate and accomplished," he says of them: "The channels arising from the head are known as 'hair-born' (śirasija).
Here, thirty-two channels emerge from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), like rivers from the Himavat mountain.
The sixth exposition: "For the arrangement of the bone-garland remains established by way of its solid nature;
however, the channel at Devīkoṭa, which is soft, is considered to be Laṅkeśvarī. (23)
She who constantly carries the skull and dwells within the entire body is Drumacchāyā in Mālava; she is the Sovereign of Jinas residing in the heart.
The Ḍākinīs known as the Upapīṭhas are the mothers of the world;
they are the sky-farers (Khecarīs) situated in the Citta-cakra, established in the Pīṭhas and Upapīṭhas.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtikā* are those which effect the collection of semen (*śukra*), blood (*rakta*), and both; they are the source of the production of all the constituent elements (*dhātu*) of the body, and consist of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, having as their essence body, speech, and mind.
Among them, the names of the thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) are: Śrīhevajra, Abhedya, Sūkṣmarūpā, Divyā, Vāmā, and Vāminī.
Born of karma, real, a consecration, a fault, excrement, and a mother.
She is Śarvarī, Śītadā, and Coṣmā; Lalanā, Avadhūtī, and Rasanā;
Pravaṇā, Hṛṣṭavadanā, Sāmānyā, and Hetudāyikā; Viyogā, Premaṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī, and likewise Sumanā.
Trivṛtā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā.
Including Kātyāyanī, these are thirty-two; together with the four nāḍīs of the junctions (*sandhyā*), they are thirty-six.
Excluding the eight beginning with Trivṛttā and those beginning with Avadhūtī, the remaining twenty-four, starting with Abhedya and Pracaṇḍā, are to be understood [as the goddesses].
The channel that carries the eye, situated in Kāmarūpa, is renowned as Airāvatī; it is cultivated by the perception of forms. || 26 ||
Oḍrā is known as the bile-carrying channel Mahābhairavikā;
these two ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga, are designated as belonging to the sacred field (kṣetra). ||27||
Born from Triśakuna, Vāyuvegā is in Kośala; she is divine, a consumer of wine, and possesses lungs and a succession of entrails. 28.
Among these, the twenty-four elements such as nails and teeth should be understood as the fragments and skull-pieces and so forth.

Regarding the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the *ḍākinīs* of the channel-seats (*nāḍī-pīṭha*): she is "Indestructible" (*Abhedya*) because she brings forth the indestructible nails and teeth; she is "Subtle Formed" (*Sūkṣmarūpā*) at the crown because she carries the extremely subtle hair of the head.
She is *Divyā* because she carries the skin and impurities (*tvang-mala*) shining on the exterior;

she is *Vāmā* because she carries the full flesh in the left ear; she is *Vāmanī* because, upon its arising, she takes the form of a dwarf (*vāmana*) due to the production of the element of beings (*sattvadhātu*), or because she carries the sinews, or because she vomits what has been eaten in the left ear upon its arising.

Because it is as indestructible as the back of a tortoise, it is the "bone-garland" (*asthimālā*); because it carries [the nectar] from the karma-born [channel], it is the "karma-born" (*karmajā*); because it contemplates the *vukka* at the midpoint between the eyebrows, it is the "contemplative" (*bhāvikī*); because it sprinkles [nectar] into the two eyes, it is the "sprinkling" (*sekā*); and because it pours forth the essence of nectar from the heart, it resides in the two armpits.
These eight channels, the Khecaryas, located in the primary and secondary seats (*pīṭha-upapīṭha*), reside in the wheel of the mind (*cittacakra*) along with their means (*sopāya*).

They are called "defects" (*doṣa*) because they are corrupted by their own respective objects; that is, they undergo transformation (*vikriyate*) due to those objects. The channel carrying the visual element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is located in the two armpits, because the mind is transformed by the sight of the armpits, and because hatred arises from the thought "this is mine"—thus, "hatred" and "defect" are synonyms.
It carries what is called bile (pitta) as excrement; thus, by the Creator's impelling, it is [placed] upon the two breasts.

Above the lungs, like a mother bird, the channel (nāḍī) is situated—[the reading "sthitā" is supported by Ja.; "phusphusā" by Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Ca. Cha.; "nālaphūphūsā" by Ja.; "annalābhā" by Va.; "mālā" by Ja.; "vastravahā" by Ja.; "sūkṣmā" by Ka. Kha.; "yāt" by Kha.; "sudhī" by Kha.; "budhaṃ" by Kha. Gha.; "bhāvakikī" by Kha. Cha.; "hṛdayāt" by Ka. Kha. Gha.—this is the universal reading; however, the adopted reading is "manovikṣateḥ" by Kha. Gha. Cha.; "cittā" by Ca.; "vakṣayoḥ" by Kha. Cha.; "ūrdhva" by Ka.; "ūrdhva" by Kha. Cha.; "upakṣetrasamuddiṣṭe" by Bho. the two Ḍākinīs, the Mothers of Yoga, [Śyāmādevī] in Kaliṅga, are stationed at the sides. ||29||
Subhadrā is indeed proclaimed to reside in Udra, while in Lampāka they are celebrated as Chandoha; these two are the Ḍākinīs, the Mothers of Yoga. 30.
Hayakarṇā, residing in Kāñcī, always carries excrement; and Khagānanā, situated in the middle of Sīmānta on the Himalayas, does the same.

Upacchandoha and Vikhyāta are the two renowned Ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga; they reside in the wheel of speech, while the channels (nāḍīs) are situated as the messengers who move upon the earth. ||32||

Because she generates longing for the Mother and because she gives birth to the world, she is the *Mātarā*. Because she causes the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) to sleep within the strings of intestines at the navel, she is the *Śavarī*. Because she generates the conceptualization of night, she remains at the tip of the nose, having turned back the mechanisms of the string of qualities (*guṇavarti*) and the network of fat. She is the *Śītadā* (Cool-Giver) because she carries that [flow]; she is the *Ūṣmā* (Heat) in the mouth and belly because she conveys the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*); she is the *Pravaṇā* (Flowing) in the throat because she carries excrement; she is the *Praṇavā* through the transposition of syllables. She is the carrier of Vairocana in the heart, the *Sīmanta* (Parting of the Hair) in the center of the *varaṭaka* (the central part of the lotus), because she flows there. Due to the joy of salutation and the touch of the hands, and because of the state of blissful joy (*sānanda-nandana*) of Wisdom and Means, she is the *Meḍhra* (Penis). These eight channels—known as the Field (*kṣetra*), Sub-field (*upakṣetra*), Grove (*chandoha*), and Sub-grove (*upachandoha*)—are the *Bhūcarīs* (Earth-Walkers) within the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*). Thus they are gathered together.

The two fields (*kṣetra*) are fully described—Ja; the two secondary fields (*upakṣetra*) are Samu—Ḍha; and Ca-Ja are on the sides—Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa; Daṃtu—Ña. Ṭha; Dastu—Ḍha; situated as carriers of the binding noose—Ja; they say—Ṭa. Ḍa; Bhadrā carries the breath and the belly—Ja; and she is established—Ja; and the two well-known [channels]—Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Cha. Ña. Ṭa. Ṭha; Nyotaraḥ—Gha; also in the ear—Ka; Karṇāpi—Kha; known as Karṇeti—Ga; Karṇīti—Gha; and in the ear—Ja; located at the waist—Ḍha; situated as carrying feces and urine—Ja; in every way—Ṭa. Ṭha. Ḍa; Śrīmānta—Kha; Śrīvanta—Gha; Sīmanta—Ṭa; Maṇivahā—Ja; or also Gā—Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Ca. Cha. Ña; Kāpi—Gha; Chandaḥ—Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Ca. Cha; Dohe—Ṭha. Ḍa; Nyotaraḥ—Gha; in the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*)—Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Ca. Cha; in the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*)—Ṭa; the channels situated in the speech-wheel are the terrestrial *ḍākinīs*—Ja; in the heart—Ka. Kha. Ga. Gha. Ṅa. Ca. Cha. Ṭha; because of the fire, [the channel] Śuṣmā—Ca; Sīmānto—Kha. Gha. Cha; the center of the pustule—Bho; in the middle—Ca. Cha; the skin—Kha. Gha; and that skin—Cha. Ca. Cha; in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "She who dwells in the abode of the dead (*pretādhivāsinī*), who is of phlegmatic nature, the swift-moving wheel (*cakraveginī*), she constantly carries pus, residing in the household deity. (33)
The supreme sovereign Ḍākinī is renowned as Khaṇḍarohā; indeed, these two Ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga, are famous as the *melāpaka*. 34.
The channel known as Lohitā, located in Saurāṣṭra, is considered to be the Ḍākinī Śauṇḍinī; it carries non-sweat and is situated in Suvarṇadvīpa. (35)

Because it carries the *śleṣman* (phlegm) which maintains the equilibrium of the elements (*dhātusāmya*), it is common [to all]; because it generally causes the loss of flesh through the consumption of meat in the secret place, or because it generates conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in the anus due to the flow of blood, it is called *vasantapuṣpā* ("Spring Flower"); because it produces passion (*prema*) by means of passion in the thighs, it is called *premāṇī*; because it produces perspiration during meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) in both [thighs], it is established everywhere; because it flows as such, it is established in the shanks; because it produces the signs of accomplishment (*siddhanimitta*) or because it is unchanging toward them, it is the cause of bodily nourishment; because it carries fat (*medas*), it is the "Cause-Giver" (*hetudāyikā*); because it causes the face to burn with tears or grief in the toes of the feet, it is *pāvakī*; because it generates mental joy (*saumanasya*) for yogins through spittle on the soles of the feet, it is *sumanā*; and because it carries phlegm (*siṅghāṇaka*) on the soles of the feet up to the knees, it is *kātyāyanī*. These are the eight channels (*nāḍī*) known as the *melāpaka*, *upamelāpaka*, *śmaśāna*, and *upaśmaśāna*, residing in the underworld (*pātālavāsinī*) within the body wheel (*kāyacakra*). Having moved far away from the explanation of the channels of the pledge wheel (*samayacakra*), he says: "In the previous one, the verbal [gate]" (6.40). This means that prior to the verbal gate is the body gate (*kāyadvāra*). In that [gate], the eight channels beginning with the eyes—located in the right [eyes, ears, and nostrils] and the left [eyes, ears, and nostrils], as well as in the mouth and anus—are to be understood as being situated in the pledge wheel (*samayacakra*), well-known by those very names.

Because of the performance of the ritual characterized by the enjoyment of sense objects, this is the etymology of the *nāḍīs*. The etymology of the *pīṭhas* has been stated previously; now the etymology of the *ḍākinīs* is being stated here. It has been established many times that all *ḍākinīs* indeed originate from the family (*kula*) of Vārāhī; they are defined precisely through their non-difference from her. In this regard: she whose ferocity (*caṇḍatva*) is completely pacified is *Pracaṇḍā*; that is to say, having attained the abode of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). She is *Caṇḍākṣī* because she possesses two fierce (*caṇḍa*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), or burning (*dāha*) channels (*nāḍī*) other than the left. Because she illuminates both [channels] by means of the middle one, she is the carrier of the self in the form of fire-color (*agnivarṇa-ātmavāhinī*). *Ja*: she who is moistened (*klinna*). *Ña*: she who is eternal (*nitya*). *Ṭa*: she who is the deity in the secret place (*guhya*). *Ḍha*: *Khaṇḍeśvarī*. *Bho*: in the *pakesu* [reading *ke su* in Ña, *kaṃ tu* in Ṭa, Ṭha, Ḍa; *kinī* in Ṅa]. *Ka*, *Kha*, *Ga*, *Gha*, *Ṅa*, *Ca*, *Cha*: she is renowned (*khyātā*). *Ja*: she carries beneficial flowers (*hitapuṣpavahā*). *Bho*: she is overcome by redness (*lohitākrāntā*). *Ja*: she carries sweat and tears (*svedabāṣpavahā*). *Jaṃ*: gold (*svarṇa*). *Ja*, *Ṭa*, *Ṭha*, *Ḍa*, *Ḍha*: she is highly esteemed (*saṃmatā*). *Kha*, *Gha*, *Cha*: by means of love (*premaṇā*). *Kha*: those very [things] are fat (*medaṃ*). *Ka*: because of calculation (*kalanāt*). *Ka*: eight (*aṣṭau*). *Kha*, *Gha*, *Cha*: in the waters (*vārike*). *Ka*: in the ears (*śrotra*). *Ka*: these are called [the *nāḍīs*]. "She who is agitated (*samākulā*), whose limbs are brilliantly radiant (*sudīptāṅgī*), is considered to be *Cakravarmiṇī*."
These two ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga, are declared to be present at the assembly (*melāpaka*). ||36||
But there stands the river named Suvīrā, which carries fat and marrow; she is known as the mighty Sindhu, and there is also the Śokā, who carries tears. || 37 ||
When these two, the Ḍākinīs and the Yogamātṛs, are stationed in the cremation ground, she who carries a shield is Śuṣkāmarī, while Marī is the Cakravartinī.
Because she is endowed with radiance, she is *Prabhāvatī*;
because her nose is great in its secret, heart, and mouth, she is *Mahānāsā*; and she is like the *Pīṭha* and *Ḍākinīs* in being true to their names.

She whose nature is that of a hero (vīra) is Vīramatī; according to the statement, "The Hero resides in the center of the navel. She is Kharvarī because she is harsh (khara) due to the burning of the three wheels, yet she is excellent (varā) because of their subsequent nourishment.
Laṅkā is the city of the body; within it, she is the sovereign mistress, the Laṅkeśvarī.
Like the cool shade of a tree that provides refreshment, she is "Drumacchāyā" (Tree-Shade).
Thus, these names of the Ḍākinīs of the Upapīṭhas are etymologically significant.
Thus are the sky-farers (*khecarī*) of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*):
Airāvatī, who flows with speed like the elephant Airāvata;
and Mahābhairavā, [so called] because she pierces the knot of the third *ūlo*.
Vāyuvegā is she whose speed and velocity are like that of the wind, moving below, above, and in the ten directions.

Surābhakṣī is she who consumes *surā* (wine) and *sudhā* (nectar) even within the two *olīs*; thus, the *kṣetra*, *upakṣetra*, and *ḍākinīs* of the *jñāna-olī* are given names according to their literal meaning (*sānvarthāḥ*).
She is dark-complexioned (*śyāmā*) because she arises before dawn, and she is a goddess (*devī*) because she sports in all the cakras; thus she is Śyāmādevī.
She is Subhadrā because her satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) is beautiful (*śobhana*), auspicious (*bhadra*), and beneficial (*kalyāṇa*).
She is Hayakarṇā because she emerges through the right ear like a horse.

In the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), however, there are the external *ḍākinīs* who dwell in the underworld; and at the eastern gate of speech (*vācika*), there are four kinds of *ḍākinīs*. ||40||
Because their faces have the form of birds, they are called "Bird-faced" (*khagānanā*); thus, the names of the *pacchando*, *ho*, and *pacchando-ha-ḍākinīs* are etymologically significant.
In the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), they are the "Earth-walkers" (*bhūcaryas*).
Because her speed of going and coming is like that of a wheel upon wheels, she is Cakravegā;
because she first shatters the Tathāgatalocanā and others, and then mounts them again and generates them, she is Khaṇḍarohā;
and because she possesses the intoxicant of wine, she is Śauṇḍinī.
Her armor and equipment are the wheels themselves; thus she is "Cakravarmiṇī" (She whose Armor is the Wheel).
The Ḍākinīs of the Melāpakas and Upamelāpakas have names that correspond to their actual nature.
She is "Suvīrā" because she perfectly originates from the syllable *Vīrā*.
She who possesses great strength in going and coming is Mahābalā;
she whose nature it is to move within wheels is Cakravartinī;
and she whose valor is great in exertion is Mahāvīryā.
Thus, the etymologies of the *ḍākinīs* of the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) and secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) have been given.
Now, the etymology of the *vīra* is stated:
because he "seizes" (*kalayati*)—that is, impels—the *bodhicitta* located in the head (*khaṇḍa*), which is situated in the skull, by means of his nails and teeth, he is called *Khaṇḍakapālī*.
He is Mahākaṅkāla because he drives away (kālayati) the great (mahān) "Ka" (the head), which is situated at the crest (śikhāsthitam) and consists of the hair and body-hair;
he is Kaṅkāla because, having reached the root of the ear, he impels the impurity of the skin;
and he is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭra because his back possesses a formidable (vikaṭā) fang made of flesh.
The etymology of *pīṭhavīra* is as follows:
*surāvairī* (the enemy of the gods) is the initiator from the left ear;
residing between the eyebrows, because he initiates the garland of immeasurable bones (*asthimālā*), he is Amitābha, being identical with that.

Vajraprabha is so called because his radiance is like that of a diamond-jewel, and because he abides in the eyes as the initiator of speech (*vukka*). Vajradeha is so called because his body is firm like a diamond, and because he initiates the heart from the base of the arms.
This is the etymological explanation of the *upapīṭha*.

He is Aṅkurika because he generates the "eye-sprout" from his two armpits;
he is Vajrajaṭila because he generates the bile element in the form of a mass of vajras from his two breasts;
and he is Mahāvīra because he initiates the lungs, which cause fear even to great vajras, from his navel.

Because he carries phlegm (*śleṣman*) capable of sustaining the secret body, he is Mahābala;
because he causes yellow-colored pus to flow from the secret place, he is Ratnavajra.
Hayagrīva is so called because he causes blood to flow from the thighs of the powerful one;
Ākāśagarbha is so called because he causes sweat to flow through the pores of the skin and the hollows of the hair-follicles from the shanks—
this is the etymological explanation of the heroes of the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka*.
He is Śrī Heruka because he causes the fat (*medas*) in the form of the indestructible *hūṃ* syllable to flow from the toes;
he is Padmanarteśvara because he causes the bodhicitta in the form of seminal fluid (*āśrava*) belonging to Padmanarteśvara to flow from the tops of the feet;
and he is Vairocana because he causes the white-colored phlegm (*kheṭa*) to flow from the two thumbs.
Because he causes the flow of *siṅghāṇa* (nasal mucus), which is as white as the moon, from the two knees, he is Vajrasattva;
this is the etymological definition of the heroes (*vīra*) of the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) and secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*).

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Arrangement of the Thirty-seven Channel-Wheels within the Body of the Tathāgata," in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*. It should be understood that there are seventy-two [channels] belonging to these yoginīs—who flow through the left and right [nostrils], who were previously identified along with the Ḍākinīs, who reside in the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and who possess their respective names—due to their authority over dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*).

This is the meaning: beginning with the passage, "In the wheel of body, speech, and mind, twenty-four [perfections] are proclaimed," and ending with, "those whose nature is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are established within one's own body," these points have been demonstrated by the intervening text; the application of these terms is easy to understand. Thus ends the detailed explanation in the sixth instruction of the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, the manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).

The channel-wheel of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the *anusmṛtyupasthāna* of body, which is Ḍākinī;
the *anusmṛtyupasthāna* of feeling is Lāmā;

The application of mindfulness to the mind is material. ||2||

Now, with the words beginning with "atha," he states the seventh instruction in order to demonstrate that the yoginīs in the form of the channels (*nāḍī*) have the nature of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*): "of one or another," and so forth, as before. (1)

It is now demonstrated that these channels (*nāḍīs*), which exist by nature as the *ḍākinīs* and others at the bodily gateways such as the heart and the head, also possess the nature of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). This is established by the passage beginning with "The *ḍākinī* is the application of mindfulness to the body" (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*).

Here, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must train accordingly in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, which are subsumed within the five paths.
In that regard, what are the five paths?
The path of accumulation, the path of preparation, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
Among these, what is the path of accumulation?
It consists of twelve factors.
Which twelve?
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power.
In that regard, what is the path of preparation?
There are ten dharmas. Which ten?
The five faculties and the five powers.
In that regard, what is the path of seeing? It consists of seven factors.
What are the seven?
The seven factors of enlightenment. In that regard, what is the path of cultivation?
The factors of the path.
How many factors of the path are there?
The noble eightfold path.
What is the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣamārga)?
The final moment of the final [type of] knowledge of the path.
For what purpose are these factors conducive to enlightenment?
Or from where do these phenomena arise?
What is awakening? He says: Awakening is that by which one realizes the true nature of all things as the self-nature [of the Self]. Is it limited or is it all-pervasive?
He said: "It should be seen in the *Pariśiṣṭa*.

Now, in place of the prose passage beginning with "atha anyatamasya," the reading in the Ja manuscript is as follows: "Henceforth I shall proclaim the thirty-seven-fold Dharma; the great Dharma of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), which bestows the fruit of all desires."
And it is of the nature of form. It is both pervasive and limited.

For instance, the enlightenment characterized by the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas, which is limited because they accept phenomena as having substantial existence (*dravyatva*).

Being liberated in such a manner, they would fall into the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas; that enlightenment is called "limited" because it prioritizes only one's own self-interest and is therefore not pure.

However, enlightenment characterized by the selflessness of both [person and phenomena], namely *samyaksaṃbodhi*, is "pervasive" because of its all-encompassing nature, as it abides as the true reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena. In the realization of that [enlightenment], the "factors" (*raṅga*) are the means, which are the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The limbs (*aṅga*), the means (*upāya*), the wings (*pakṣya*), and the causes of manifestation (*abhivyaktikaraṇa*) are synonyms. And why are they called "dharmas"?

They are called *dharmas* because they are cherished (*priyante*) by Bodhisattvas established on the path and are fixed within their minds; they are comprised within the side of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*), because the path-constituting being is exclusively wholesome due to its being untainted (*anāśrava*).
However, their status as wholesome yet with-outflows (kuśala-sāsrava) depends on the practitioner due to the distinctions among the paths.
It should be understood that these five paths are subsumed under two categories.
Under which two?
By means of the mundane path and by means of the supramundane path.
Among these, how many factors are there in the mundane path?
There are twenty-two factors.
Which ones?
Those known as the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and the faculties and powers.
Among these, how many factors are there in the supramundane path?
Fifteen. Which ones?
The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.
In that regard, what are the four foundations of mindfulness?
It is said: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

Therein, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is as follows: here, this entire body—in its entirety, whether belonging to one's own or another's continuum, and extending throughout the three realms.

When this [body] is investigated, it is first of all not one, because the whole (*avayavin*) is unestablished; and its non-establishment is due to the observation of defects such as being cooked or uncooked, colored or colorless. Since multiplicity is impossible if unity is unestablished, and since [the body] is divisible into atoms, the aggregation of atoms is untenable; or, if that were accepted, the entire universe would result in being nothing but atoms. Therefore, because it is devoid of both [unity and multiplicity], this body is empty. The application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the stabilization of the mind in proximity to that mindfulness which [perceives] "this body is empty."

In this way, feeling (*vedanā*) as well—consisting of the six groups of consciousness because it is dependent upon them—is eighteenfold due to the distinctions of pleasure and so forth, as well as the past and so on; yet, because that [feeling] too is non-existent due to the distinctions of the past and so forth among pleasure and the rest, it is empty. Thus, the establishment of mindfulness within one's own mind is the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*). Likewise, since the existence of the mind prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with the object of knowledge is not established, the mind is empty. That which is the establishment of mindfulness [regarding this] is the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*).

Thus, because phenomena—distinguished by categories such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are empty as previously stated, that application of mindfulness which is the presence of recollection is the *dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*, the path of the Bodhisattva; for it consists of the fivefold aggregate (*pañcātmaka-dhātuka*).
Regarding this, the seventh instruction is: "The generation of the power of aspiration is *Pracaṇḍā*."
Caṇḍākṣī is the arising of the power of vigor; Prabhāvatī is the arising of the power of investigation; Mahānāsā is the arising of the power of mind. (3)

Through the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the correct awakening regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); through the two middle ones, regarding feeling and consciousness; and through the last one, regarding perception and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). This is because of the commonality of the term "dharma" with the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

However, in the Śrāvaka view, the distinction is that the four applications of mindfulness have the characteristics of impermanence, impurity, suffering, and non-self, serving as the antidotes to the four perversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self.
In the Mantra view, however, the Ḍākinīs, whose nature is self-awareness, should be known as the *dharmatā* of the body and so forth.
To that end, he says: "The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī," and so forth. (2)
Regarding the question "How many bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are there?", he says, stepping aside slightly: "There are four bases of psychic power:
the basis of psychic power of desire (chanda), the basis of psychic power of energy (vīrya), the basis of psychic power of investigation (mīmāṃsā), and the basis of psychic power of mind (citta).
Among these, what is the basis of psychic power of desire?
The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration through desire;
the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration through energy;
the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration through investigation.
The basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is concentration of mind accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment.
The meaning of these sūtras is as follows: here, there are six defects for every kind of concentration. Namely: "laziness, loss of the object, lethargy, excitement, and lack of effort."
By combining these two types of laxity, there are five faults.
For the purpose of abandoning them, there are eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
What are the eight?
"Faith, aspiration, vigor, and pliancy as the fourth;
mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity as the eighth.
In this context, the antidote to laziness is the engagement in wholesome action through faith.
Through zeal, their intention is accompanied by aspiration;
through vigor, the abandonment of laziness;
and through pliancy, the realization of abandonment.

This very desire is called the basis of psychic power (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*). Through mindfulness, one abandons the loss of the object of focus; through clear comprehension, one abandons lethargy and excitement.
These two are the bases of psychic power consisting of energy and investigation.
When the abandonment [of the hindrances] depends upon volition and equanimity as the exertions [respectively], that is called the base of psychic power consisting of mind.
For this very reason, these are said to be the four energies.
Therefore, it is said in the *Samādhirājasūtra*: "And because of being possessed of non-existence" (na ca bhūtvā-mayatvāt). [Variant readings: *gṛhītaḥ* (ka. kha. gha.
cha.), *samanvāgata* (ka. kha. gha. cha.), *mayatvāt* (ca.)].
And laziness (kausīdya). [The variants read] *cha* and *ga*, *gha*, *cha*.
The support (*ālambana*) is the thorough application (*sampradhāraṇa*). [The variants read] *ga*, *gha*, *cha*.
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "The faculty of faith is Vīramatī;
the faculty of energy is Kharvarī;
the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī."
The faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā;
the faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī. (4)

Based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and transformed by relinquishment; through dissociation from conditioned things, one is endowed with the abandonment of substantiality and manifestation—this is the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting of five factors.
When condensed, the four bases of psychic power comprise twenty types.
Thus it is said.
What is called *ṛddhi*?
It is "success" (*ṛddhi*), because the root *ṛdh* is listed in the *Dhātupārāyaṇa* with the meaning "to increase.

Consequently, since all the qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)—attain increase (*vṛddhi*) therein, that [increase] is perfect enlightenment (*saddhiḥ samyaksaṃbodhiḥ*). The bases (*pāda*) of this [enlightenment], being the causes for its attainment like feet, are thus the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Although the means (*upāya*) of the path is common [to all], these alone possess a double number of feet, because they represent the excellence of the antidote to the defects of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Having this as their nature, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā are the *ḍākinīs* of the seat (*pīṭha*) in the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*). ||3||
In that regard, how many faculties are there? Five.
Which five?
[The five faculties are] faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Among these, on the path of preparation (prayogamārga), there are four factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya): the stages of heat (ūṣmagata), the summits (mūrdhagata), receptivity (kṣāntigata), and the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
Therein, as the bodhisattva brings forth the untainted concentrations (anāsravasamādhi), "heat" (ūṣma) arises like a precursor sign from fire.
That which has arisen from the fire of knowledge of the mind is called "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*);

that same [state], when it has reached its culmination and is accompanied by resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), is the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*); and when that very mind endures through identity with that [object], it is "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
That which emerges immediately after that very patience (*kṣānti*) is the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). By way of metaphorical designation, this is the associated state (*saṃprayoga*).
In that regard, for the sake of the first two factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), faith and the others are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Among them, faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction of the mind regarding the future supramundane path, or regarding the Three Jewels and so forth; that is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) encourages one to exert effort toward those qualities (*dharmas*) brought forth by the faculty of faith;
and that [energy] is of four kinds: the energy of undertaking, the energy of non-retrogression, the energy of investigation, and the energy of practice.
The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is that by which the qualities brought forth by the faculty of energy are repeatedly brought to mind and not forgotten.

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is that which, by means of the mind, establishes those phenomena brought forth by the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) within the mind, having set aside all other internal essences.

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is that which investigates those phenomena brought forth by the faculty of concentration through the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*). Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṅa, Ca, Cha.
In the Smṛti— ka, kha, ga.

one whose faculties are clear through conviction—kha.
And the preparatory purification (parikarma) in the recitation consists of the transposition of the sequence— gha, cha,
and dharma— and by means of this.
Vimāraka, vihāra-ca. Chapter Seven: 55. "The Power of Faith is Mahābhairavī."
Vīryabalā is Vāyuvegā; Smṛtibala is Surābhakṣī;
Samādhibalā is Śyāmādevī.
Subhadrā possesses the power of wisdom. || 5 ||
Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor;
Cakravegā is the factor of awakening that is joy.
Praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga was Khaṇḍarohā; Dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga was Śauṇḍinī;
Smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga was Cakravarmiṇī.
The factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is well-established. 6.

Now, why is it called an "indriya"? It is an indriya because of its power (*prabhava*) over wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*). With the exception of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which produces joy regarding the affliction and purification of the five aggregates, the four ḍākinīs—Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā—are to be known as the purities of faith, vigor, mindfulness, and meditative concentration. ||4||

In that regard, how many powers (*bala*) are there? Five. Which ones? They are precisely those previously mentioned: faith and the rest. What is the distinction between the faculties (*indriya*) and the powers? It is said: when faith and the others are turned away from their opposites, they receive the designation of "faculties"; however, when they cannot be turned back by their adversaries—namely, lack of faith, sloth-and-torpor, forgetfulness, distraction, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), which is a synonym for faulty wisdom—they become the "five powers. This is the distinction.

By means of the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) previously mentioned, Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, Subhadrā, and Viśuddhā are to be known as purified within the wheel of speech (vākcakra). || 5 ||
In that regard, how many factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are there? Seven.

Which seven? They are: the factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), the factor of enlightenment of vigor (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga), the factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga), the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga).
These are the factors of enlightenment on the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
Enlightenment is unobstructed knowledge;
that by which the vision of truth is concentrated in the mind is the factor of enlightenment called concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
that by which there is enthusiasm for that very [vision] is vigor (*vīrya*), the factor of enlightenment.
That by which one makes the mind free from doubt regarding that very [object] is the factor of awakening called joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Through that very joy, because of the pliancy (*karmanya*) of body, speech, and mind, and through the abandonment of the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it becomes exceedingly cool; this is the factor of awakening called tranquility (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The thorough knowledge of the true nature of reality is the factor of awakening called the investigation of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Pure power—ka.
