In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: Right View is Mahābalā,
Right Resolve is Cakravartinī, and Right Speech is Mahāvīryā.
Right action is Kākāsyā, right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā,
and right effort is Śvānāsyā.
Right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā;
right concentration is the Blessed One, Śrī Heruka. ||7||
Among these, even equanimity (*upekṣā*) is a factor of awakening (*saṃbodhyaṅga*);
from among them, concentration (*samādhi*) and vigor (*vīrya*) are to be known as having the nature of the factors of awakening. [These correspond respectively] to Hayakarṇā and Khaḍgānanā;
such is the purification of the heroic goddesses of speech (*vākcakravīrā*).
Through the five remaining [perfections], beginning with joy, Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, and Suvīrā are purified. ||6||
And what is that Noble Eightfold Path?
Which eight? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Among these, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the wisdom that realizes the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is right view, as is the view of the existence of the next world.
Furthermore, right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is that which, though based on what has been seen and attained, takes selflessness (*nairātmya*) as its object;
right speech (*samyagvāk*) is the teaching to sentient beings that illuminates the meaning of what one has seen for oneself;
right action (*samyakkarmānta*) is exclusively wholesome physical activity, or the intimidating of others through [supernatural powers] such as *ṛddhi* for the sake of disciplining them.
Seeking robes and other requisites solely for the purpose of sustaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
The application of one’s own mind, body, and speech to their respective activities throughout all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) is right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*).
And it is said: "In whatever way the Son of the Victor proceeds within the various spheres of direct perception during his course..."
In whatever way it is appropriate for the sake of establishing beings in a state of equality through skillful means, he applies himself to that toward sentient beings. Thus,
on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the object of focus,
and the one-pointed mind that is immovable is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).

The interval that appears after the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantapratibhāsā bhūmi*) is where the three initial Great Powerful Ones (*mahābalā*), who possess great heroism (*mahāvīryā*), are purified;
this is the purification of the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*),
which is right action (*samyakkarmānta*) and Kākāsyā.
Right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā;
right mindfulness is Sūkarāsyā;
and the production of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī.
The protection of wholesome states that have arisen is Yamadūtī;
the abandonment of unwholesome states that have arisen is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī; and the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen is Yamamathanī. ||8||

Thus, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, being pure, reside within the body; all the channels situated within the body abide by assuming the colors, arms, and postures of the deities. || 9 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the exposition known as the Purity of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment and the Channels, in the *Śrī Vasantatilakā*. Thus is the purity of the female gatekeepers, the Perfect Samādhi, the Blessed Lord Śrī Herukavajra;
[this is] the purity of the pericarp of the wisdom-lotus. 7.
Yamadāḍhī is that which brings about the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas;
Yamadūtī is the protector of arisen wholesome dharmas.

The goddess Yamadaṃṣṭrī, who causes the abandonment of arisen unwholesome dharmas, and Yamamathanī, who prevents the arising of unarisen unwholesome dharmas—this is the purification of the corner goddesses of the Samaya-maṇḍala. || 8 ||
These thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, when categorized by their distinctions, consist in substance of ten items; they are subsumed within the five faculties and the five powers,
while the foundations of mindfulness are included within the power of mindfulness or the power of wisdom.
The bases of psychic power [are included] in the power of wisdom or in vigor;
the right efforts are in vigor;
the power of concentration is in the factor of enlightenment called concentration.
The power of energy is in the factor of enlightenment of investigation;
the power of wisdom is in the factor of enlightenment of investigation;
the power of mindfulness is in the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.

The power of faith is included in the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary within the factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). As for the inclusion of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) within the eightfold path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), it is as follows: right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) are subsumed under the factors of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The factor of enlightenment that is energy is [associated with] right effort;

the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena is [associated with] right view; and right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three constitute the practice of pure ethical discipline.

Likewise, right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—by including the factor of enlightenment of tranquility and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity among these five factors of enlightenment, there are ten items;
and these are subsumed within the threefold powers of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

In this context, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the three aspects of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), which is the practice of pure morality; right effort is the fruit of that practice of pure morality; right view, right intention, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) constitute the fourfold aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*); and right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration (*samādhis-kandha*).
Thus, both ethical discipline and concentration are subsumed within wisdom, according to the principle that "wisdom alone is the awakening to phenomena."
In this way, it should be understood that the thirty-seven [channels] are subsumed by ten, the ten by three, and the three by one.

This is what is meant: here, the thirty-seven channels—which were previously described as having the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the form of Ḍākinīs—extending from the head down to the knees, are comprised within ten channels: four ending at the navel-cakra, eight in the group of eight doors, and one in the center in the form of the *avadhūtī*, which rests upon the bodily door.
Those ten are further subsumed within the three channels beginning with Lalanā, and those three are, in turn, subsumed within the central channel.

Thus, having its very nature as Vajravārāhī, [the central channel] avadhūtī is such that this entire collection of channels, having manifested, converges back into that very place. By this, the dual nature of the conventional and the ultimate is revealed,
and that itself is the accumulation of the path of union (yuganaddha).
As it has been said: "Just as many clouds, possessing various shapes and colors, arise from the expanse of the sky and indeed return to dissolution therein."
In the same way, all primordial natures (*prakṛtis*), having their cause in the three appearances, enter the entire luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) after having experienced all objects.

Thus, because of such statements as "form itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is form," and because of the statement, "What talk can there be of ultimate reality apart from conventional reality? [it follows that they do so].

By this, both those who belong to other schools and our own fellow Buddhists, such as the proponents of formless representation-only (*nirākāra-vijñaptivāda*), are refuted, because they are characterized by dogmatic attachment to a distinction between the conventional and the ultimate. Enough of this digression; let us return to the subject at hand.
Thus, these [deities] in the form of channels (nāḍī) exist within the internal self;

externally, however, they are established in the maṇḍala-cakra according to the specific dispositions of sentient beings, residing in the sacred seats (pīṭha) such as Pullīramalaya and so forth. Having been described as the seventh [chapter], they sport, delight, and investigate while bestowing grace in the form of field-born (kṣetraja) [beings].
Likewise, within the internal self as well, their mouths and other features are present.

All the egg-like structures (nāṇḍyaḥ), having emerged from the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), manifest their faces at the extremities of the vajra and lotus; their sprouts are individually manifold, and the arms possess colors due to the coloring of the elements (dhātu). For instance, the nails and teeth are white, while the hair of the head and body is black.
The skin-secretion is blackish-red,
the flesh is red in color, and the sinews are white.
The garland of bones is white, the palate is black,
and the heart is white and red.
The eyes are white;
the bile is yellow; and the lungs are red.
The intestines are white and without quality;
the belly is dark, and the feces are yellow.
The hair-parting is red and white;
phlegm is white;
and pus is pale like the moon.
Blood is indeed red;
sweat has the color of fire; fat is white.
The tear is white like a pearl, the snot is blackish-white,
and the nasal mucus is yellow or white; such is the distinction of colors.
Their configuration exists in the form of *ālīḍha* and other postures through the movement of the left and right in a curved manner; their weapons are established by their very nature.

Through the purification of the sword (*kartī*) and skull-cup (*kapāla*), their innate (*sahaja*) nature, which pierces the impurity of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-mala*), is to be understood here.
Regarding this, there are verses: "Those whose essence is consciousness attained through the severance of the impurity of conceptual construction..."
They are established in innate bliss, free from the duality of the grasped and the grasper.
The ten known as the Ḍākinīs and others, who bestow the fruit of Buddhahood upon the world by mere touch, are the conceptualizations residing within the wheel.
O Great Hero, whose nature is the Element (dhātu), you who abide forever in this world with an indivisible and other such natures, together with the twenty-four [deities].
If the channels and heroes are situated within one's own body, then how is it that deluded people wander through the sacred seats of Pullīra and so forth with detachment?
Having completely renounced all external things as well as the darkness of mental constructs, liberation is attained by the yogi who is disciplined in internal yoga.

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the seventh instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).

• | • • The Eighth Exposition: Now, I shall fully explain the ritual procedures for the mandala, fire-offering (homa), yoga, recitation (japa), meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), and so forth, pertaining to the body of a certain Tathāgata, in both their external and internal forms.

It is perfectly established by the deities, Heruka and the rest, who possess the characteristics of the thirty-seven factors conducive to great enlightenment and exist in the form of the channels (nāḍī).
The body is a delightful mandala with four gates as previously described,
standing supported by eight pillars that are its own constituent limbs.
Now, in order to reveal that the external mandala, yoga, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, are actually established within the internal self, he says "Then, of another... and so on;
this is easy to understand because it has been explained previously.
In that context, the body itself is presented as the mandala.
The connection is with the phrase "the orb of the body."
Of what kind?
"Thirty-seven," and so forth;

he speaks of the purity of the supported maṇḍala, stating that those channels which are established through the purity of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) exist in the very form of the ḍākinīs and others residing within the wisdom, mind, speech, and body samaya-wheels.
For what reason?

Because here, the *ḍākinīs* are said to have a nature that is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), objectless (*nirālamba*), and unobstructed (*nirāvaraṇa*). According to the statement: "The syllable *ḍe* (or *ḍai*) signifies the Buddha-element (*buddhadhātu*) in the sky of space; those who move through all of space and have attained accomplishment (*siddha*) are called *ḍākinīs*."

And because the channels move within the great sky of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*), they alone are called *ḍākinīs*, since through contact with them, the non-conceptual reality (*avikalpatattva*) arises for both.
Having explained that which is to be contained (*ādheya*), he describes the mandala as the support (*ādhāra*) with the words "the body is the mandala," and so forth.
In this context, the body itself is the mandala because it is the locus for the yoginīs and vīras, who consist of the forms of the channels (*nāḍī*) and elements (*dhātu*) of mind, speech, and body.
For this very reason, the eighth instruction states: "Because of its equality, it is proclaimed to be square by means of its entire being."
It is said to consist of three wheels in the form of body, speech, and mind.
On the filaments at the summit of the mountain, beginning with Vairambha and so forth in due order,
that mandala indeed arose through the sequence of the stages of the Guru.
The Vairambha wind is situated at the soles of the feet, shaped like a bow; likewise, fire is situated in the triangular region of the sacrum.
"Delightful," because it does not depend on external dust, raṅgas, and so forth. To show that the external maṇḍala with its four gates is just like the internal one, he says:
"In that maṇḍala of the body, there are four gates known as the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth; or else, 'as previously stated' means that those four gates exist according to their division.
First, the gate of the mind (*cittadvāra*) is in the left and right channels (*nāḍī*).
The four beginning with the *ātmapīṭha* constitute the second, the door of speech. The ninefold body-door is twofold through the division of lower and upper. Thus, there are four doors.
It is called "eight-pillared" because it is endowed with the pillars of the eight enemies.
Internally, it is endowed with the pillars of the channels (nāḍīs) such as the eyes and so forth.
Just as the external mandala is square, so too the bodily mandala should be understood as square by virtue of its balanced proportions.
Whence comes its equality?
Just as this body has a fixed measure from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, so too, with the arms extended, it possesses that same measure.

The external mandala, consisting of the mandalas of mind, speech, and body, comprises three wheels (*cakra*) and twenty-four [sites]; likewise, within the self (*adhyātman*), there is the internal triad of wheels endowed with twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*), beginning from the head and ending at the knees, which serve as the support for the channels (*nāḍī*) of mind, speech, and body.
3–4 || The brief thematic outline begins with the words "the pollen of the mountain peak" (*girimastakañjalaka*) and so forth.

This [reality] is presented as the Universal Lotus (*viśvapadma*), situated upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, which rests above the four spheres (*maṇḍala*) beginning with wind; likewise, within the microcosm (*adhyātman*), it is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru as the body-sphere marked by the [same] spheres.
5 || He states the detailed explanation: from the words "the wind is situated on the sole of the foot" up to "in manifest and unmanifest form," the state of being marked by mandalas is described.
On the sole of the foot—that is, beneath the foot—the wind is situated.
Because it has the shape of a bow and because it is a specific commencement (*viśiṣṭārambha*), it is called Vairambha.

The suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). And the action consisting of the movement of the feet is like that of Vaikṛta. In the *Vasantatilakā* with commentary, [it says]: "Varuṇa, who is indeed circular in form, resides at its edge;

and in the heart, the earth is likewise square on all sides. The king of mountains, Sumeru, is indeed in the form of a staff-like skeleton; situated upon the top portion of that is a thirty-two-petaled lotus. Arisen from the vowels and consonants, the thirty-two-fold mind of awakening—that which is located in the center of the lotus is called the lunar disc."
9. That which is situated in the middle of the head is called the brain; in its center is the syllable *haṃ*, the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound in the form of a point (*bindu*).
Thus it is said. By this, the function and configuration of the wind-mandala have been described.

Above that, in this region of the three hips—the hip-region—there is the fire-mandala of women and men, which is triangular, naturally brilliant due to its being joined with red jewels, and is thus established.
Above that, due to the fusion with the fluidity of the circular garland of mantras, the watery mandala is naturally situated in the region of the abdomen.
Above that, in the heart, the eyes, and the chest, resides the square earth mandala, resembling gold.
That which is above it, the region of the neck known by the synonym *kaṅkāla*, is to be understood as Mount Meru, endowed with eight peaks such as the eyes, because its four petals consist of jewels.

Regarding that Meru, those thirty-two channels—beginning with Abhedya—which are located in the center of its summit, should be understood as the *viśvapadma* (universal lotus), the seat of the Blessed One.
Within that, the very brain-matter, which is the mass of the thirty-two bodhicittas consisting of vowels and consonants, is the moon mandala, the special seat of the Blessed One.
Indeed, no inherent distinction among seats is established in the tantras, because the reality of purity (*viśuddhitattva*) is never intended to be expressed [in such conventional terms].
The differentiation of the seats is due to the inclination of individuals;
for this very reason, they explain that in some cases the heroes and yoginīs situated upon the triple wheel have moon-maṇḍala seats, while in others they have sun-seats.
6-63 || The eighth exposition: That is the root of all worlds, both of the stable and of those whose nature is mobile; it exists in the form of a seed, manifest through its unmanifest form.

11–12. From that, the form of all embodied beings first arose; it flows in the form of nectar and remains established day and night. By that very [nectar], which brings satisfaction to the fire, the *nāda* is split; by that, the mandala indeed becomes complete—of this there is no doubt.
13. "In its center," and so forth.

In the center of that brain is the syllable *haṃ* of the Unstruck (*anāhata*) sound; because it flows with spreading nectar and is of the nature of being perceived as a drop (*bindu*), it is called the "Drop.
Since it is the cause of all entities, whether stable or moving, it is the locus of perfect establishment (*pūrṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Therefore, it is manifest in the form of a seed, yet unmanifest in the form of the ultimate *bodhicitta*.

For this very reason, the body of all embodied beings—whether footless, one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether born from an egg, from moisture, from a womb, or by spontaneous generation; whether among animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, gods, asuras, or humans—is produced from the very beginning and remains as nothing other than the flowing nectar of this [bodhicitta], by virtue of the union of mother and father.

That is the true nature of the Blessed Heruka, because all phenomena are pervaded by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*); for that [nature] remains whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, since it is primordially unarisen. Because all phenomena arise dependently, they lack arising; and precisely for this reason, cessation is not established. Here, nothing whatsoever arises, nor does anything die.
Saṃsāra itself must be known as abiding in the form and appearance of the mind.
Because of this statement, even when there is the conceptualization of arising and ceasing, there is no objective support (nirālamba) in the case of the existence of a real entity.
Even when there is an appearing object of support, because that [appearing object] is like an illusion, the entire collection of entities should be understood as ineffable, unceasing, and unarisen.

10–12 || He speaks of the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means: By that very [union], abiding in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), either within one’s own body or mounted upon the mandala, by that which brings satisfaction through the fire of gnosis (*jñāna*) whose nature is the mandala-circle, the *nāda* [is produced]. From the syllable *kārā* situated in the pericarp of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*)—[in the portion] *ga, gha, ṅa, ca, ṭa, ṭha, ña*—the *hūṃ* syllable is the *stiga* (or *stika*). It is the blazing circle at the waist. The door is to be pierced. Abiding in the *ukā*, it is full. It is indeed the deceased. There is no "many-footed" (*bahupada*). It is the mother. For the sake of knowing the Dharma. The body-mandala. That very thing is called the mandala, the supreme essence of all things; because it grasps (*lāti*) or takes (*gṛhṇāti*) that, the body is considered the mandala.

14. It is "shattered" (*bhidyate*), meaning that having been moved from its own place, it is uprooted by being subjected to the breaking of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅga*) due to its addiction to the snares of the stage (*raṅgapāśa*) which has attained the nature of the moving [breath]. And it is said: "Indeed, *nāda*—having become the single cause of all phonemes (*varṇa*) that differentiate words and sentences—is established in the region of the navel."

And Vāyu and Upavāyu, with respect to the activities of Kṛta such as rising and so forth, have resorted to a state of alternation through their functioning in the form of exhalation (*recaka*) and the rest.
That very same basis is said to be tenfold in its intermediate form; through the union of the churner and the churning, it brings about great bliss.
By means of its upward flaming, it burns the aggregates, sense-faculties, and so forth; having the very form of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), it is the agent of universal destruction.
The Bindu, in the form of the moon, brings delight to the world; in the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), it assumes the form of the unstruck syllable (Anāhatākṣara).
In the Great Bliss, however, the droplets of the consciousness of awakening, resembling the moon, pulsating within the periphery of the yellow wheel, remain present even as they flow forth.
He alone is the life-breath of living beings; he alone is the supreme syllable; he alone is all-pervading; he alone resides within every body.
The resonance (nāda), nourished by this, shall attain the state of perfect contentment; this is declared to be the Vasantatilakā yoga.

Therefore, by that very [means], the mandala consisting of the four seats, or the mandala of Nirmāṇa and so forth, is declared to be complete; even externally, the mandala becomes complete through the Lord of the Mandala together with his respective consort, and not otherwise. || 13 ||

Regarding the term *maṇḍala*: it is the circle (*maṇḍala*) consisting of the letters u, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ta, and na; it is that which grasps (*gṛhṇāti*), and it is that which takes (*lāti*). It is the delight (*rīrama*). By means of the [letters] beginning with d, i, nā, and kāla, there is the vibration (*sphuraṇa*). It is the wind (*vāyu*), or the wheel (*cakra*) of the winds. It is the lion (*hari*). It is that which strikes the vibration (*sphuraṇa*). Even as it flows down, it is the distinction of its own nature (*svasvabheda*). The eighth instruction: "Indeed, the wheel of the thirty-seven great channels is considered the *maṇḍala*. The *bodhicitta* is the great jewel; the *maṇḍala* is the *maṇḍala* of reality (*tattva*). (15)

Pervading the universe in both external and internal forms, it remains established; the external form consists of sound and the other objects of the senses, which set the six sense organs in motion. || 16 ||
But within, the perfected substances such as semen and so forth are established; indeed, for the Vajra-holders, [these exist] through the bodhicitta that is both external and internal. (17)

In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, by the passage beginning "that very mandala," it is stated that the body itself is called the mandala because it encompasses the supported mandala—which consists of the channels (*nāḍī*), elements (*dhātu*), and the intrinsic nature of the *Vasantatilakā*, namely the Ḍākinīs, Heroes, Śrī Heruka, and Vajravārāhī—since [the term] *maṇḍala* is derived from the root *lā* (or *dā*) meaning "to give" (following the prefix *maṇḍa-*), according to the rule for forming the suffix. 14.

He speaks of internal purity with the words beginning "thirty-seven" and so forth: those thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) which are of the nature of consciousness—through their purity, the previously mentioned wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) itself is the mandala. He speaks of the purity of the heroes (*vīra*) with the words beginning "awakening mind" (*bodhicitta*) and so forth: the twenty-four pulsations of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*) which are of the nature of the elements—that very thing, because it is the essence of the mandala, is to be known as the mandala of the circle of goddesses and also as the mandala of the heroes (*vīramaṇḍala*), for it grasps that essential core. || 15 ||

The emanated mandala (*nirmitamaṇḍala*) is twofold: the external, which is square and so forth; and the internal, the womb-mandala (*garbhamaṇḍala*), which consists of the three wheels and so forth. Here, however, the external refers to the head and the *Jālandhara* [pīṭhas] and so forth, while the internal consists of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the elements (*dhātu*). For this very reason, one should know that this mandala does not belong to me alone, but belongs to this entire universe of the five destinies (*pañcagati*). Therefore, it is said: "It remains pervading the universe. Furthermore, the internal mandala is worshipped by means of the external mandala’s offerings of form, sound, and so forth. Within the internal mandala, however, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) exist within the interior of the skull-cup (*kapāla*) for the sake of the worship of bliss. Here, on the other hand, the external sense-doors are worshipped by means of the five qualities of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) such as form and so forth; whereas internally, the accomplished substances (*siddhadravya*)—the substances consisting of the five voids (*pañcavyoma*) which are established by their own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*)—are present. To that end, it says: "The external, however, is form, sound, and so forth," and so on. The external is shown to the disciples for the purpose of bestowing the coarse and subtle commitments (*samaya*). [In this context,] the gross and subtle... the stainless... the great mandala... O Viśvarūpa! ...by the Vajrī... for the sake of the mandala... by means of the meaning of the syllable *la*... of the mandala... in the petal of the skull... for the worship of the mouth... "established by their own nature" is not found in manuscript Gha. ...by way of the gross and subtle nature of the world-friend, of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through the arising of the meaning of the commitment (*samaya*). (Verse 18)
Therefore, from this maṇḍala, one attains Buddhahood in this very life, as well as the state of a Śrāvaka, a Buddha, and likewise a Pratyekabuddha. (19)

From this maṇḍala, there is the manifestation of the gods beginning with Brahmā; [this occurs] through the internal [elements] such as semen and so forth, and likewise through the external [objects] such as form and so forth. //20//

By means of the bodhicitta divided according to its distinctions, by Vajradhara—the achiever of Buddhahood for the entire world—and through the cause of being joyful in bestowing the pledge of both Buddhahood and the state of a Bodhisattva, that very state is attained from that very mandala. ||16-17||
To that end, he says: "By means of the distinction between the gross and the subtle" (di).
Among these, the gross consists of the twenty-four elements;
the subtle is the *bodhicitta*.
Alternatively, the gross impurities (*mala*) that have emerged from the nine gates are to be melted; the subtle heart of awakening (*bodhi-hṛdaya*) is the melter (*drāvaka*).

And it is said: "Having attained a twofold state through the distinction of gross and subtle—the gross being the ninefold substance and the subtle being awakening, which is one's own nature—these substances become perfected (*siddha*) by way of the classification of the melting substances.
The central leader within the outer maṇḍala performs emanations as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Samyaksambuddhas, Brahmā, and so forth, for the sake of sentient beings.
The *śrāvakas* are the nine gates because they flow internally;
the *pratyekabuddhas* are the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, because of their unconditioned nature;
and the *samyaksaṃbuddhas* are Ānanda and the others.
Body, speech, and mind are Brahmā and the others.
Since all these are produced from this very mandala, it is the determination of the mandala. (18.163)
He describes the external and internal *homa*: "By means of the internal [substances], semen and so forth," and so on.

Here, in the external [rite], the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*) is satiated by the teachers with offerings of sesame seeds through the mouth of the pledge-fire (*samayāgni*). In exactly the same way, the mandala of the Buddhas and their Sons, consisting of the five aggregates and so forth, is satiated by the objects of the senses such as form, by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), and by semen and the rest produced through meditative union (*samāpatti*).
This *homa* should be understood as blazing with the heat of burning, because the fire of wisdom (*prajñāgni*) is ignited by the flaming of the *caṇḍālī*. (20–203)

*gadvindu*—ña, ṭa, ḍa; *piṇā-ṇam*—ḍhaṃ; *tu ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha re tu*—ghaṃ; *śakrādyaiḥ*—ghaṃ; *bāhyarū*—ṭha, ḍha; *buddhatvasādhakena*—ca; *cha*; "in its own form" (*svarūpeṇa*) is the reading in the root text; *bhāga*—gha, cha; *jvalanam*—cha; *saṃprāpya*—ka, kha, gaṃ, gha, ṅa; *rastu*—ṭa, ḍa; *saṃguhyaiḥ*—ga; absent in kha, gha, cha; *sattvam*—ka; *srava*—cha; *jvalanadhīḥ*—kha. The eighth instruction: "Homage is performed with oblations in the intensely blazing fire of Wisdom (*prajñā*), specifically for the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. (21)
In that same way, yoga is declared to be the worship of those ḍākinīs who possess divine forms, because by means of it they are worshipped. ||22||
This skull of the head is called the vessel for the oblation; the tongue is said to be the *śruva* ladle, and the heart is the moon, consisting of the *lalanā*. ||23||
The vessel is designated as the mouth, and the sacrificial pit is the circle of the navel; the fire of Brahmā, fanned by the winds of karma, resides in the triple junction. (24)
He states the worship: "Of the six sense-bases and elements," and so forth.
Here, according to the principle previously stated, the five aggregates are the five *ḍākas*; the six sense-bases are the six universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla;
and the four elements are the goddesses of gnosis (*jñānadevī*).
The thirty-six *ḍākinīs* are the [thirty-six] channels (*nāḍī*).
Thus, the yoga which consists of the non-dual union of wisdom and means through these [channels] appearing in the form of deities and so forth—that is to be understood as worship.
And it is said: "Through the practice of the state of selflessness, the cultivation of the deity's form is the great equality, the worship that accomplishes all Buddhas."
For this very reason, he says: "Because they have been honored by him. (21–22)
He states the ancillaries of the previously mentioned *homa* with the verse beginning "This skull is the head" (*śiraḥ kapālametattu*).
This very skull on the head is the vessel for the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhājana*), because it serves as the support for the oblation of moon-butter; it is nothing else.
Likewise, the *lalanā* and *rasanā* located on the left and right [sides] are to be known respectively as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, because they carry the substance downward in due order.

In the *nirmāṇacakra*, the navel region is the sacrificial fire-pit (*vahnikuṇḍa*), because the oblation is poured there. Through the union of the churning-stick and the churning-base, the fire of Brahma—which is the essence of reality (*tattvamaya*)—arises from that action. It remains blazing below that, in the triangle of the secret place (*guhya*), by its very nature.

The supplementary statement is that even outside [the body], the Brahma-fire is praised for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), and it arises from the friction of the kindling sticks (*araṇi*). || 23-24 ||
One should cast [it]— with "ḍa mahājvalau" (ka, kha, ṅa, ca), or with "mahojjalaiḥ" (ṭa,
ṭha); [this is] yoga (ka, kha), or sacrifice (ña).
The people—O!
O Haviḥbhuj! O Hṛccakraka! (various manuscript readings: ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, bho).
-tmikāṃ - ka, kha, ga; -tmikā - gha;
pātīti - ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca;
trikaṭi - ka, kha, ga; trikaṭake - gha.
That which is called "the sound is the mantra" (*nādaṃ tu mantra*) [in the *Vasantatilakā*] refers to the repetition (*japa*) and the turning back (*āvartana*),
through the yoga of the non-duality of the mandala. ||25||
But the manifestation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is this innate form (*sahajarūpa*) of the Maṇḍala and so forth of the Victors (*jināḥ*).
Having explained the fire-oblation (*homa*), he speaks of the recitation (*jāpa*): "The resonance (*nāda*) is said to be the mantra," and so on.
This very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), which was previously mentioned as being articulated from the region of the navel, is called "mantra" because it is the cause of all mantras.
The repetition (*jāpa*) is said to be the revolving [of the mantra] through the sequence beginning with its entry;

by this, it is stated that this natural repetition (*prakṛtijāpa*) is common to all the world. And it is said: he states the conclusion—"But this is the innate form (*sahajarūpa*) of the Victors, beginning with the mandala."

For all the Jinas and all sentient beings, this mandala and so forth—known as the mandala, fire-offering (homa), sacrifice (yāga), recitation (jāpa), and meditative cultivation (bhāvanā)—is the innate form (sahajarūpa) abiding in its own nature, and not artificial. However, that which is artificial is taught solely for the sake of entering into the innate state; thus, all sentient beings are indeed Vajradharas. Regarding these mandalas, one might wonder: "What is external, presided over by the Master (ācārya), and what is internal? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Master is the King of Mind (cittarāja), in the form of the presiding deity of the mandala."
This very holder of the mind-vajra, established as the nature of self-cognition, [is represented by] ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha;
me, taṃ, tu, bhā, va, cha, mudrā, and ka, ca.
The mantra is said to be: *ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha*;
the radiance (*bhāsa*) is *ga gha ṅa cha*; the innate form (*sahajārūpa*) is *ka kha gaṃ*; the reality (*vastu*) is *ja ṭa ṭha ḍa ga gha ṅa*;
and having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one recites] *kha cha*.
In the mantra:
(ka) non-existence— (kha), (gha), (cha) existence— (kha), (gha), (cha).
‘There is no artificiality’—ka; ‘artificiality, artificial mantra’—kha, dha;
‘yoga’—ka; ‘the nature of form’—gha.

The eighth instruction: The teacher is indeed the King of Mind; in the form of the presiding master of the mandala, everything here—the mandala and so forth—should be understood exactly as it has been described. || 26 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, the instruction on the determination of the ritual procedures for the mandala, fire offering, yoga, recitation, meditative cultivation, and so forth, in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*. 8.
That very person who understands the previously mentioned mandalas without distinction is the Ācārya; he is called an Ācārya because he practices the remaining conduct (*ācaraṇa*) in its presence.
For this very reason, it is said: "in the form of the presiding lord of the mandala."
Here, the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be understood as elided. He states the extended application (*atideśa*): "Everything here is to be understood exactly as it was taught, beginning with the mandala.
This means that whatever mandalas and so forth have not been mentioned here—such as the mandala, the *upachāra*, the *rāja*, and the *vajra*—[are to be understood].
*Mantraiva*—ka. gha. ṅa. ca. cha; *mantavyam evamādi*—ka. kha.; *kartavyaṃ homādikaṃ yathāvidhi*—ja.

Following this, in the *Ja* manuscript, these verses from the *Ḍākārṇava* appear: In the *Ḍākārṇava*: "The mouth is declared to be the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the sun and moon are the two vessels, and the *śruva* ladle is the non-dual teacher; there, he offers the oblation whose nature is pure consciousness."
Agni is this entire universe, the mantra of the Ḍākinīs characterized by primordial nature;
she is declared to be the Siddhā Nālī, just like rice-grain produced from paddy.
Alternatively, that which is always pure food is the noble *bodhicitta*; blood should be known as honey, and *dūrvā* grass as the vital winds such as *prāṇa*.
Urine and feces, sandalwood and musk, what is called the "red flower," phlegm, spittle, and milk-rice.
O gods, fuel consists of nails, teeth, bones, skin, clothing, and in brief, hair and body hair; these are situated within the center of the fire-pit.
One should understand that another subtle kind of element, the offering of various grains of rice, is the *pūrṇāhuti*; through this sequence, there is the accomplishment of the *ḍākinī*.
All the sense faculties dance and sing; their latent impressions [manifest as] various musical instruments with great sound, and they partake of food through compassion and other [virtuous emotions].
Having cultivated great power as the sovereign over all living beings, one shall become satisfied by that; through the fire-oblation (homa), success in all rites is attained.
There, among the foremost realms of all worlds, he sports with the mind;
at whatever time there may be bliss, at that very time it proceeds.
But for one who bestows curses and favors through the vision of the inner self via fire-offerings,
the middle [channel] is at the end for the sake of attaining mundane and supramundane knowledge.
The great mind indeed carries along the ultimate reality within all the joints;
having consumed that which has arisen at that time, it consumes the impression (vāsanā) created by the Buddha.
In the case of oblations, *māyā* has the sense of "characteristic."
Regarding the abandonments of hundreds of thousands and tens of millions, you should know that through these two, *laya* (dissolution) is produced therein; O "Śrī," O nihilist!
[This is found] in the *Tilaka*—Ja.
*vanāvidhi* — ga, gha, ṅa, cha; *ṅa*, *ca*, *ja*; *yogapūjājapa* — bho;
and the word *śabda* — gha.
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, the fifth chapter (*ja*)—

containing the ritual instruments, the thread-measurement, the acquisition of the ground, the invocation, the installation, the dismissal, the accomplishment of the mandala, the consecration, the bathing, the offerings, and so forth— is to be understood as occurring within that very body-mandala; that is to say, they are to be known [as being there].

To explain: the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) is the thread (*sūtra*); blood, semen, feces, urine, and so forth are the colored powders (*maṇḍala-rajas*); the twenty-four channels that encompass the twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*) are the grounds (*bhūmi*). The circumambulation (*paribhrama*) of these by way of their dissolution and so on is the "seizing of the ground" (*bhū-parigraha*). The invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites are performed by way of entry and so on. The accomplishment of the mandala (*maṇḍala-sādhana*) occurs through the flame of gnosis (*jñānolkā*). Here, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the circle of goddesses and deities seated upon the lotus throne takes place through the torrential stream from the *vajramaṇi* flask. This tasting of the tongue (*rasanā-svāda*) of the outflows (*niṣyanda*) is the "oblation" (*bali*). || 26 ||

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the eighth chapter of the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishing the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 8.
There is nothing to be known— [this is] the perfection of the stages (bhūmi-parikarman) and the excellence of knowledge.
And this much is the *sāt* [suffix],
as well as the *gha* and *tilaka*.
In the *paṭala*—ka;
in the *tilaka*—ka;
in the *pikāṭīkā*—gha; "in the *ṭīkā*" does not exist in ca.
The Ninth Exposition: Now I shall explain the extraction of the mantra-circle for a certain Tathāgata-body. ||1||
The delightful triangular mandala, which issues forth from the Vajrāralli, is renowned as the Dharmodayā and is also called the *bhaga* of women. (2)
In its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp; there, the eight groups [of consonants], mixed with vowels and semi-vowels, are situated. ||3||

Regarding the previously mentioned recitation of mantras, as to what that mantra is, he provides its extraction (uddhāra) by means of the ninth instruction beginning with "atha" and so forth: "Of any one whatsoever"—meaning, the mantra which is established by the very nature of any given being; from that, the origin of all mantras is demonstrated. || 1 ||

In that regard, having drawn a triangular mandala on the outside and having painted an eight-petaled lotus within it, one should place the letter *A* in its central pericarp and the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*) upon the petals according to the division of eight by eight. Then, through the detailed sequence beginning with "the fifth of the fourth" and "the fifth of the fifth," one should extract the root mantras and so forth. As for the internal [correspondence], this triangle is the primary seat (*mūlapīṭha*) together with the eight channels (*nāḍī*). Therein resides the Lord *A*, situated in the midst of the vowels and consonants along with the eight groups (*varga*), abiding in the form of all letters, words, sentences, great sentences, and so on; from him alone these letters manifest.

And they produce those words, which in turn produce sentences and great sentences, extending as far as the infinite eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings according to the distinctions of worldly phenomena; all of this originates from the phonemes and so forth.

And because the relationship between support and supported is intended to be expressed between the navel and the secret place, it is said that the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) alone is the support of the mantra. || 2–3 ||

Thus, mantras whose lineage is the letter *a* and which originate from the letter *a* perform and bring about the collection of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth in their proper form; otherwise, mantras do not act if their true nature (*tattva*) is not fully understood.
Now, for another [mantra]—*ṭa. ḍa.*; now for this one—*bho*; now I shall explain another, O Dear One, the procedure for the extraction (*uddhāra*) of mantras—*ja*.
The extraction of all mantras—*ña. ṭa. ṭha. ḍaṃ*.
Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti: *ṭa*, *vajrāvalī*—*ḍha*, the triangle—*ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja*;
the *vastri*—the petals—*ka kha ca ja ṇa*.
Then—kha.
cha. | [The] corner-maṇḍala—kha, ca, cha | [One should] contemplate—kha, cha.
In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, [it is said]: "They perform the aggregate of actions for embodied beings in the form of mantras;
indeed, the fifty syllables are established as the Vedas and so forth. (4)
Likewise: "The nature of the class of mantras is the single supreme syllable.
By the mere knowledge of that, mantras become performers of action."
Thus it is said.
For this very reason, we do not accept that mantras consist of the nature of phonemes;
for [phonemes] are not capable of being the cause even for the bending of a blade of grass.
Thus it is said; therefore he says: "They perform the aggregate of actions for embodied beings in the form of mantras.
By the words "the fifty syllables," and so forth, he states their number.
Because the vowels (*āli*) become twofold by way of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), they amount to sixty-four.
In that regard, having divided the vowel-group (*ālivarga*) into two, thirty-two phonemes (*varṇa*) arise;
likewise, from the placement of the two *rakṣas* above and below, there are exactly thirty-two *kālas*.
In its fundamental sense, however, it consists directly of fifty phonemes.

By means of those phonemes, according to the tradition of other schools (*paranikāya*), it encompasses the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*); yet, according to the tradition of its own school (*svanikāya*), the letter *A* exists by relying upon the five branches of knowledge.
And it has been said: "He who is not bound by the ten [phonemes] situated within the middle of one to nine..."
One should know that as unbound; he knows the supreme state.
He who knows the vowels and consonants, which follow the number nine,
as unbound by mutual conjunction— he is the Teacher of the World.
Thus: "The Vedas, the four auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya,
the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."

Thus ends the position of the other schools. The Tenth Explanation: "Now, I shall proclaim the gnosis of great bliss in the form of the three bodies—the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation—of a certain Tathāgata’s body. (1)
The wheel located at the head and the navel is established in the form of the letter E; the wheel reaching the heart and the throat is considered to resemble the letter Vaṃ.

Now, for the purpose of establishing the innate (*sahaja*) which is the expressed meaning (*vācya*)—having as its nature the three bodies beginning with the Dharma-body, the four wheels, the *Vasantatilaka*, the etymological explanations (*nirukti*), the mantras, and the fourfold *yoni* (or *dyauli*) consisting of the five vowels and so forth—the tenth instruction begins with the words "Then" (*atha*) and so on.
The word "then" (*atha*) signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*) in relation to the preceding instruction; [it refers to] any one of those [preceding topics].
"In the form of the Dharma and so forth" means in the form of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*).
"I shall explain the innate (*sahaja*) as the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*": this is the brief statement (*uddeśa*).
This is what is meant: all sentient beings indeed consist of the innate of the three bodies (*trikāya-sahaja-maya*), because they are endowed with the three. (1)
Regarding the passage beginning with "the wheel situated at the head and the navel," etc.:
the two wheels situated between the head and the navel are of the shape of the letter *E*, because they are equal to the *dharmodaya* below and share the same nature as the earth.
Above, even the pericarp of the lotus at the *uṣṇīṣa* is triangular in shape, because its intrinsic nature is that of the *dharmodaya*.
Likewise, even the two wheels located in the heart and the throat have the form of the syllable *vaṃ*.

Beginning from "in the center of the navel" and ending with "the lotus is remembered as having eight petals," it is established that the four wheels, beginning with the *nirmāṇa*, have respectively sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, and eight petals; this is because they correspond in nature to the *daṇḍas*, the transitions (*saṃkrāntis*), and the watches (*praharas*) [of the day].

Just as there is a division into *daṇḍas* and so forth externally through the movement of the sun, so too internally through the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); since that [movement] is based precisely upon the wheels, these are the *kālacakra*s. (3–4)

By the passage beginning with "sixty-four petals" and ending with "situated all around," it is demonstrated that these four are not only of the nature of the specific times of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), but also possess the nature of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth.

In this context, the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*) is the emanation body, because it is the source of the arising of all sentient beings—the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*)—in the form of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The heart wheel (*hṛccakra*) is the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), because it withdraws the forms of the aggregates and elements, such as the syllable *haṃ* and others.

The throat-cakra is the *saṃbhogakāya*, because it bestows the enjoyment of the nectar of the Dharma and because it is the source of the [Dharma] horse. The head-cakra is great gnosis (*mahājñāna*), the *svabhāvakāya*, because its essential nature is the ultimate *bodhicitta*.
And it is said: "The three bodies are situated within the body in the form of cakras; the thorough knowledge of the three bodies is known as the cakra of great bliss."

The tenth instruction: "That which is called the manifest bodhicitta is condensed and undisturbed. *pramāṇastadgata* (kha); *nartena* (kha); *tatreṣveva* (ka), *tatreṣu* (kha), *tatreṣṭhe* (prabhā-ca-cha); *cina* (gha).daśamo nirdeśaḥ: 'vyaktasaṃbodhicittākhyaṃ piṇḍībhūtamanāvilam' || 10 ||

The supreme, stainless form of Śrī Vajrasattva, free from dualities, is known as Śrī Heruka; however, the tantra itself is the form of the wood-worm (ghuṇa). ||23||
Alas! Having attained the hand of the True Doctrine and being established in the three tantras, he remains like a wood-worm, having abandoned both passion and dispassion. ||24||
The *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* have been explained; now he speaks of the *dharmakāya* with the words "when that sun has set," and so forth.

When that sun known as the *nirmāṇakāya* has set—that is, when the moon has entered into it—the two manifestations, having attained a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), [merge]. Of that *bodhicitta*—meaning of both the moon and the sun—it is a massed, untroubled state, free from the stain of dualistic conceptualization; this is the *dharmakāya*, which is the connection with what follows.
Of what nature is it?

It is that in which there is the cessation of the path of saṃsāra—the state of equilibrium between the two individuals—and the conceptualization thereof; it is that wherein there is the pacification of the two manifestations, namely the *saṃbhoga-kāya* and the *nirmāṇa-kāya*. Therefore, it is a compound in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*).
It is "Auspicious" (*śiva*) because of its innate nature (*sahajatva*), and it is "beyond duality" (*nirdvandva*) because it is free from the two mutually opposed sides.
Because he is self-cognizable, he is supreme;
because he is free from afflictions, he is pure.

*Vajra* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and *sattva* is compassion (*karuṇā*); because he is based upon these, his nature is that of Vajrasattva. He is Śrī Heruka because he is the means consisting of the three gates of liberation, and because he is the form of the goal to be attained through the gate of liberation that is natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*).

That very [reality] is called the *dharmakāya* because it protects the mind; that very [reality] is the *mantra* because it devours, as if with saliva, the web of afflictions such as passion; and that very [reality] is the *ghuṇa* (woodworm) [because it consumes the wood of ignorance]. || 21–23 ||

If it is objected: "But in the *Yoginītantras* the 'woodworm' (*ghuṇa*) alone is specified, whereas it is not mentioned in the *Kriyā* and other tantras; how then can the *dharmakāya* be non-pervasive? It is said in reply: "By 'laughter' and so forth"—in the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* tantras there is mutual laughter between wisdom and method; in the *Yoga* tantra, however, it is looking; and in both the *Yoga* and *Caryā* tantras, it is taking hands. And this is merely an illustration.

In the Mahāyogatantra, it is *āśleṣa* (embrace), and in the Yoginītantras, *dvandva* (union) is taught—[where] the intrinsic nature... [is] Heruka, who is indeed proclaimed as all the gods; that which is the goal is the tranquil, non-dual, supreme bliss, the very nature of Vajrasattva, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and undisturbed (*nirākula*).

In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, [it is said]: "Shaken by the winds of karma, it blazes within the circle of the navel. (Chapter 86)
The one well-known as Vārāhī is remembered as the Vasantatilakā. || 32 ||
With a body possessing hundreds of thousands of hair-pores, and with a radiance equal to a hundred flashes of lightning,
[he abides] within the pores and joints during the times of deity-yoga.

The Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, whose nature consists of the three activities, has been described. Now, in order to show the Blessed Lady Vārāhī, who is non-different from him, [the text] says: Within the navel-mandala of this very Śrī Heruka, whose self-nature is the innate (*sahaja*), there is a consciousness in the form of fire—born from the union of the churned and the churning, kindled by the wind of karma—which is his innate wisdom (*prajñā*) established by its own nature, like the moonlight of the moon.

She alone is Vārāhī; she is called Vārāhī because she impels (*īrayati*) and causes to flow (*srāvayati*) by means of the two syllables *vā* and *ra*, representing the wind (*mātariśvan*) and the fire (*hutabhuj*), and not because she has a sow’s face.
Vasanta is like a sectarian mark (tilaka) consisting of the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth; for it has been previously established that she is satisfied upon attaining him. || 31–32 ||

He states her measure with the words beginning "bālāgra" (the tip of a hair): she whose limb—that is, her very form—is like a hundred-thousandth part, a portion measuring one lakh, of the tip of a hair;
by this, her extreme subtlety is established, since she is accessible only to the knowledge of yogins.
And it is said: "That wisdom which abides pervasively and is perceivable by great beings is declared by Vararuci.
It is radiant with a brilliance like the flash of lightning, resembling a streak of cloud-born light, shining intensely with splendor.

The *devatāyoga* is the yoga of the non-duality of wisdom and means. At that time, on that occasion, that very flame of the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgnijvālā*) issues forth from all the pores and joints of the yogin’s body. Having overcome the gods and asuras—the conceptualizations of the aggregates and the sense-faculties—it burns the fuel of the conceptualizations of the aggregates and elements, which exist in the form of knots within the *dharmacakra* and *saṃbhogacakra*. Emerging through the right nostril, it enters the apertures of those [beings] situated in the ten directions via the opening at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). Having burned their four wheels, it emerges again through the left nostril and enters through the crown aperture, possessing the brilliance of a hundred thousand rising suns and a radiance equal to a hundred lightning flashes.

The tenth exposition: Emerging toward all directions, threatening the gods and asuras, she repeatedly consumes the wheel of dharma within the wheel of enjoyment.
Having emerged from the heart through the channel of the nose on the right side, it likewise pervades the ten directions through the aperture located in the treasury of the *ūrṇā*. 35.
Having entered through the left nostril of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
one should set ablaze the wheel at the crown of the head and emerge.
And again, through the previously mentioned aperture, she enters the crest-lock (śikhā);
she generates bliss for the Buddhas who have been burnt, and having reached the navel-mandala, she remains as before. ||37||
Thus, in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*, the tenth [chapter] is known as the *Śrī-Heruka-Vasanta-Vajravārāhī-Tilakā*, preceded by the embrace of the three bodies: the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation.

It is the exposition of the Tathāgatas who abide in each respective object, having the nature of thirty-four syllables and the twelve vowels and four measures; it concerns the secret emanations of the knowledge of the mantras and the movement of the tantras, and the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies within the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*) consisting of the four lotuses.
As before, it effects the nourishment of the Tathāgatas who have been burnt, and it becomes stable and dissolves into the navel-mandala.

And it is said: "From the union of the churner and the churning, the fire of gnosis, impelled here by the wind of karma, dissolves into the circle of the navel; blazing with radiance, having incinerated the Sugatas situated in the *samaya-cakra*, it [incinerates] the Means (*upāya*) situated in the *saṃbhoga-cakra* three times... In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary: "The sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, pills, the subterranean realm, the yakṣa-maidens, the three worlds, the lamp, and those [powers] residing in mercury—these are the accomplishments (*siddhis*) that follow from karma."

Having performed a circumambulation, [the wind] enters the Tathāgatas stationed in the ten directions through the opening known as Oḍḍiyāna—which is located in the *ūrṇā* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows) and serves as the gateway for piercing the vital points (*marmodghāṭana*)—and through the golden door known as Jālandhara. Having entered, it burns the four previously mentioned wheels of those Tathāgatas, exits through the aforementioned door, reaches the stream of milk, and produces bliss (*ānanda*) for the Tathāgatas who have been burned.
Thus, in the *Tantrolijñānolī*, it is said:
"The twelve vowels are situated on the left and right sides" (by this, the *mantroli* is indicated; however, in the investigation of the *dharmakāya*, it is the *guhyoli*).

By the statement, "The twelve vowels are situated on the left and right sides," and by the passage beginning with "Likewise, her innate wisdom (*sahajā prajñā*)... and ending with "...having incinerated the wheel, one should emerge," as well as by the statement, "And he should again produce bliss for the Buddhas who have been incinerated," and by the statement, "Having reached the navel-center, she remains as before," the four *olayas*—known as Mantra, Tantra, Jñāna, and Guhya—are described.

Likewise, regarding the arrangement of the five vowels and so forth within the four wheels beginning with the Nirmāṇa-cakra, it has been stated in brief by such passages as: "The twofold doubling of the alphabet (*alikāli*), the placement of the five seed-syllables beginning with *HŪṂ*, the placement of the neuter seed-syllables, the placement of the long Brahmans, and the placement of the syllable of the Unstruck (*anāhata*) surrounded by the thirty-two vowels"; and further, "In the center of the Nirmāṇa-cakra, the letter *A*—the supreme syllable—is the foremost form of the letters surrounded by the eight classes (*varga*). For a "detailed exposition" (*nirdeśa*) follows a "brief indication" (*uddeśa*), since a brief indication is a presentation in summary.
The phrase "the detailed exposition" is the ellipsis;
"this exposition" means the section [of the text].
The eight great accomplishments previously mentioned, beginning with the sword and the collyrium, have their meanings made clear.
It has been established that those [attainments] arise from understanding the previously mentioned method for the practice of the *Vasantatilaka*;

thus, demonstrating that this concerns individuals of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya-pudgala*) by excluding those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya-sattva*), he says "from the summary" (*uddeśāt*) and so forth.
This is the tenth instruction on the guru’s samādhi, as pointed out by the jewel-like dust from the lotus feet of the Guru.

All those who possess great supernatural powers (*maharddhi*) in their own abodes, endowed with the five objects of desire—all of them are encompassed by the power arising from the application of the *Vasantatilaka*. Thus, having received the oral instruction of the Guru and the command of the venerable protector Heruka Bhaṭṭāraka, and having fixed in mind that which was revealed in a dream, this *Vasantatilaka* has been clarified through speech—both externally and internally, in terms of its essential nature and through meditative visualization—by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, who observes the conduct of the yogic observance (*caryāvratin*), for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect. And because the goddess Vajravārāhī is the "Spring" (*vasanta*) and Heruka is the "Glory" (*śrī*), it is called *Vasantatilaka*; this is also the title of the treatise.

Thus ends the *Vasantatilakā*. Those who are adorned and graced by the diadems that distinguish the jewels of realized reality, as well as others who have been inspired and brought forth with enthusiasm by the Blessed Tathāgatas—the preeminent among the Victors—through words of every step and sentence consisting of the syllables of reality, experienced through the grace of the instructions known as Prajñā down to the level of the Ācārya: whatever has been thus experienced is seen exactly so in all the various Sūtras and Tantras.

And it is said in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*: "Conviction arises from scripture, conviction likewise from the guru, conviction from oneself, and conviction from another; [the truth] is to be grasped through these four convictions," and so forth.

For this very reason, regarding those who hold to both the external and the internal—just as *calakānvi* and *calaṃkā* were together with one named *sārdhaka*, by whom meditation is not clear through the words of meditation, nor is there awakening to yoga—there is no *tilaka* for the completion of the *syāpa*, and no *tilaka* for the completion of *kaṃ*. *Gha*.
Henceforth—may there be prosperity! Written on the eleventh day of the month of Vaiśākha in the [Vikrama] year, completed and auspicious.

[He visualizes] the one named Heruka, who holds a snake and a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in his [right] hand, a hell-being and a goat-head with his four left arms, and in his right [hands] he bears a curved knife (*kartī*), a trident (*triśūla*), an axe (*paraśu*), and a *ḍamaru* drum. — Auspicious Year. Thus ends this [work] of Vārāhī. Likewise, from the instruction on Śrī Heruka, this is the treatise titled *Vasantatilaka*;
thus it is called *Yogarājavasantatilaka*. [The verse beginning: "Of those phenomena... (the *Ye dharmā* verse).

In the *Vasantatilakā* with its commentary, they receive instruction through the similarity [of the external] with the internal, because of the statement: "Just as it is internally, so too is the external restraint revealed. Furthermore, for those who possess the Vajra-Ḍākas within their own hearts alone and not externally, this *Vasantatilakā* was composed by me; for they grasp the object of knowledge firmly through faith. Thus, showing the completion of the work by way of revealing his own nature to one who grasps through firm faith, the author says: "Thus, by the venerable Guru-Buddha... and so forth.

This work entitled *Vasantatilaka*, consisting of ten chapters, has been completed by me, Kṛṣṇa, who has received the command of my own Vajra-guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas; who abides in the body of the Tathāgata, and who observes the vows of conduct. This means that because it summarizes the meaning of all tantras, there is no dependence on anything else.

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the tenth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, the manual for the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*). Thus ends the *Vasantatilaka-ṭīkā*. He proclaims: "And thus, and indeed thus—from this point forward: 'Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. By whatever merit has been gained through this writing, may people thereby become sons of the Victorious One (*jinaputra*).

May [all beings] always have minds distressed by the terrible cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Written by Dharmarāja on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa in the year [marked by] wind, fire, a drop, and the moon (1430), on Thursday; it has reached completion. May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds! On the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Rādha (Vaiśākha) in the same year, on Monday, this commentary on the *Vasantatilaka* was caused to be written by Jīvaratna.
May there be auspiciousness.

Now, the appendix: furthermore, regarding the channel-wheel (*nāḍicakra*) of a certain Tathāgata, there are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*), sub-channels (*nāḍikā*), and secondary sub-channels (*upanāḍī*). There are one hundred and twenty names for these, which follow the body. They are not [merely] supported by the [gross] body.
The preeminence of the channels (*nāḍī*) is now described: The channels, their locations, and the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) are twenty-four in number.
Among them, three channels are all-pervading and take refuge within them. (3) In Pullīramalaya, at the head, the channels that carry the teeth are situated;
in Jālandhara, at the site of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the channel carries the afflictions and body hair. (4) In Oḍiyāna, at the right ear, the channel carries the impurities of the skin.
In the *arbuda* [region] at the back of the neck, the channel carries lymph (*pṛṣita*). || 5 || At the *goḍāvalī* on the left ear, the channel carries sinews (*snāyu*);
between the eyebrows, it always carries bone (*asthi*). || 6 ||

The goddess Rāmeśvarī resides at Devīkoṭa; Mārave is at Kāmarūpa; Cakṣu is the channel (nāḍī) that flows upward; and the channel that flows to the heart is situated in the region of the two shoulders. || 7 ||
In the location of the two armpits, the Cakṣu channel always carries [the wind];
in the pair of breasts, the Oḍra channel always carries bile.
At the navel, in the region of the female organ, there is a channel carrying the lungs;
and at the tip of the nose in Kośala, the Antamālā-carrying [channel] is situated.
In Muṣasthāna among the Kaliṅgas, the Guṇavatī always carries [the breath];
but in Lampāka, at the region of the throat, the Nāḍī always carries the belly [wind].

The channel in the region of the heart is Kāñcī; the channel in the region of Meḍhra is Himālaya; the channel at the Liṅga is Pretādhivāsinī; the channel in the region of Guḍa is Gurudevatā; and the channel situated in the middle of the Sīmānta is Vipravāhinī. ||11||
The channel carrying phlegm is also the channel carrying pus. || 12 ||

It is seen in the general *mātṛkā*s. In the *Vasantatilakā*: in Saurāṣṭra, it is in the pair of thighs; in Suvarṇadvīpa, it is in the shanks; and in Nakhara, it should be known as being in the toes of the feet. In Sindhu, the channel (*nāḍī*) located on the instep of the foot is the one that always carries perspiration. (13)
Always carrying intoxication, she flows as embodied tears.
The Maru [lineage] always carries the burden at the position of the two thumbs;
Kulatā, who rides upon a young lion, remains stationed at the two knees. 15.

Situated among them is the *lalanā* channel on the right, and the channel known as *rasanā* is said to be enclosed by the central portion. Resembling the *kadara* flower and ignited like a lamp of oil and fire, she is to be known as *avadhūtī*. She is the most preeminent of all channels; for this very reason, the others depend upon her. These are the *yoni*-channels:
the one carrying urine and the one carrying blood. (16)
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus,
she hangs with her face turned downwards.
She brings forth the thought of awakening and bestows innate bliss. || 18 ||
The channels, beginning with lalanā, are the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, and Parāpagā rivers. ||16||
O-faced one, you should know that those [energies] beginning with Saṃbhoga-kāya, having become unified, have resorted to the body. ||20||
The three principal channels in a woman, beginning with Lalanā and the others, are established such that Lalanā has the nature of wisdom (prajñā) and Rasana has the nature of means (upāya). ||21||
In the central region is the Avadhūtī; Lalanā is the Saṃbhogakāya, and Rasanā is the Dharmakāya—thus these channels are all devoid of subject and object, and constitute the Nirmāṇakāya body. ||22||
She is considered the embodiment of the three bodies, the one who brings about the purity of the physical form. ||23||
The mass produced from that collection becomes a cluster transcending form; therefore, by means of inconceivable yoga, in whatever manner it may be, it is both the deity-nature and the deity itself.
Consisting of suchness, all-pervading, and established in the state beyond the aggregate,
the yogi, having attained identity with that, shall obtain Buddhahood. ||25||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning the method of the sequence of the wheel of channels, within the *Vasantatattva*.
Appendix 2: Now I shall further explain another supreme mandala of the body, by the mere knowledge of which one attains nirvāṇa.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to great enlightenment are established in mandalas in the form of the channels of Vajrasattva and the five ḍākinīs.
With four gates and corners, with a multicolored *viśvadalapadma*, and with Mahāsaṃvara, Heruka, and the others.
The circle of the body, mercury, should be known from the mouth of the Guru;
it is the wind situated at the soles of the feet, known as Bhairambha, shaped like a bow.
The triangular fire-maṇḍala should be known as being located in the region of the three folds [of the navel];
the water-maṇḍala, which is circular in shape, is situated in the abdomen.
The circle of the earth is the heart, and it is square;
the syllable Kaṅkāra is declared to be the armor, as is Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains.
Situated in the center of that region of the head, produced from vowels and consonants,
is a lotus with thirty-two petals located in the middle of the heart,
representing the thirty-two marks of a Buddha.
The lunar disc consisting of nectar situated in the middle of the head is called the *mastaka*;
in its center is the syllable *haṃ*, in the form of a bindu, which is the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound.
That seed of all worlds, both moving and stationary, exists as their very seed-nature in both manifest and unmanifest forms; from it,
the bodies of all embodied beings are produced and arise.
Established day and night in the form of the nectar of the Śrāvaka [vehicle],
by that very means desire arises as the cause for the creation of the world;
thus the complete five-maṇḍala comes to be— of this there is no doubt.
The body is said to be the mandala; it is the supreme mandala that brings an end to the ocean of saṃsāra.
This body is considered the mandala, for the wheel of the thirty-seven great channels is indeed remembered as the mandala.
The great maṇḍala is the maṇḍala of the great jewel of bodhicitta.
Pervading and established as both external and internal forms, the universe exists; externally, it is proclaimed as form, sound, and so forth, along with the six sense organs,
while internally, the substances for accomplishment such as semen and the like are well-established.
And by means of the vajra-holder’s bodhicitta, which exists both externally and internally in the form of the gross and the subtle, and which has the nature of the kinsman of the world,
[he is the essence] of the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and likewise of the Samayas.
For the Śrāvakas, the Buddhas, and likewise the Pratyekabuddhas,

as well as for all the gods beginning with Brahmā, the homa is performed from this maṇḍala by means of the internal semen and so forth, as well as the external forms and so forth, and likewise by means of oblations, into the wisdom-fire which is indeed greatly blazing.

The sacrificial worship of the six sense-bases, the aggregates, and so forth— specifically those in the form of deities, as well as those ḍākinīs— is thus proclaimed; when worshipped by everyone, it is worshipped by oneself.
The head and the neck are said to be the vessel for the oblation;
the *dhruvā* is called the tongue, the heart is of the nature of the *lalanā*,
and the navel-circle is designated as the sacrificial bowl (*pātrī*).
The fire of Brahma, fanned by the wind of karma, resides at the three joints;
that which is called the sound (nāda) is the mantra, and its recitation (japa) becomes the sowing of seeds.
Regarding meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), the state of being is the mandala through non-dual yoga.
This mandala and so forth of the Victors is of the nature of the co-emergent (*sahaja*); it is the very substance of the Master’s mind.
In its true nature, everything belonging to the mandala—including the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and other rites—must be performed right here according to the ritual procedure.
Henceforth, I shall explain the nature of the Great Mantra;

indeed, by the mere knowledge of that mantra, one reaches the further shore oneself. By the power of the mantra-deity alone, which bestows my ultimate reality, [one masters] the mantra that is the presiding deity among all mantra-kings in every respect.
I am the supreme among all the Vedas; furthermore,
the wise one should know that the king of letters called Praṇava is Vināyaka.
In the Tathāgata Vajraḍāka and also in Nānāḍākeśvara,
the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* exists within all names as Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Māyā, Mātrā, Viśākṣarā, and Parā.
"Vajra-he-he-ru-ru-ka and Mahāsaṃvara-mātrikā;
two *hai*s, two *phaṭ*s, and with *svāhā*—this is the great mantra of the Buddhas. This mere teaching has been revealed by me, not for ordinary persons, nor for those lacking in discernment."
By means of the seed-syllable of the Goddess Lakṣmī, Śrī is produced everywhere; likewise, by means of the seed-syllable of Lajjā, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ come under one's control;
and through the nature of the Māyā-bīja, there is the destruction of all sins.
The thirty-two syllable mantra bestows the ultimate reality:
the letter *śa* is declared to be semen (*śukra*), the letter *ra* is born from passion (*rajas*),
and the letter *ī* is said to be the union (*mīlana*) of the three worlds beginning with Īśvara.
The syllable *ha* is declared to be joy; the syllable *ra* arises from passion (*rajas*);
the syllable *ī* is said to be the closing of the eyes, pertaining to the three worlds beginning with Īśvara;
the syllable *ka* is declared as "who? or "where?"; and the syllable *la* refers to the lord of the gods and others.
The letter *ī* is declared to be the closing [of the eyes], pertaining to the three worlds beginning with Īśvara;
the form *śuśya* is called *śuśya*, consisting of the half-moon and Ratneśa;
the line is Lord Amitābha, and the letter *ha* is Vairocana.
The syllable *ukāra* is declared to be unfailing, as are the Buddha-Ḍākas and so forth; likewise,
the two *phaṭ*s and that which ends with *svāhā*— I speak the truth, the absolute truth—
along with Vārāhī and the Ḍākinīs, by means of these four seed-syllables.
At its end, O Goddess, the root mantra is declared as before;
there is no other mantra for me, nor is there any greater mantra than this one for you,
which should be known as the bestower of the ultimate truth and the destroyer of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Indeed, there is no mantra equal to it found in the three worlds; it is the mantra that bestows the state of Nirvana in every age throughout the triple realm,
the mantra that grants great bliss, the sovereign lord of all kings of mantras, the all-pervading one.
A suitable place should indeed be prepared for an ordinary person who has blossomed [in realization];
having established the thirty-seven syllables, there is the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśvara),
as well as Vīreśvarī, who bestows the fruits of the activities of the mind.
The forty-eight root [mantras] likewise bestow their fruit; they must not be given to ordinary people but should be guarded with great effort.
By the power of these great mantras, the state of the Three Jewels shall be attained, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others will certainly be present at all times.
One should certainly take the final letter of the western [direction], and likewise the final letter of the northern;
one should take the second letter of the southeast, and there again and again.
The fire-seed (ra) is in the southwest, and likewise Varuṇa (va) is in the northeast;
the third letter of that which begins with the third letter [of the first group] is the third letter of the western [group];
and again, the last letter of the northern [group] is at the beginning of the first [group].
The second syllable of Īśāna and the first syllable of that same [deity];
the fire-seed (RA) in the southwest and likewise the first [syllable] in the northeast;
taking the letter RA from the rakṣasa [direction] and the second syllable from the southeast.
From the Daitya [seed-syllable], the fire-seed (*agnibīja*) is to be taken; likewise, from Agni, the wind (*pavana*).
This is said to be the first syllable of the mantra’s vowel;
the second letter is *śo*.
The fifth syllable, joined with the *visarga* and occupied by the fourth square; the ninth syllable, occupied by the second square and adorned at its lower part by the letter *ra*;
they know this as the sixth syllable. The tenth [syllable] is likewise occupied by that same [fourth square]. And by the fourth [square], [the eleventh is formed].
The twelfth is occupied by that very same [deity], and the thirteenth is likewise occupied by that very same one.
In the fourteenth, one should visualize Varuṇa in the lower portion.
The supreme fifteenth syllable is occupied by the second square.
