"Having understood this, O great mantra-master, you must always know the cause in all positions, as well as the extraction of the mantra and its practical application. One should take the first of the west and the fourth of the north."

One should take Varuṇa from the northeast and again the last [letter] of the south. One should take the first seed-syllable of the middle and likewise the last of the north; one should take the first of the middle and the final seed-syllable of the north.
One should take Varuṇa from the northeast; the seed-syllable of the southern face is in the southeast.
The letter of the wind [Ya] is said to be the second pada in the southeast.
The third [syllable] is occupied by the square and is illuminated by that which is below the first.
In the fifth square, the second syllable is adorned below;
the first of the northern [group], however, is the sixth, illuminated below.
The eighth syllable is equal to that, and the tenth is likewise traversed by it—the turning of the wheel of Dharma, pierced by the second square.
The destroyer of all misfortune,
the untroubled bestower of all accomplishments,
the second seed-syllable of the Daityas. || 2 ||
One should take the third of the west, the first seed-syllable of the west, and again the first of the south. Then the fourth of the north, the second syllable of the Daityas,
the last of the south, and the fourth of the north.
The syllable *daitya* (dai), *agni* (ra), and likewise *īśāna* (ma) and *varuṇa* (va) are to be grasped;
together with the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*) and wind (*ya*), they constitute the third word of the mantra.
They know the first syllable to be that which occupies the eleventh square.
In the *Vasantatilakā* meter, the third [syllable] is adorned with fire (the letter *ra*),
the second syllable is topped by the ninth square (the letter *na*),
and it is likewise adorned below with fire (*ra*) by means of the first syllable of the right-hand line.
One should place the third [syllable] in the middle and arrange it in the lower sections.
They know the fifth syllable to be that which occupies the fourth square and the eighth square;
one should then provide for the tenth syllable.
The tenth [vowel] conjoined with the second [consonant] is the supreme subduer of the wicked;
it brings about the subjugation of gods, asuras, and humans in their respective places. It consists of the seed-syllable preceded by fire (RA) and the first letter of the western [group] (PA).
The second seed-syllable of Vāyu and likewise the one following Īśāna;
again, the letter that is the second of Vāyu located at the end of the West (maṃ);
and the first of the West, which is the seed-syllable of Fire and Wind.
They call the fourth word the illuminator of all things.
One should arrange the fifth syllable below the letter *ra* in its lower parts.
The sixth [syllable] is from the sixth square, and the seventh is the second again.
Indeed, the imperishable state of the Omniscient One is adorned below by Fire (Ra).
Then take Īśāna (Ha), Varuṇa (Va), and Kāra (Ra);
again, the first seed-syllable of the West (Sa), and the fifth word of the East-facing one (Na), which is the third of the Yoginīs belonging to Raudra (Ū). || 4 ||
One should grasp Īśāna in the west, and then Pavana in the southeast;
[he is] the awakener of all.

The first syllable is occupied by the third square; by that same [syllable], the fourth seed-syllable is occupied. The fifth is "So" (Śo), which is beautiful; it is occupied by two squares. With the seat and the fifth word, one should employ them in all rites.
The first seed-syllable is the middle one; then that same syllable again is the imperishable (akṣara). One should take the Vāyavya and Māhendra [syllables], and then again the last one of the North.
The seed-syllable is the Vāyavya and Pārthiva, and the fourth of the North.

The seed-syllable of fire (Ra) is the last letter of the southern [vowel-series]; again, the third letter of the middle [vowel-series] is to be taken as the seed-syllable of fire and wind (Ra). One should then add the fifth vowel and so forth, which effects both emanation and reabsorption.
The first syllable, which pervades all, is occupied by the third *rākṣasa* (the letter *ra*). That very same [syllable] is occupied by the fourth seed-syllable; that is the supreme *śobhana*.
The fifth [syllable] is occupied by two squares and is the excellent seat of Varuṇa (*va*).
And one should employ the fifth *pada* there in all ritual activities. The first syllable is beautiful when occupied by eleven [units];
the second syllable is said to be that which is occupied by the second square.
The fourth and fifth syllables are likewise overlaid by that very [syllable],
adorned with the eighth and ninth squares.
One should know that the tenth [syllable], which is occupied by two squares and pierced from below by fire,
accomplishes all desires.

One should take the sixth syllable, which is the first of the middle [row]; then the lower seed-syllable of Vāyu; then take the fourth of the north; having extracted Agni and Pavana, one should extract the mantra called Kaṣa, which is situated in the ninth square.
Likewise; likewise, the first of the south;
the third of the east, the pervasive one whose first syllable is "pra."
The second syllable.
The seventh step is imperishable.
The third cell is indeed adorned; they know the seat of the fifth [vowel] to be from the measure of the fifth cell.
Then, the sixth syllable is occupied by the second cell. (7)

The third from the east is to be taken; having taken the [square] of Īśāna and Varuṇa, the eighth step is to be known as that occupied by the second square, occupied by the second square, occupied by the fourth square, and occupied by the second square—
the seed-syllable of Vāyu located below, in the corner of Pavana and Agni.
The destroyer of all evils;
the foremost syllable on the seat of Varuṇa.
They know the second syllable as being designated by the fourth syllable.
Together with the seventh syllable,
one should know that the western [syllable] causes the destruction of all enemies.
Therein, one should take the seed-syllable of the Nairṛta-fire from the first syllable of the north;
the second seed-syllable is the first letter of the north.
In the *Vasantatilakā*, one should take the second [syllable] of the southwest, the first seed-syllable of the west, and the second syllable of the southeast, which is Vajrasattva.
The wind element and the earth element are to be grasped, along with the seed-syllables of fire and wind;
this is the heart that crushes the ḍākinīs of the mantra of the ninth syllable.
The seat [is formed] from the fifth square, adorned with the second letter;
that same [letter] is placed upon the third letters, and the fourth is superimposed from the second square.
One should know that the fifth [syllable] comes from the ninth square, the eighth from the sixth square,
and the seat (āsana) from the second square as it is traversed by the nine.
The first seed-syllable of the middle [row], likewise the one belonging to Vāyu and Mahendra;
the first seed-syllable of the west, and having taken the final of that very same [west], having again taken the final of the north, the first of the west once more;
the third of the middle [row] should be taken, and the final syllable of the south.
The syllable of the Nairṛta-fire is to be grasped;
likewise, the first of the northern [syllables] is the first seed-syllable of the Daitya-fire.
Taking the first of the west and again the last of the north;
taking the first of the west and then the wind [letter] in the southeast.
And the twelfth mantra-syllable is indeed the subjugator of all yogis.
They know that the first letter, occupied by the second cell and itself occupied by the one from the eastern gate, is the seat of the second.
Then,
again, the sixth syllable, which is occupied by the third square.
The sixth is the seat of the Koṣṭhaka, and the fourth.
The third [syllable] of the middle [group] is the first syllable.

Taking the third square from the northeast (Īśāna) and the west (Varuṇa), the second seed-syllable from the north (Uttara) and the southwest (Nairṛtya), and again the wind (Pavana) in the southeast (Agni), which is filled with the seventh syllable;
the eighth syllable is thus adorned.
"The tenth word"—thus is the corruption of the mantra.
Furthermore, the second syllable, which is marked by the second square and begins with the letter 'U', should be known as the seat [of the deity] together with the eleventh head-letter.
They know it as the five-syllabled mantra.

One should place the sixth vowel (ū) upon the support of the sixth square, the fourth letter (jha) joined with fire (ra) below the square occupied by the fourth [vowel] (ī), the fifth seat (na) in the eighth [square], and the ninth [letter] (ma) occupied by two squares, which causes fear even to the Great Terrifier (Mahābhaya). ||10||
Taking the first syllable of the middle [line] from Īśāna and Varuṇa,
and again taking the first of the southern [line] and the last of the northern [line].
The middle [vowel] is the second seed; in the northeast is the second syllable.
Again, she herself should take the seed-syllables of the southwest and fire.
The syllable of Īśāna and Varuṇa, which destroys the army of Māra,
and the gathering of fire and wind—
this eleventh mantra-word is occupied by the third cell, seated upon the fifth cell, beautiful with the essence of the first letter.
And [the same applies] to the syllables of the fourth [line].
The sixth is conjoined with the second; then again, the seventh and the ninth. || 11 ||
In the tenth and eleventh squares, below the eleventh square traversed, is the Sun; it is immovable for the rite of subjugation.
It is indeed occupied by the second square. ||12||
One should take the second [syllable] of Vāyavya, then again the second of Īśāna; the third seed-syllable of Pūrva and the second syllable of Vāyavya;
the third seed-syllable of Paścima, the fire-syllable of Nairṛtya, and having taken Īśāna and Varuṇa, the seed-syllable of Vāyu and Pārthiva.
She herself should give it in the lower part; she should give the fourth of the northern [syllable];
having taken the middle one first, [she takes] the syllables of Nairṛti and Agni;
and having taken Pavana in the fire, [this is] the thirteenth word of the mantra.
And the producer of all bliss for those who do not waver from the path to enlightenment;
they know the eleventh syllable as being occupied by the second case-ending,
and the sixth [syllable] as being occupied by the fourth, which is the fifth seat of the fourth.
Eleven types of living beings dwell within the dung. ||13||
Having extracted the seed-syllable of knowledge (*jñānabīja*), she herself should again extract it;
first, the middle [vowel] is to be taken, and the syllables of Nairṛti and Agni.
One should take the first of the eastern [group], and she herself should form the seat.

Taking the letter *ra* from the Rākṣasa [group], the final letter of the southern [group] (*ma*), the seed-syllable of Vasantatilakā, the final letter of the northern [group] extracted [as *va*], the second letter of the middle [group] (*bha*),
and taking fire (*ra*) and wind (*ya*), one obtains the fourteen-syllabled immutable mantra.
Again, the third syllable is occupied by the second square;
the fourth is occupied by the ninth; the fifth is the second syllable;
and likewise the eighth and ninth are joined with the seat of the fifth square.
The fourteenth letter, located at the end of the northern [row] and marked by the second square, should be taken. ||14||

In reverse order, one should extract Īśāna; likewise, the second seed-syllable in the southeast is that same one again. Then, having taken the last letter of the south (ma), one should take the last letter of the north again.
Taking the wind (ya) from the fire (ra), that same seed-syllable is again the fifteenth word, a mantra for eradication and conceptualization;
it is joined with the second cell and is the second-syllable mantra.
One should give the last [letter] of the north [group], and for the third [deity],
the second [letter] joined with the second square; the Lord of the fourth syllable,
conjoined with the third of the sixth [group] and ignited from below by fire.
The seventh [letter], conjoined with the second, resides in the mouth of the Yoginīs. ||15||

The second seed-syllable of Vāyu, the [seed] of Īśāna and Varuṇa, the fourth of the North, the first of the West, the second seed-syllable of Vāyu, the first of the West, the second of Vāyu should be taken, and likewise the very last of the South again.
And again:

The first seed-syllable is the middle one; the son of the fire and the *Nairṛta* [R] is in the southeast; the wind-seed (*Ya*) is the sixteenth word of the mantra. The second [word] is conjoined with *Repha* (*Ra*); the third seat is the sixth [word]. The eleventh is the crown; five [syllables] from the sixth, ending in the second cell.
Having taken the seat (āsana), the son of fire (vahni-putra), and the tenth from the two compartments (dvikoṣṭhaka),
then taking the last of the north, likewise the other Īśāna,
the first seed-syllable of the middle [row], and again the one belonging to Vāyu and Pārthiva;
One should take the first letter of the north, likewise the first of the west,
and the third of the middle; then, taking the first letter of the west and the third of the east,
one should again place the wind (v) in the southeast (fire).
The seventeenth syllable is the mantra-seat of Kālāntara;

it is joined with the second cell and likewise occupied by the fourth. Occupied by the seat of *na*, it is further occupied by the fourth and the eleventh. The eighth is the mantra-syllable of the second [letter], and the fifth is likewise occupied by that very same one.
The sixth [syllable] is occupied by the third;

from the second square in the seventh [row], the mantra is to be taken: first the third, then the middle, then the first seed-syllable; then the first of the northern [row], and the middle and first seed-syllables; having taken the wind [letter] in the southeast, that syllable joined with the second square, and likewise the fourth in the seventh square.
The source of all happiness.
Likewise, first the right [hand].
The earthly [element] is from the northwest;
and at its very ends is the syllable.
Likewise, the first [syllable] of the south is the eighteenth word of the mantra.
But for the second [mantra]:
the sixth syllable is in the fifth [square],
and the seventh syllable is likewise the eighth of the second square.
And from the position of the minister, he turns the wheel of Dharma for living beings.
The second seed-syllable of the middle [finger], the first of the right [hand],
the third to be taken from the middle [finger], and the first of the middle [finger].
First, the [seed-syllable] of the North; then the second seed-syllable in the southeast (Agni); the fourth of the North; the fourth of that same [North]; then the wind-element and the earth-element;
and then the earth-element in the northwest (Vāyukoṇaka).
Likewise, the last [syllable] of the western [quarter];
and again, the son of Agni [is placed] in the Daitya [quarter].
One should grasp the nineteenth square from the southern edge;
it is the seat of Varuṇa, consisting of two cells, and is joined with the second syllable.
The crown consists of eleven squares; the fifth is joined with two squares.
It is illuminated by the lower part, not by that which is below the lower part.
The seventh [syllable] is from the sixth square; the ninth is by means of three squares; the eleventh for the head is from the second; the thirteenth pada is in the seventh;
and the twelfth syllable is in the third.
The mantra is the coemergent reality.
From the *Vasantatilakā*, the last [syllable] of the north is to be taken;
from the other *īṇa* square, the second seed-syllable of Vāyu, and again the last of the north.
The third seed-syllable of the west, the final letter of the north,
the second of the middle [line], and the earth-letter of the wind.
Having taken the wind (v) from the fire (ra), the twentieth word of the mantra,

joined with the second cell (the letter *u*), the second syllable, the fourth, the fifth seat (the letter *e*), the sixth with the seventh *repha* (the letter *r*), and the mantra that is a great terror (*mahāsantrāsana*), the wise one should take Īśāna (the letter *i*) and Varuṇa (the letter *va*).
The fifth syllable,
and the eighth from the pair of squares.
But it is terrifying to the nāgas.
The middle [syllable] is the fourth letter;
having taken the first from the east, it is the seed-syllable of Agni in the southwest.
The seat is the final letter of the northern [syllable], the third letter of that very same [syllable],
the seed-syllable of Nairṛti and Agni, and the fourth letter of the western [syllable].
In the southwest is the seed-syllable of fire, and likewise in the south is the syllable *maṃ*;
this twenty-first word is entirely free from all terror.
The seat is the conjunction of the second cell, and likewise the wind;
thus, the first syllable is the letter *ra*, with the pair situated below it.
The seventh [letter] is situated on the head of the fourth [vowel], joined to the second square.
But by the seventh [syllable]:

the eighth, which is the abode of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhyālaya*), is conjoined with the second and overlaid by the tenth upon the crown; it is the mantra that bestows the accomplishment of mudrās.
One should take the Īśāna and Vāruṇa [syllables], as well as the first western one;
likewise, the second syllable there is the Vāyu and Māhendra [syllables].
The fourth seed-syllable of the middle [direction], and again the last of the north;
one should likewise make the fourth of the west joined with the letter *ra*.
Having grasped the southern [finger], the middle one first;
likewise, in the Rākṣasa [direction] is the seed-syllable of fire, and in the southeast is the seed-syllable of wind.
One should perform the rite of liberation using the twenty-two-syllable mantra,
joined with the first syllable of the primary mantra from the seventh square.
The second [syllable] is from the tenth [row], the fourth syllable is from the eleventh [row];
from the second cell, Citta is the one who bestows fearlessness upon the Caityas.
The last [letter] of the northern [quarter] is to be taken, and the one following it belongs to Īśāna;
in that very same place, the [letter] of Varuṇa is to be taken, and again the fourth of the middle [quarter].
One should likewise offer the seat with the syllable *na* in the western direction;
furthermore, one should take the seed-syllables of Īśāna, Varuṇa, Daitya, and Agni.
Taking the twenty-third syllable from the end of the southern [line],
and joined with the second square, the second syllable is beautiful.
The third, the third again, and the fifth by that same [count];
the sixth from the second square, and likewise the third and the seventh.
The eighth [syllable] from the seventh cell is the one that possesses the terrible waters of saṃsāra.
The fire-syllable (RA) is the second seed, and likewise the first of the former;
one should provide the seat of the letter RA, and again the last of the western [syllables].
The second letter of Vāyu (Ya) is to be taken, as well as the fourth of the North (U);
the final seed-syllable of the South (Ra), and the first syllable of the Middle (A).
The seed-syllable of Nairṛti and Agni, and again Pavana in the fire [syllable];
this twenty-fourth word of the mantra is for the splitting of the head.

The fifth [syllable] is the third letter of the fourth [line] of the northern [section]; the third [syllable] is [formed] with the fifth; the seat is [formed] from the second [letter] of the square, adorned by the third letter.
One should adorn that very [place] with the supreme, innate awakening. ||27||

The last [syllable] of the north, along with the subsequent [syllables], should be taken from the compartments of Īśa; having drawn the first [syllable] of the north, one takes the second syllable from Agni as well.
The remainder: having first taken the western [syllable], there is the seed-syllable of Ravi (the Sun) in the southwest corner;
the fourth seed-syllable of the west is the seed-syllable of Ravi in the southwest.
Taking the syllable of Īśāna and the syllable of Varuṇa, and the second syllable of Vāyu together with its following letter,
one should place the seed-syllable of Agni in the corner of Īśāna and in the southwest (Nairṛtya).
One should take the twenty-eighth word of the mantra from the end of the southern [row],
and the second syllable of the mantra joined to the second square.
One should join the third with the third, and again the fourth with that same one;
furthermore, one should join the sixth with the fifth in the lower positions.
One should join the third with the seventh; the tenth from the second square;
the eleventh by that same [path]; then again the twelfth from the third; the thirteenth from the seventh square; and Mahākaruṇā herself. ||28||
In the wind [letter] is the second seed-syllable joined with *ra*;
the last letter of the north [direction] is to be taken, followed by the fire [letter] of the Daityas (*na*).
The third of the northern [quarter] belongs to Vāyu,
while the fourth of the western [quarter] is again assigned to the seat of Varuṇa, pertaining to the earth.
The second seed-syllable of Vāyu, then again the last of the western [group], and the nineteenth [syllable] of the mantra which accomplishes all;
joined with the syllable from the second square, this is the third syllable of the mantra.
In the eleventh [syllable], one should place the all-pervading Lord, who consists of the seventh letter.
In the third [house] the eighth sign, and likewise in the seventh the ninth; this mantra has been proclaimed for the accomplishment of various siddhis. ||26||
The great lord joined with Ravi occupies the first seat on the right.

One should take the second [syllable] from the northeast corner and from Agni; the second from the southwest corner and the second seed-syllable from Vāyu; and having taken the solar [syllable] from the southwest, the first and the supreme [syllables] from the center.
In the *rākṣasa* [cell], one should take the fire [syllable] (*agni*) and the first letter of the middle [line];

in the fire [cell], one should take the wind [syllable] (*pavana*), which is the thirtieth word of the mantra and is joined to the third cell; by that same [means], one should join the second [syllable] as it is occupied by the eleventh.

The first syllable is the all-pervading Lord in the Vasantatilakā meter; then the second, fourth, eighth, and likewise the sixth syllables, each by its own nature, are entirely free from delusion. || 30 ||
The second seed-syllable is that of Vāyu, and the [seed] of Varuṇa joined with Ravi; the third [syllable] is the seed-syllable Maṃ, which belongs to the western direction and to the middle [channel].
Again, the last letter of the western [direction] is in the southwest; then, having extracted that same second letter once more, as well as the last letter of the southern [direction].
In the northwest, the second [syllable] is to be taken; then again, the seat starting from the west:
the fourth of the north and likewise the final one of the west.
One should take the fourth letter of the western [group], which belongs to Varuṇa;
joined with the letter *ra*, that indeed constitutes the seed-syllable of Īśā-Varuṇa.

Taking the final letter of the southern [group], the seed-syllable of the wind in the fire— there has never been, nor will there ever be, a mantra equal to this recited mantra that grants accomplishment.
The third syllable of the mantra is occupied by the second cell;
the fourth is joined with that same [second] and adorned by the eleventh.
The fifth [syllable] is from the second square, while the sixth is likewise the ninth;
the ninth is surmounted by a bindu, and the twelfth is again in the third [square].
The thirteenth [is joined] with the second, and the fifteenth with that same one; the thirty-first mantra-word is the source of all bliss. || 31 ||
Having extracted the first square from the west, one should likewise give the supreme seat of Vajrasattva as the first.
In the northwest (Vāyu), one should take the fourth letter from the end of the Earth (Pārthiva) group;
likewise, in the southwest (Nairṛtya), the seed-syllable of Fire and the final letter of the west.

The first [syllable] is the third [letter] conjoined with the eleventh; the fourth is from the second square; the fifth is indeed by the fifth; the seventh is indeed by the seventh; this is the terrifying mantra of the Bhairavīs, consisting of the third and sixth syllables.
The thirty-second word fulfills Vajrasattva. || 32 ||
The second seed-syllable of Vāyu, the last of the North, the supreme Vajrasattva in the Southwest, and the first letter of the Middle.

One should take the remainder of the northern [syllable], the first of the western [syllable] likewise, the final one of that very same [western syllable], and again the third of that [same western syllable].
And having taken the fire and the wind, one should take the thirty-third step, which is the fifth seat of the first and the seventh of the second.
The seat of the third [deity] is from the fifth square; the first is the origin, and the fifth, occupied by the fourth and eleventh, is from the three squares.
From the seventh and eighth squares, the second and so forth are always ignited;
these are the leaders of the mantra who abandon the forms of the grasped and the grasper. ||33||
First, taking the middle [vowel], there is the seat, the son of fire (ra);
then the fourth of the western [group] (ta), and the seed-syllable of Īśa (ha) and Varuṇa (va).
The fourth from the middle [line] is established as the seat of the Sun;
and again, the fourth from the western [line] is in the northeast corner.
Likewise, having taken the fire-seed (ra) from the Daitya (the letter *da*), the southern *ti* (the letter *ma*), and the wind (*ya*) from the fire, one obtains the thirty-fourth word.
The third [syllable] is occupied by the ninth cell; indeed, they know the mantra for crossing over the miserable states (*durgatyuttaraṇa*) to be the last [syllable] of the north,
the first letter, and the second, sixth, and eighth syllables.
The self-arisen sound is beginningless. ||34||
One should first take the central [syllable] from the northeast corner; the second seed-syllable is in the southeast;
the first seed-syllable is in the west; and likewise, the [seed-syllable] of Mahendra is in the northwest.

First, the middle [syllable] is to be grasped; then the initial syllable of the western [group] is to be joined with the seat at the end of the northern [group], and again the final syllable of the western [group]. This is the thirty-fifth word concerning the emptiness of all phenomena.
The second syllable is joined to the second square on the ground; the fifth is with the third square; the seventh is with the ninth; and the two sevenths [are with the] eleventh. (35)
One should place the third [syllable] of the north, and likewise the third of the west;
one should give that as the fourth seat. Likewise, the first of the middle [line], the first of the south, the second seed-syllable in the northwest (vāyu), and in the northeast (īśāna) corner.
Furthermore, O Vāyu, he should take the second [syllable] from the *Vasantatilaka*, conjoined with the letter *ra*; he should then extract the mantra known as *kaṣa*.
One should take the last [letter] of the southern [group] and again the last [letter] of the western [group].
The second seed-syllable in the southwest is the seat for the first and the subsequent [syllables];
the third of the western [group] and the final letter of that very same group,
having taken the wind from the southeast, is the thirty-sixth word of the mantra.

In the first [square], the fifth seat is marked by the ninth; the third and fourth are marked by the third; and from the second cell, the thirteenth is marked by that same [number]—this is the *tilaka* for those who possess knowledge. 36.
Having extracted the syllable that is the form of gnosis (jñāna), taking the last of the northern [syllables] and the last syllable of the western [syllables],
this is considered the seat at the eastern gate;
furthermore, the first of the western [syllables] is Īśa and Vāruṇa.
One should cause the second syllable of the Nairṛta [direction] to be conjoined with the letter *ra*;
likewise, take the first seed-syllable of the North and the last of the South;
and having taken the Fire and the Wind, one obtains the thirty-seventh word.

The first [syllable] is occupied by the second square; by that same [square], the sixth is occupied. In the conjunctions of the "Flame-Ambrosia" (jvālāmṛta), the second syllable and the eighth syllable constitute the mantra, which is a festival for all people. ||37||

In the wind [letter], the second is to be taken; the letter of the Lord of Varuṇa joined with *ra* is for the middle [channel]. By that same [method], the first of the middle [channel] is joined with *repha*; likewise, the last of the northern [channel] joined with *ra*, and the first of the northern [channel] joined with the letter of the Lord (Īśāna) and Varuṇa.

One should take the first syllable from the end of the third line, as well as its final syllable; likewise, one should take "pavana" (wind) from the southeast. This thirty-eight-syllable mantra, joined with the second square, is known by the wise as that which pacifies all afflictions; its eighth syllable is particularly significant. ||38||
Taking the third of the northern [syllable], the third of the western,
and its very last, as well as the first of the middle [group],
the seed-syllable of the Rākṣasa-fire, and the seed-syllable of the wind of the mantra conjoined with the eleventh [vowel] in the fire-position.
The first letter remains as a supplement; they know the fifth letter to be situated in the second square, and one should take the wind (the letter Ya) in the southeast; this is the forty-first word.
They know the seat of the fifth square to be the first step; the second from two squares, the fourth from the fourth, the eighth from that same [fourth], and the ninth from the second square. (41)
First, from the north, take the destroyer of the lord of the Rākṣasas;
then, taking the first from the middle, the seat of the moon-gate;
thereafter, the first from the west, and the seed-syllable of fire and wind.
One should take the first [letter] of the west, mounted upon Vajrasattva;
then take the last [letter] of the north, and again the first of the west.
The seat of the letter *ra* is right there, and likewise the last [letter] of the west.
In the *Vasantatilakā*, one takes the second seed-syllable in the fire [element], then the last of the west, again the wind in the fire, and the forty-second word;
the fifth and eleventh [syllables] are mounted upon it, and the seventh by that same [means].
The great Bhaga-mantra is said to consist of nine syllables from the two squares. 42.
Cause the last [letter] of the north to be grasped along with the one in the northeast corner; one should personally extract the letter called *ka* from the southeast corner and the southwest corner;
the first seed-syllable of the middle [line] is that of the Rākṣasa and the son of Fire (Ra).
And one should cause Agni and Pavana to grasp the forty-third step,
which is indeed the second, fourth, and sixth.
One should know that the second cell among the letters belongs to the Yoga-protecting Self;
furthermore, the third [cell] belongs to the Western [direction], and the second to the South-Western (Nairṛta) direction.
One should offer a seat beginning with the south, and likewise ending with the west.
And Īśā should cause Varuṇa to seize the third [portion] in the west;
and the earthly [deity] in the wind-corner (northwest), which is the fourth of the west.
Take the fire (Ra) and the wind (Ya), and the first syllable of the middle [name];
then the son of fire (Va) in the southwest (Nairṛtya), and again the fire (Ra) and the wind (Ya).

Occupying the ninth cell and joined from the second cell of the mantra, take the first syllable of the middle [mantra] which is the abode of all phenomena, and then the second and the sixth syllables.
Forty-five words. ||44||
The fourth letter of the western [vowel-group] is illuminated by the sun (RA), and the second letter of Vāyu (YA) is likewise.
One should take the second syllable from the north; then, having again taken the fire-seed (ra) from the east as before, likewise take the final syllable from the south.
And at the end of that is the seed-syllable of Vāyu, which is the forty-sixth word. ||45||
The first syllable, adorned by the ninth square, is joined with the third, fifth, and seventh squares, which are themselves conjoined with the second squares. ||46||
Having extracted the third [syllable] from the third square, and the third of the western [direction] joined with the seat of the Sun (ravi), and the third of the eastern [direction].
The earth element is in the northwest, and from that, the second syllable joined with the letter *ra*;
the water element is in the northwest, and the second syllable [is likewise].
The western [section] consists of three squares, as does the northeast; the seat of Varuṇa is in the west, the first [seat] is in the west, and the final [seat] is in the north.
One should take the forty-seventh syllable from the end; it is excellent when the first is occupied by the eleventh.
By the second [syllable] comes the third, and by that very same [syllable] the eighth;
by that very same [syllable] the tenth and the seventh—the mantra which is equal to all on earth. (47)
One should cause the third letter of the middle [group], joined with the letter *ra*, to be made;
then the second seed-syllable of Vāyu, followed by the seat beginning with the West.
Taking the [syllable] belonging to Īśāna and Varuṇa, taking the third of the western [group], and taking the seat of Ravi, one should cause the first of the northern [group] to be given.
Taking the Vāruṇa [square] from the Īśāna [corner], the third from the west,
and the last from the north, one should place them in the northeast corner.

The last letter of the north [row] should be taken, along with the first letter of the west [row] joined to the second square, and likewise joined to the sixth, the eleventh, and the seventh square; this forty-eighth-word mantra was spoken by the Hero.
At its sound, the gods, nāgas, and all other beings dwelling in the forests were struck with terror.

This is the power of the mantra; it has not existed in the past, nor will it exist in the future, due to the majestic influence of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, as expressed in this second-syllable mantra.
But the ninth is the Perfection of Wisdom itself.
The Naga King Mantra.
Being satisfied, all the mantras beginning with Oṃ, as well as those ending in Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ, will grant accomplishment to the great-souled one who has performed a hundred thousand recitations.
And by the application of short and long pronunciations of the words,
they become lords of yakṣas and universal monarchs.
The leaders such as Mañjuvajra and others are accomplished merely by recitation, and the practitioners of mantra become those whose success is attained through recitation alone.
It should be known from the time of their movement according to the lineage sequence of the Yoginīs.
For the purpose of destroying all obstacles, one should cause ten thousand recitations (*jāpa*) to be performed, sequentially for each single step and for the beginning and end of each syllable:

*oṃ a ka ā kha i ga ī gha u ṅa ū ca ṛ cha ṛ ja lṛ jha lṛ ña e ṭa ai ṭha o ḍa au ḍha aṃ ṇa aḥ ta aḥ tha aṃ da au dha au na a i pa e pha ba la ba lṛ bha ṛ ma ṛ ya ū ra ula ī vai śa ā ṣa aṃ sa oṃ ha aṃ kṣa haḥ*.

ka kā kha khā ga gā gha ghā ṅa ṅā | ca cā cha chā ja jā jha jhā ña ñā | ṭa ṭā ṭha ṭhā ḍa ḍā ḍha ḍhā ṇa ṇā | ta tā tha thā da dā dha dhā na nā | pa pā pha phā ba bā bha bhā ma mā | ya yā ra rā la lā va vā śa śā ṣa ṣā sa sā ha hā kṣa kṣā ||

Kṣa kṣāṃ ha hāṃ sa sāṃ ṣa ṣāṃ śa śāṃ va vāṃ la lāṃ ra rāṃ ya yāṃ ma māṃ bha bhāṃ ba bāṃ pha phāṃ pa pāṃ na nāṃ dha dhāṃ da dāṃ tha thāṃ ta tāṃ ṇa ṇāṃ ḍha ḍhāṃ ḍa ḍāṃ ṭha ṭhāṃ ṭa ṭāṃ ña ñāṃ jha jhāṃ ja jāṃ cha chāṃ ca cāṃ ṅa ṅāṃ gha ghāṃ ga gāṃ kha khāṃ ka kāṃ.

ka ca kha cha ga ja gha jhaṅa ña | ka ṭa kha ṭha ga ḍa gha ḍha ṅa ṇa | ka ta kha tha ga da gha dha ṅa na | ka pa kha pha ga ba gha bha ṅa ma | ya va la śa ṣa sa ha kṣa aḥ aḥ | ka ha kasa ka ṣa ka śa ka va ka la ka ra ka ya kama ka bha ka ba kapha kapa ka na ka dha ka da ka tha ka ta kaṇa ka ḍha ka ḍa ka ṭha ka ṭa ka a ka jha ka ja ka cha ka ca ka ṅa ka gha ka ga ka kha | kuhu kusu kuṣu ku śu ku vu ku lu ku ru kuyu ku mu ku bhu ku bu ku phu kupu ku nu ku dhu ku du kuthu ku tu ku ṇu ku ḍhu ku ḍu ku ṭhu ku ṭu ku ña ku jhu ku juṃ ku chu ku cu kuṅa ku ghu ku gu kukhu | bandhaya bandhāpaya | ga gajjaya sośaya tarjjaya sphoṭaya vidveṣaya mohaya trāsaya māraya kampāvaya | duru khura bhara jara viṣa haiṃ daha paca bhañja madhye hrī~ haiṃ cala macala krūracetāya phaṭ.

Repel the enemies, HŪṂ! Repel the clouds, HRĪṂ! Release, paralyze, devour, and strike with pride! To the one who hangs from the garland at the end of the secret [place], to the sky-walker, HŪṂ! To the earth-walker, ĀḤ! To the subterranean walker, OṂ! To the water-walker, VAṂ! To the land-walker, LEṂ! To the dweller on the mountain peaks, HEṂ! Of the Nāgas dwelling in the seven subterranean realms, seize! JÑĀṂ JYAṂ JYĀṂ! Act, act! KHA RA KHA RU GA RA GU RU GHARA GHRU ṄARA RU CARA CURU CHARA CHURU JARA JURU JHARA JHRU ARA!

juru ṭara ru ṭhara ṭhuru ḍara ḍuru dara duru ra guru tara turu thara thuru dara duru dhara dhuru nara nuru para puru phala phulu bara buru bhara bhuru mara muru yara yuru rara ruru lara luru vara vuru śara śuru para puru sara suru hara huru kṣara kṣuru haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ huṃ hūṃ haiṃ haiṃ ho ho haiṃ haiṃ:

Roar! O you who are born together with the gods of innate birth! O you who possess all bodies! HŪṂ! Victory! Victorious one! HŪṂ! Move! HŪṂ! Spread forth! HŪṂ! To Agni! HEṂ! To Varuṇa! HŪṂ! To Anala! HŪṂ! To Dharā! To Ākāśa! HŪṂ! To the remover of all diseases! HŪṂ! To the consumer of poison! HŪṂ! To the driver of the machine! HŪṂ! To Kālāgni! HŪṂ! To Deva! HŪṂ! To Yama! HŪṂ! To Kubera! HŪṂ! To Daitya! HŪṂ! To Indra! HŪṂ! To Bhūta! HŪṂ! To all sentient beings! HŪṂ! To the Wheel of Dharma! To the Dharmadhātu! HŪṂ! To the mouth! HEṂ! To the eye! To the one wearing a garland of skulls! HŪṂ! To the arm! HŪṂ! To the weapon! HŪṂ! To the foot! HŪṂ! To the crown of matted hair! HŪṂ! MASA GASA RASA BHARA MAṬA ḌAṬA KHAṬA MUÑCA! O you who are dear to the terrible darkness! HI! GHUṬA RAMA! O you whose form is the ultimate truth! To the performer of peace! To the increaser of prosperity! To the one whose form is the world-protectors! To the form of all bodies! To the trees, shrubs, and creepers! To the thousand-formed one! To all things! To the slayer! To the form of the slayer! To the eater! To the form of the eater! To the incomparable! To incomparable bliss! HASA VIHASA NṚTYA NṚTYĀPAYA! To the union of the two organs! O you who are without self-nature, the Great Soul! To the warder-off of a thousand streams! To the cutter of various malevolent spells! CUMBA PHULU CULU HEṂ HEṂ HEṂ HĪ HŪṂ HI HŪṂ HO HEṂ HU HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HE HEṂ HE HEṂ HO HEṂ HO HEṂ HEṂ HEṂ HAḤ HŪṂ HRĪṂ KROḤ HIṂ HUṂ HUṂ HO HĪṂ HAṂ HĀṂ HAṂ HĀṂ KUCA DAKA MAṬA RAṬHA DAṬHA JAṬA MADAHŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
This is the mantra of the great root.
This auspicious [teaching] must be concealed, concealed, concealed with great effort.
The syllable *ukāra* is declared to be infallible, as are the Buddha-Ḍākas and so forth;

likewise, the two *phaṭ*s and that which ends with *svāhā*—I tell you this truly, truly. Together with Vārāhī and the Ḍākinīs, by means of these four seed-syllables, at the end of that, O Goddess, the root mantra is proclaimed as before.
I have no other mantra; this is your great mantra.
It should be known as the bestower of the ultimate truth and the ender of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Indeed, there is nothing equal to that mantra in the three worlds;
it is the mantra that bestows the state of nirvāṇa throughout every age within the triple realm.
This sovereign lord of kings of mantras, the pervasive one who bestows great bliss and is worthy [of practice],
is indeed not for the common person who is merely in the state of blossoming flowers.
The Lord of the Thirty-Seven Heroes bestows the fruit when the thirty-seven limbs are likewise arranged; Vīreśvarī is the forty-eighth root for the work of painting.
For in that very way, it bestows the fruit through diligent effort.

It must not be given to ordinary persons; it should be guarded by means of the power of the great mantra. The state of the Three Jewels will certainly be attained, and the status of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others will certainly be attained at all times.
Oṃ śrī hrīḥ klīṃ vajra he he ruru ka ka mahāsaṃvara ḍākinījālasaṃvara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
One should thus contemplate [the visualization] throughout all mantras.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the instruction on the explanation of the nature of the Great Root Mantra, in the Vasantatilaka.
Hereafter, I shall indeed declare the place for practice,
which is secret, supremely delightful, and present everywhere within the temple.
One should practice in a secluded place or even in one's own gardens;
everywhere, one is fortunate through universal trust, by means of the universal vows in all respects.
One should accomplish all tasks in every way as one pleases,
everywhere— in monasteries, forest hermitages, and on the summits of mountains.
One should accomplish the various and manifold activities of a Buddha,
established in a cremation ground, a temple, or the abodes of the Mothers and so forth.
The various activities of the glorious Vajradhara are accomplished in delightful lotus groves and at the confluences of rivers.
The activities of the glorious Padmadhara are accomplished in the ultimate sense within delightful royal capitals and indeed within royal gardens.
He should accomplish the remaining royal duties, both manifold and diverse,
indeed upon various mountains and along the blue waters of the rivers.
When the foreign kingdoms have been subdued, one should accomplish the Vajra-horse;
[one should accomplish] the lotus-red form of the Buddhas and the variegated Vajrapāṇi.
The color of Lokeśa is white, while that of Śrīvajrabhāskara is yellow;
as for the outer canopy and the ornaments of the banner, they may be of any color.
For this is indeed the complete consecration of the glorious Paramāśva, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Abode of All Sadhanas," in the Vasantatilaka.
The Supplement: *Vasantatilaka* composed by Daśabalācārya. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Homage to the lotus feet of the true Guru.

I pay homage to the glorious Vajrasattva, the supreme teacher of the world, who is praised by all the Buddhas; he who, abiding upon Mount Meru, has manifested in various forms to dispel the fear of darkness.

He is the source of the Dharma for the sages, the complete mandala of the Conqueror’s qualities, the Vajradhātu whose singular form is universal bliss, consisting of supreme Śiva for the sake of the liberation of embodied beings.

In this regard, is Śrī Heruka, embraced by Nairātmyā, truly equal? Certainly not; rather, he is unequal. How so? Is he two-armed, or is he four-armed? With his two arms, he embraces the Vajra and Vajra-bell, while Śrī Herukī has two arms. She wears an elephant hide as her garment and is generated from the *Śrī-nona* (the venerable womb). Nairātmyā has a white face, is devoted to the sexual union (*liṅga-anurāgin*), and holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a *khaṭvāṅga*. He abides in the nature of the thirty-seven factors conducive to great enlightenment (*mahābodhipakṣadharma*) within Great Bliss. How does he abide? Within the channel-wheels (*nāḍicakra*) of his own limbs. How is it that he is adorned with the four petals as the primary [elements], the five vowels as the doors, and the thirty-four consonants as the measures (*mātrā*)? Regarding those who abide in the divisions of the wheels of body, speech, and mind—how do they abide in those divisions?

How is it that within the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), which is the very nature of the Four Joys (*caturānanda*), the ten [sites] beginning with the *pīṭhas* are situated in their differentiated state? What is the Lord of the Grounds (*bhūmīśvara*) of these ten, beginning with the *pīṭhas*?
It is the form of Great Peace (*mahāśānta*).

What is its form? It is the form of space (*vyoma*). What should one do? One should effect the yoga of one's own body with all beings as its limbs. Śrī Heruka is the state of supreme cessation (*paramanivṛtipada*), and he is the arising Vasantatilakā. What is "Vasanta"? It is the form of the channel (*nāḍī*). Like *śuṣma*, like passion (*rajas*), and like a spear (*śūla*), it is the venerable Swift One (*Śrītvarita*). Having quickly entered the subtle channel, it resides in the heart, throbbing with a brilliance like fever. What is "one's own body"? It is the brilliance shining in the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) within the wheel of enjoyment (*saṃbhogacakra*). What are the arms of this supreme bliss? They are sixteen arms.
The body, embraced by Mahākālī and the others, accumulates the expansion of the three bodies;
through the force of the *praṇava* within the wheel of channels and the channels themselves, what could the *saṃbhoga-cakra* not accomplish for the world?
It brings about the bliss of one's own and others' welfare.
For that [purpose], he fashioned the *cakra* with a division extending upward; emerging from the *yogapīṭha* in both external and internal form.
How was it?
In its internal form, according to the sequence of the Śrīcakrasamvara.

The venerable Vajraḍākinī is perfected, residing within one’s own body as Cakrasaṃvara. How is she twelve-armed? She becomes so by being filled with the twelve supports (*ādhāra*). Therefore, in the *nirmāṇacakra*, that which is the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is called "cessation" (*virama*); how does she become the cessation-bliss? In the *sukhacakra*, how are there eighteen arms? The venerable Ḍākinī is perfected; she possesses a form terrifying through passion. By means of the *sukhacakra* and the force of the wind, she goes upward halfway into the *nirmāṇacakra*.
For those with extremely meager interest, however, [the practice] is clear by means of the cause for subjugation.
By what cause?
It is the action of the causes of wind and fire; how does it become so? It is called the "Vajra-skin" as described in the Maṇḍala.
One should perform artificial fire-offerings (homa), artificial temples, and likewise artificial recitation (japa).
One should produce sound; what sound? Just as a certain monkey is well-employed by those seeking their own ends.
There is that which moves upward and that which moves downward, and thirty-seven flames rising above.

Thus, in the case of Śrī Heruka, the agent of action becomes the object; from that sound "tasta," it is known as the scripture composed by the sages. Just as the Buddha is beyond conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), yet likewise not devoid of conceptual construction, so too how could there be a discourse on reality that is truly pure knowledge?
What could one do with a nature that is already perfectly pure?
In the world of conventional practice, one always desires to act with propriety according to one’s own nature within the mundane sphere.
If one acts entirely in accordance with the mundane nature while relying upon the scriptures, is one liberated? Where is one liberated?

In the *Vasantatilaka*, the first [chapter], titled "The Exposition of the Nature of the Four Previous Joys by Means of the Linga," [concerns] the path of the relationship between the agent of the ritual action and the object to be grasped.
Now, therefore, I shall explain how the body comes to possess the form of its respective deity:
the Buddha is Vairocana as his form, while sensation is Vajrasūrya.
Padmanarteśvara is perception (saṃjñā), Vajrarāṭaka is mental formations (saṃskāra);
Vajrasattva is consciousness (vijñāna), while Heruka is all form (sarvarūpa).
The eye is called Locanā, and likewise Māmakī is the ear;
Pāṇḍarā is the nose, and Tārā is remembered as the mouth.
The activity belongs to Vajradhāteśvarī; these five are the gross deities.
But Heruka, the Supreme Lord, is the element of all the yantras.
The earth element is known as Pātaṇī, while water is remembered as Māriṇī;
the fire element is Ākarṣaṇā, and wind is considered Narteśvarī.
Padmajvālinī is undisturbed;

she is said to be the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) and is likewise established upon an eight-petaled [lotus]. Upon those eight petals are Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Dhaṣmarī, Puṣkasī, Savarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombinī.
These are thus declared to be the eightfold [retinue]. What is called Śrī Nairātmyā?
"Based on arising and destruction, existence and nirvāṇa are one's own.
Thus ends the second chapter, the instruction explaining the forms of the deities and yoginīs such as Vairocana and others, within the *Vasantatilaka* concerning the stability of the body.
[In the] Vasantatilaka [Tantra]: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the description of the nature of the Avadhūta, beginning with the vajra-pañjali of body, speech, and mind.
The single heroic Śrī Heruka emanates as the five named deities.
And likewise in the Ātma, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and Vāruṇa [regions].
The movement of the wheel is upon the wheel; it stands blazing above and to the side.
And the principal Śrī Heruka is proclaimed as half-and-half.
Through its door, by means of the upper door of Śrī Heruka, are the elements;
the Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, while below is the emission.
In the performance of coming and going through the forms of invocation and so forth,
the Buddhas, Ḍākinīs, and Yogamātṛs are indeed of three kinds.
"Is she, the Mother of Yoga, perfected as the form of innate being (sahaja) by Śrī Heruka?
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Distinctions of the Doors of the Nature of the Yantra," in the *Vasantatilaka*.

Now, therefore, I shall explain the ten seats (*pīṭha*) and the stages (*bhūmi*). The Blessed One is the Lord of the Ten Stages. Having come to the seat of Oḍḍiyāna, he rests; in what does he rest? Beginning from the place of the forehead, there is the determination of the wheel of the letter *hai*. What is that wheel? It is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), where the thirty-two drops of bodhicitta are withdrawn.
These are known as the eight Khecarī Yoginīs and the others who move upon the earth, existing both internally and externally in the form of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth.

And all those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) are situated within them. Why are they situated above? They are situated within the wheels of body, speech, and mind; by what differentiation of locations? By the differentiation of twenty-four [sites].
The ten channels beginning with the pīṭhas.
What are the ten channels? How is the locus differentiated by its own nature?
How is that which abides as the innate differentiated?
What is it that abides? The vajra-lotus abides. What is it that abides? The innate (*sahaja*) abides.
These very stages, beginning with *muditā*, have been thus described.

The stage of *muditā*, however, is the *ālaya* of the bodhisattvas. What is the *ālaya* of the bodhisattvas? It is the *ālaya* of those whose own nature consists of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth; specifically, it is the *ālaya* of all the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth of all the Buddhas.

What is the Buddhahood of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? What are the supreme [perfections] that carry it forth? For the sake of others, what is the nature of that benefit for others? Regarding the thirty-two types of bodhicitta, when do they reach fulfillment? What constitutes that fulfillment? Does Buddhahood come together with the fulfillment of the Buddhas so as to become proximate? What does "proximate" mean?
Wherever else, in what place, and in what manner does Buddhahood abide within one's own body?
What is considered the nectar of the Buddha’s gnosis to abide in? And what is it considered to be?
The pīṭha, the upapīṭha, and likewise the kṣetra;
the chanda, and another which is the upachandoha.
The meeting place (melāpaka) and likewise the secondary meeting place (upamelāpaka),
the cremation ground (śmaśāna) and the secondary cremation ground (upaśmaśāna), as well as the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth— these are the ten stages (bhūmi).
Thus, having entered the center of the nine-streamed *vasantatilakā* [cakra], where has he gone?
Having arrived at all the channels (*nāḍī*), from where has he come?
This is the fourth instruction, the description of the nature of the ground (*bhūmi*).

Now, therefore, I shall describe the nature of the channels situated within the *bhaga*. What is their nature? They are of the nature of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*. What is their purpose? Having pierced through what within the three bodies (*trikāya*), and having united with what?
[The locations are] the head, the Malaya region, the crest (*śikhā*), and likewise Jālandhara.

The recollection (*anusmṛti*) of the channel-wheel (*cakranāḍikā*), the place of that [wheel] which is the place of the recollection of the sensation of the five channels, the five channels as the place of the recollection of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*), and the ten channels as the place of the recollection of mind (*cittānusmṛti*)—likewise, together with the root, there are twelve supports (*ādhāra*). Thus it is; what becomes of them through the division of the twenty-four sacred seats (*pīṭha*)?
These are born from one's own body; does the triangle (*trikoṇa*) within one's own body differ in all its locations according to their divisions?
What is the distinction regarding the state? What is the distinction regarding the state by means of the thunderbolt (*vajra*)?
Is everything divided according to the state? What would it do, though it abides both externally and internally? [It is] the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Buddhas.
What are the *bhūmis*? They are declared to be the locations of all the channels (*nāḍīs*) everywhere;
in these locations, the *ḍākinīs* abide in the form of channels.

Thus, in the *Vasantatilaka*, this is the fifth chapter, which provides an exposition through the distinction and non-distinction of the ten *bhūmis*, beginning with the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*). || 5 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the wheel of channels (nāḍicakra). I indicate that there is a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp situated in the center of the heart. What should one do?
Within its center is a channel having the nature of a blazing fire.
What is its nature?
It resembles a *kaḍarī* flower, hanging with its face turned downward;
situated in its center is a hero, no larger than a mustard seed.
What should Śrī Heruka do? The syllable *huṃ* is the unstruck sound (*anāhata*).
What is the unstruck sound? It is like snow.

Where has it been declared that spring—the delighter of the hearts of embodied beings—resides? Is it the elephant, or the tilaka flowers shaken by the winds of karma? Or is it the blazing fire in the circle of the navel, which, having attained spring, remains satisfied and established through its own offspring?
The single hero Śrī Heruka is known as Vasantatilakā;
how has he become so? O Vārāhī, how is it that the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, have become the radiant Vārāhī?

One face is red in color, with loose hair, three eyes, naked, and accompanied by a dog; she is described as possessing all flavors, mounted upon a corpse, and likewise holding a skull-cup and a knife. Thus Vārāhī is remembered in the *Vasantatilaka* through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, appearing in three ways according to the exits from the gates.
In the *Vasantatilaka*, he effects the coming and going of all embodied beings;
does Śrī Heruka abide in the body? Yes, he abides in the body.
What is this that remains? It is the single *pluta* vowel of three morae (*trimātra*) uttered suddenly. It is the venerable Heruka, the supreme resort of the four yogis.

How is the yogi? He is born from the syllable *huṃ*, whose face is the Vedas; he resembles a dense cloud of smoke, dark blue and red, and intensely yellow. He is adorned with a crown of matted hair, a vajra, the Viśva-vajra, and the *suṣka-mudrā*.

Holding a vajra and bell at the base of the two [arms], with an elephant hide and a *ḍamaru* drum above, bearing a knife, noose, and trident; holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a vessel, and a noose; adorned with a garland of severed heads; treading in the *āliḍha* posture upon Māra; with Bhairava and Kālarātri beneath his feet; beautified by the six mudrās; delighting in the nine aesthetic sentiments (*navarasa*); clad in a tiger skin; the single form of Wisdom and Means; possessing the radiance of ten suns—to that Heruka, the glorious Saṃvara, belongs that glorious Vīra, the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *anāhata*.
What is the unstruck sound (*anāhata*)?
It is the great elements such as earth and so forth, as well as the nature of the four joys for one who is devoted to the four yogas.
What is it that the one devoted to yoga becomes? It is the Ḍākinīs, as well as Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī,
who exist in the form of supreme bliss consisting of action and agent.
He sports here at his ease in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva;
and what do those situated in the four petals and in the cardinal directions play?
What should one do? The five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the hands have become the very form of that worship.

Therein, in the wheel of body, speech, and mind of Śrī Heruka, twenty-four [deities] are proclaimed, established in their respective places by relying on the divisions of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth.
The channels that arise from the head are known as the *śiraja* (head-born);
they consist of the forms of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.

Among them, the principal channel is in the city of Pullīramalaya; there resides Pracaṇḍā, who has a golden complexion, a white face, and a terrifying form, possessing six arms and holding a curved knife (*kartī*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), as well as a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*).
Adorned with the two garments of passion and so forth, she wears the skin of the great savor; she is likewise supreme among those embraced by desire. || 1 ||
In Jāraṃdhara, however, is Caṇḍākṣī:

she has one face, is naked, possesses three eyes, and has a face like a cloud; she is adorned with a garland of severed heads, has six arms, a gentle form, and holds a khaṭvāṅga staff and a ḍamaru drum.

She holds a vajra, a bell, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup; she is endowed with necklaces, half-necklaces, and anklets, and is well-furnished with a terrifying mass of matted hair; her tongue is lolling and she is fearsome. || 2 ||

In Oḍiyāna is Prabhāmatī, who has one face and three eyes; she holds a *kartika*, a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in her right hands, while her left hands hold a goad and a noose; she is adorned with a garland of Rudrākṣa beads, possesses a mass of matted hair, and is decorated with necklaces and anklets. || 3 ||

But Arbuda, with a face pale-red like the evening twilight, naked, holding a vajra and a bell, as well as a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, a curved knife, and a skull-cup, sports here at his pleasure with a female jackal. || 4 ||
Anahā is known as Vīramatī; she has one face and six arms, is yellow in color, and likewise has matted hair.
She holds a bell, a vajra, a goad, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga, and a ḍamaru;
she wears the six mudrās, and is likewise embraced by the Goddess. || 5 ||
At Rāmeśvara, however, there is the goddess Kharvarī, who kisses the Liṅga while embracing it; she has one face, a dark complexion, and is adorned with three eyes.

With six arms, her hands are engaged in embracing the Liṅga, holding a khaṭvāṅga, a parśu, a ḍamaru, and a vessel; likewise, she possesses the six mudrās and is equal in luster to the wind of destruction. || 6 ||

At Devīkoṭa, however, there is the goddess Laṅkeśvarī; she has one face, a white face, and a white countenance, adorned with six arms. She holds a vajra, a bell, a trident, and so forth, as well as a *ḍamaru* drum, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a sword. Bearing various weapons of pleasure, she embraces [her consort] and is both passionate and free from passion.
In Mālava, Drumacchāyā is red in color, three-eyed, and six-armed; she embraces [her consort] and holds a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, a vajra-bell, a goad, and a wheel.
Adorned with the six mudrās, she is the embodiment of sound and action, delighting in taste and water, and is exceedingly fierce and laughing. || 8 ||
In Kāmarūpa, there are Tanakakṣī and Airāvatī; likewise Ekavaktrā, Śyāmavadanā, and Bhujāṣaṇmukhī;
and likewise Vajrakhaṭvāṅga, Ḍamaru, Ghaṇṭā, and Kati, adorned with severed heads.
She is endowed with the subtle essence pervading her mass of matted hair. || 6 ||
Śrī Bhairavī is remembered as having two pairs of lower garments,
being of a single color with a blue body, and likewise possessing twelve arms;
she holds a vajra, a bell, an elephant hide, a curved knife, a skull-cup, and a severed head.
Holding a trident, a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, a goad, a noose, a discus, and a sword, as well as various other auspicious weapons, she is red-limbed and brings about welfare. || 10 ||

Triśakuna, Vāyuvega, Śyāmābhā, Liṅginī, Bhujāravi, Karā, Vajrapāśa, Muṇḍadhāriṇī, Khaṭvāṅga, Ḍamaru, Vīpicarma, Aṅkuśā, Triśūlaka, and Baddhamuṣṭi; he has three faces—red, dark, and black—and his body is pure with bliss. || 11 ||

In the [four] corners and at the tips of the nose, twelve arms are extended; they hold a vajra, a bell, a human skin, a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru drum, as well as a vajra, a trident, a goad, a noose, and a Brahma-head. They possess various ornaments, are black in color, and are laughing. || 12 ||

Embraced by Śyāmādevī upon his face, he is said to have twelve arms; he possesses the vajra and vajra-liṅga, the khaṭvāṅga, the utpala, the trident, the curved knife, and the skull-cup, as well as the elephant hide, the khaṭvāṅga, the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), and the bell.
Dark blue and black, his body bears the five mudrās, and he both kisses and embraces [his consort]. || 13 ||

In Lampāka, Subhadrāṅgā has a white face; likewise, Dharā is embraced by Bhujāprabhākarāliṅgi. She holds a vajra, a bell, a severed head, a khaṭvāṅga, and a goad in her hands, as well as an elephant hide, a skin, and another hand displays the yonimudrā, while with the other two she holds a trident and a vessel for the sacrificial knife; thus she sports in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, her body being white.

In the heart is Hayakarṇā, who has one face and the color of the sun; she is reddish like saffron and possesses eighteen arms. In her right hands she holds a vajra, a parasol, a tooth, a trident, a sword, a discus, a sword, a chain, and a goad; likewise, in her left hands she holds a bell, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga, a vessel, a Brahma-head, a lotus, a banner, an umbrella, and a mountain.
She stands embraced by Mahāprajñā, and she is passionately devoted to the embrace of Kādyā. ||15||

In the *Vasantatilakā*, on Himālaya, there are the bird-faced goddesses with four faces and eighteen arms. They are dark blue, yellow, and red; in their right hands they hold a thunderbolt, a universal [banner], a thunderbolt, a sword, a discus, a goad, a tusk, an arrow, and a small knife; with two hands they hold an elephant hide; in the left [hands] they hold a water-pot, a skull of Brahmā, a noose, a tethered animal, and a *khaṭvāṅga*; they are endowed with the six mudrās, and possess a bell, a vessel, the gesture of fearlessness, and a terrifying appearance. (16)

And Cakraveginī, presided over by a preta, is black in color with four faces— white, dark blue, and red— and has two arms; she holds an elephant hide in her two hands, and likewise, in her right hands, she holds a vajra, a goad, a flaying knife, a *ḍamaru* drum, a trident, and a sword.

In her left hands she holds a bell, a noose, a vessel, a headless trunk as a banner, a parasol, and a vajra; reddish-brown at the peak of her crest, she sports amidst various displays of vigor and laughter.

The deity of the house is located in the place of the molasses; she has eighteen arms and five faces, and her form is fierce. She is dark blue, yellow, red, saffron-colored, and black, and she shines with the six mudrās as ornaments. With two hands she holds an elephant hide, and another hand displays the *dhenu-mudrā*. Furthermore, she holds a vajra, a skull-bowl, a trident, a flaying knife, and a *ḍamaru* drum in her right hands; and in her left hands, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a bell, a noose, a vessel, and a battle-axe. The goddess Parvatī likewise holds a thunderbolt and a citron in her hands, and she shines with the ornaments of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). 18.
Saurāṣṭra, Sauḍinī, the well-known Anagnaka, Paromaga, Khaṭvāṅga, Ṣaḍvaktrā, Muṇḍā, and likewise Aliṅgiti;
their complexions are respectively black, dark, red, white, yellow, and ash-colored.
Her body wears a garland of flowers, and a long necklace of severed heads hangs down.

With her two hands she displays the *yonimudrā*, while in her right [hands] she holds a vajra, a battle-axe, a *ḍamaru* drum, a flaying knife, a hook, and a wheel; likewise, in her left [hands] she holds a bell, a noose, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a vessel, a skull-banner, and a parasol. She is clothed in a tiger skin, possesses the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and has a smiling face. || 16 ||
On Suvarṇadvīpa, she is the sovereign Cakravartinī, red in color, with matted locks and beautifully adorned with garlands of severed heads; she is resplendent with ornaments of human bone,
possesses eighteen arms, and is radiant with the full array of erotic adornments.
To the right are Vajrapārśva, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Triratnaraśmi; they wear the skins of tigers and elephants,
hold rosaries and the boon-granting gesture, and in their left hands carry a bell, a khaṭvāṅga, a bow, an alms-bowl, a banner, a goad, and a staff.
She is endowed with the practice of the Vedas and is beautifully adorned with the bliss of divine play.
In the city of Naga, she is known as Suvīrā, Ṣāṇmukhī, and Kṛṣṇā;
she resides upon Hari and is white, red, smoke-colored, yellow, and green; she is exceedingly fierce, accompanied by laughter, possesses eighteen arms, and likewise embraces Suvīra.

In the left hands are the *yantra-mudrā*, the bell, the flaming lamp, the universal-vajra banner, the Brahma-skull, the axe, and the noose; and in the right hands are the vajra, the trident, the *ḍamaru* drum, the small knife, the large sword, the battle-axe, the jewel, the cane, and the mountain.
They sport in various ways, embracing in the great bliss of wisdom and means. (21)
Mahābalā is on the Aśruvāhinī; she has four faces and is dark blue in color.
Her faces are black, red, and yellow, and she possesses eighteen arms.
She has a lolling tongue, is most terrible, and is fearsome with her prominent fangs.
In the left [hands] are a bell, a *phetadanta*, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a trident, a *muṅgala*, and so forth;
likewise, in the right [hands] are a vajra, a sword, a goad, a *ḍamaru*, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a *triśūla*, and a wheel.
With two hands holding an elephant hide, she embraces the Prajñā with passion; she is sealed with the six mudrās, and all [her limbs] are beautifully adorned with garlands of severed heads. || 22 ||
In Maru, however, there is Cakravartinī, the presiding deity of the great field; she has eight faces, is great yellow, terrifying when accompanied by Bhairava,
and her colors are red, smoky, tawny, black, dark-green, and passionate.
Having eighteen arms and a fierce appearance, she is adorned with the six root mudrās;

in her left hands, she holds a bell, an alms-bowl, a noose, a flame, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a flute, a water-pot, a thread, and an elephant hide with two hands; she is further adorned with five mudrās, while in her right hands, she holds a vajra, a knife, an axe, a *viśūra*, a *ḍamaru*, a wheel, a staff, and a skull-topped staff.
Possessing great wisdom and joined with the essences, she is beautifully adorned with the bliss of play.
Possessing great heroism, she carries the weapons of a child; she has three faces, and likewise her complexion is smoky-grey.
She is dark-blue, red, and has three eyes; she is most formidable and terrifying.
She has eighteen hands and is beautifully adorned with a garland of severed heads.

In the right [hands] are the vajra, sword, mace, goad, girdle, small bell, axe, jewel, arrow, bell, hand-drum, noose, hero, as well as the bowl, the threatening gesture, the skull-bowl, the trident, and the spear; likewise, in the left [hands] are the great laughter and the terrifying [implements], as well as perfume, flowers, and the great linga. || 24 ||

She has two arms and one face, is white in color, and is most beautiful; she embraces the vajra-bell and her waist is draped in a tiger skin. Her arm is embraced by a ḍākinī. Why [is she] four-armed? She holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and likewise a ḍamaru drum. She is black in color, terrifying, yet possesses the form of bliss;
she is adorned with the Mahāmudrā and is fearsome, accompanied by Bhairava. || 25 ||
Embracing Śyāmālā, she has four arms, holding a curved knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).

Likewise, in the form of Śrī Paramānanda, he has three faces and six arms, holding a vajra, a bell, a ḍamaru, a khaṭvāṅga, and an elephant’s skin. Adorned with necklaces and anklets, accompanied by the sound of Lāmā’s embrace, he is of great yellow color and stands in the ālīḍha posture.
Bhairavakālī and Rātri are beautifully adorned, treading upon her feet. || 26 ||

The first [face] has the form of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), is red in color and beautiful in form, four-faced, and most terrifying; it possesses a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
The second is red, black, and yellow; likewise, she has eight arms, is wrathful, holds a great goad, and is laughing.
And with her two hands, she holds a vajra, a bell, and a *ḍamaru*; likewise, another supreme goddess, Mahārāgānurāginī, holds a *khaṭvāṅga*, an axe, and a noose;
and Khaṇḍarohā, accompanied by Bhairava, is terrifying.

Red in color and exceedingly beautiful, she possesses four arms and hands; she holds a bowl, a knife, a hand-drum, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and she shines while treading upon Bhairava and Kālarātri with her feet. || 27 ||

Furthermore, from the nature of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), Ānanda arises; she is yellow in color, most formidable, with twelve arms and four faces, and is profoundly peaceful. Her [right] arms are yellow, red, dark green, and black, holding a vajra, a *ḍamaru* drum, a goad, an axe, and a trident.
In his left hands, he holds a bell, a khaṭvāṅga, a vessel, and a noose, as well as a Brahma-head;
likewise, with two hands, he holds an elephant hide while blissfully embracing Rūpiṇī.
The Great Goddess has four arms, holding a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru drum, a noose, and a sword.
The great goddess Gauravarṇā is endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) and beauty; she wears a tiger-skin lower garment and is adorned with necklaces and anklets.
The goddess Mahābhairavakālarātri is likewise devoted to embracing her consort. || 28 ||

In the corners are the two great heroes, and the deities beginning with Kākāśyā, who are blue in color and four-armed; likewise, they hold a curved knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
The goddesses beginning with Ḍākinī are passionately embracing them, adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, and the like; their tongues are lolling, and they are terrifying to behold.
Mounted upon a great preta, she is adorned with a hanging garland of severed heads;
she is the *Ḍākinī* of great passion, decorated with dried skulls. || 26 ||
Ulūkāsyā has a dark face and four arms; she is terrifying, holding a curved knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a hand-drum in her right hands,
and is beautifully embraced by goddesses such as Ḍākinī and others.
The goddess Ḍākinī has a black liṅga; she is Śubhakālinī, seated upon a great corpse-throne, and possesses a radiance equal to various splendors. || 30 ||
Śvānāsyā is red in color, four-armed, and smiling;
she holds a curved knife and a skull-cup in her right hands, while likewise holding a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaru in her left; she is embraced by Ḍākinī and is most fiercely laughing.
The goddess Ḍākinī is red in color, possessing her own natural form, adorned with the six mudrās, and seated upon a great corpse. || 31 ||
White, dark-complexioned, and extremely terrible, she is yellowish-green in color and has four arms;
the most formidable Mahāghorā embraces Ḍākinī.
Indeed, the Gholalās hold a flaying knife and a skull-cup in her right hands, as well as a khaṭvāṅga staff and a hand-drum.
The Ḍākinī is yellow in color; her nature is that of great striking.
Adorned with necklaces, gems, and the erotic sentiment, beautiful in her aesthetic flavor, she is mounted upon a great corpse and laughs with a great gaze. 32.

In the corners are the Yamadāḍhīs; Sākinī has a black face, four arms, and holds a curved knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a ḍamaru drum in her right hands, while she is embraced by a Sākinī.
Nagna, Hāhā, Kālajihvā, and likewise Rasānvitā;
Hāḍābharaṇā and Pretasaṃsthā are indeed terrifying.
She has the luster of a firefly, is yellowish-red in color, and possesses four arms;
in her right hands she holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup, as well as a khaṭvāṅga staff and a ḍamaru drum;
embraced by Hākinī, she is indeed full of great energy and is laughing.

The Hākinī goddesses are red in color and fierce; they wear great necklaces and anklets, and with their loud, terrifying laughter, they crush the Rākṣasas and others who dwell upon great corpses. || 34 ||
Yamadṛṣṭi is dark-red in color and endowed with four arms;
her right hands hold a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a ḍamaru drum.
She is embraced by a Yoginī, and there are likewise Kolāhala and Cumbikā.
The Yoginī has white and white faces; she is enamored with Kātyāyanī;
she is fierce with loud, boisterous laughter and terrifying with the sound "Huhu";
she is mounted upon Mahāśveta, who is formidable with his bared fangs. || 35 ||

Yamamathanī has dark-blue limbs and four arms; she is joined by hands and embraced by Vajradevī, who is endowed with great bliss. In her right [hands], she holds a curved knife (kartī), a skull-cup (kapāla), a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).

The Vajradevī is red in color, intensely radiant with the bliss of play, seated upon a great corpse, and terrifying with the sound "hī hī"; she is fed with human flesh and fed with the flesh of those under her control. 36.
The enjoyment of the thirty-two thousand channels resides in the Leader; but who is the Leader?
It is the solitary hero Śrī Heruka, together with Nairātmyā and Śubhakālinī.
He is of a magnificent black color, accompanied by Bhairava, and is terrifying. She has eight faces and sixteen arms; all are adorned with a multitude of hands.
At the root of the face, he is intensely black; his other faces are red, yellow, dark blue, green, and black.
His upward-facing mouth is smoke-colored, with large fangs, and is extremely fierce and terrifying.
He possesses the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction and is most fearsome with the tips of his furrowed brows.
With tawny hair standing erect on his head, three eyes, and adorned with the six mudrās; in his right hands [he holds] an elephant, horse, donkey, cow, camel, human, snake, and cat;
likewise, in his left hands [he holds] Earth, Varuṇa, Wind, Cloud, Indra, Sūrya, Yama, and Kubera;
wearing a garland of heads, his body is adorned with dried skulls.
Adorned with bone ornaments and anklets, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction, she is trampled upon by Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Mādhava.

She stands upon the four feet [of the deities] and is enamored with the embrace of Prajñā. The Blessed Lady Nairātmā experiences the bliss of the embrace of Nairātmā; she has one face and two arms, and in her right hand she holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup, adorned with the *śuṣka-mudrā*.
Naked, with hair standing on end and clad in the directions as their garment, they are indeed various great Herukas; possessing great power, they are the bliss of play.
One should thus visualize Mahāhevajra in such a state.
To Heruka, the Supreme Lord, endowed with all happiness— the Lord who is the Lord of Heroes,
the Lord of the Vīras, and the Lord of the three umbrellas of the Vajrayoginīs— [she asked]: "O Lord, what is the Lord?"
"The preta-forms are three-eyed and established as Ālikālis;
thus the Vajrayoginīs are established in the form of the channels.
These thirty-seven yoginīs of the Mind-Vajra have been proclaimed."
For these perfections of wisdom abide within the body, both moving and unmoving.
In the Vasantatilaka, the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Arrangement," concerning the wheel of twenty-seven channels, is concluded. || 6 ||
Now, therefore, [is described] the wheel of channels of the bodies (*kāya-nāḍicakra*), which is the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika-dharma*):
the application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī;
the application of mindfulness to sensation is Lāmā.
The station of the recollection of the Dharma is Khaṇḍarohā;
the application of mindfulness of the mind is Rūpiṇī;
how is it for those abiding in the distinctions of the thirty-seven channels?
Pracaṇḍā resides in the division of the six channels;
Caṇḍākṣī resides in the division of the six channels;
and Prabhāmatī resides in the division of the six channels.
The six channels abide in Mahānāsā;
these become the four-legged Ṣaṭnārighanā, Calavīramati,
and Kharvarī of the six channels and the Sahasindhu.
The six channels are Lampākeśvarī;
the six channels are Ghanadrumachāyā;
the ocean of the six channels is Airāvatī.
Whatever stability there is of the five sense-faculties, that is [stability].
The channel endowed with twelve is Mahābhairavī; the channels are Ghanadvādaśā, Vāyuvegā,
Dvādaśāṅganāḍī, Surābhakṣī, and Dvādaśākāranāḍī Śyāmādevī.
Subhadrā is the twelve-finger-breadth channel. 14.
Thus there will be five channels;
the Hayakarṇā channel carries eighteen channels,
and the Aṣṭāṅgadaśokhagānanā channel [carries] channels.
The eighteenth channel is Cakravegā;
the nineteenth channel is Khaṇḍarohā;
the eighteenth [variant] channel is Kula-Soṇḍinī.
Thus is the factor of enlightenment that is concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga). || 16 ||
In the eighteenth family is the channel Cakravarminī;
the channel Suvīrā carries eighteen [units];
the eighteenth mark is Mahābalā.
The eighteen [streams] are the carriers of the family of the universal monarchs;
