the eight and ten carriers are those of great heroism, who are perfectly [awakened].
The factor of enlightenment that is concentration. || 25 ||
Kākāśyā resides at the location of mindfulness of the body, which carries the four channels; Ulūkāśyā resides at the location of mindfulness of the body, which flows through the four channels;
Śvānāśyā resides at the location of mindfulness of feeling, which carries the flow of the four channels.
The Sukalā flows through four channels at the station of mindfulness of sensation (vedanānusmṛti);
Yamadātrī flows through four channels at the station of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānusmṛti);
and Yamadyuti flows through four channels at the station of mindfulness of phenomena.

The place of the recollection of mind (cittānusmṛti) is Yamadaṃṣṭrī, where four channels flow; the place of the recollection of mind is Yamamathanī, where it has come to the meeting of four channels. || 33 ||

Thus, for those born in the *sthānas*, there is the production of the [four] dharmas: the thirty-two *vahasthānas* are the locus of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛti*), with the Ḍākinī Śrīheruka as the lord of the sixteen *vahasthānas*; the locus of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanānusmṛti*) is the Khaṇḍarohā Śrīheruka of the twelve *vahasthānas*; the locus of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*) is the Rūpiṇī Śrīheruka of the thirty-seven *vahas*; and in the Śrī Samyak Samādhi, the Blessed One Śrīheruka is the Bhūmīśvara. || 36 ||
Thus, the channels throughout the entire body, purified by the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, abide by assuming the colors, arms, and postures of the deities.

In the *Vasantatilaka*, the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*) is the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). Now, therefore, the seventh instruction shall be explained. 7.

All the ritual activities of the great yoga—including fire offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—along with their external and internal forms, are integrated within the thirty-seven great yogas. By what are they integrated? They are integrated by means of the yogas; by what are the deities integrated? They are well-established in the form of the channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with Heruka. The four gates remain as they are, and the square mandala is proclaimed as the union of all heroes (*vīra*). The Guru-Buddha, the Guru-Dharma, and likewise the Guru-Saṅgha—therefore, that mandala has indeed arisen through the lineage of the Gurus. What is the mandala? It is the Lord of the Wheel, the heroic Śrī Heruka. Of what nature is he? He is the King of Mountains, Sumeru, in the form of a skeleton staff (*kaṅkāla-daṇḍa*). Likewise, he is the cause for the great numbers, the vessels, the fire offerings, and so forth. The single heroic Śrī Heruka is known as the *Vasantatilakā*. Why is he called "Dead" (*mṛta*) and so on? In spring (*vasanta*), the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) is known as the *tilakā*. As for the remainder: he is called the "Spring of the Khatvāṅga. Therefore, he is the Unstruck Sound (*aṇāhata*) in the form of the drop (*bindu*), remaining both moving and unmoving. What is moving and unmoving? By means of that very form of white nectar, the channel is pierced by him who brings satisfaction to the Fire. He is the one who brings satisfaction to Vārāhī. Of what nature is that very mandala? It is said to be the supreme essence of all things. What is the thirty-six-fold mandala, the benefactor, the Lord of Heroes and Heroines? It is the Lord Śrī Heruka. The *tilakās* are known to be in spring when the Yoginīs assemble. The six sense objects, such as form and so on, are the engagement of the external senses; internally, however, they are established as the substances of accomplishment, such as semen and so forth. The single heroic Śrī Heruka is the Vajrin through the Bodhicitta. The fire offering is performed with oblations; the Wisdom-Fire is intensely blazing. [It includes] the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Suras and Asuras; those who abide on the Joyful Stage (*Muditā-bhūmi*), and likewise those on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sudurjaya-bhūmi*); those who abide on the ten stages, the deities beginning with the Perfectly Awakened One (*Samyaksambuddha*), those abiding in peace, the Great Pretas, and the faculties in their proper order. The Lord, the Master of the Ten Stages, is in the Great City of the Noble Eightfold Path. Those who abide on the stages, the Heroes and Heroines, the Great Awakening, the Śrāvakas and so forth—for them there is always well-being and peace. Thus is the Leader of the Wheel. In the *Vasantatilakā*, this is the eighth chapter, the instruction on the satisfaction of the hands of the thirty-two Hero-Lords and others, concerning the ritual of the fire offering.

Now I shall fully explain the commitments (*samaya*) and so forth for those who have broken [their vows]. The Blessed One said: "The beautiful triangular mandala is known as the 'Array of Vajras' (*vajrāvalī*); it is celebrated as the 'Source of Phenomena' (*dharmodayā*), the firm method of Great Enlightenment."

The Goddess asks: "In that regard, the goddesses Alikā, Lisanmitra, and the eight groups are established, performing a collection of actions for embodied beings in the form of mantras. What are these syllables—the forms of the Vedas and so forth—called? And what, O Lord, are the mantras, the tantras, and the treatises?"

The Blessed One said: "These very forms are it; there is nothing else. Śrī Devī said: "The fifty vowels and consonants—*a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*—are known to be equal, situated upon the diamond, the spokes, and the lotus, in each petal and in the eight directions."

In the midst of these, within the pericarp, resides the Supreme Lord, the letter *A*, the foremost of all phonemes, the possessor of great meaning, O Leader of the Groups (*varganāyaka*). The powers that follow from ritual action—such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, pills, the subterranean realm, and the yakṣa women—which bring about the three worlds and reside in the mercury (*sūtaka*), and all those great supernatural powers (*mahardhi*) accompanied by the five objects of desire in their own abode; these emerge from the excellent vowels, which are the essence of the groups, situated in the midst of the eight groups. *Vasantatilakā* [verse].
The Blessed One said: The Goddess said: Whatever movement of living beings occurs, all that is indeed of the nature of mantra; for from that alone it is born.
For it is said that there is no mantra superior to this; it shall emerge as a jewel of Dharma for all embodied beings who are bound by the great knots of worldly existence.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddesses! The secret origin is being told, by the mere knowledge of which one may attain perfect enlightenment."
No mantra is fixed; rather, its accomplishment and miraculous power are established [as such]. For the supreme Lord of the Vowels is a mantra whose intrinsic nature is unarisen.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Instruction on the Determination of the Distinctions of the Conduct of the Samaya, in the Vasantatilaka.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Great Bliss-Feast (mahāsukhāśāna) which has as its essential nature the three wheels of Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa. The illustrious Mahādevī said: "The secret of all Buddhas consists of the ritual actions of yoga and so forth; the secret is known as the delightful triangle, the [sacred] syllable."
The Blessed One said: "The Śrīcakra situated at the head and navel is established in the form of the letter E; the cakra situated at the heart and throat is considered to resemble the letter Vaṃ."
A lotus with sixty-four petals is situated in the center of the navel; within the center of the nirmāṇa-cakra, it is encircled by the eight classes of letters.
The syllable HŪṂ, illuminating in color, stands in the center of the saṃbhoga-cakra, surrounded on all sides by four hands.

In the great wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-mahācakra*), the syllable *ha* is the female *hakārī*, whose form is the *bindu*. Furthermore, the remaining [explanation] states: that channel which flows upward from the navel is known as the blood-carrying channel, resting in the middle of the throat; it is the basis for the coming and going of the heroes (*vīra*) and the *ḍākinīs*.

Regarding the eight objects of mental activity during the states of sleep and waking, the venerable Goddess said: "On the left and right sides, the twelve vowels are situated facing upwards; they are described as being surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *na*."
When positioned face-down or at the sides, they are not excessively employed; the letter *kṣa* is declared to be the protector, indeed situated in the lower part.
The Blessed One said: When the moon is situated in the form of the great passion (*mahārāga*) at the throat,
and when it is always situated at the tip of the vajra in the fire of the navel, and when it is clearly manifest as a mustard seed situated in the center of the *bhaga*—
this sky, consisting of the form of the sun, is called the *nirmāṇakāya*.

The illustrious Heruka, the bliss of the Goddess, spoke. The Goddess said: When that sun, which has the form of the *nirmāṇakāya*, has set, what is that which is called the mind (*citta*) and the bodhicitta—condensed and stainless? What is "stainless"? It is that which cuts off the path of saṃsāra, the pacification of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the auspicious (*śiva*), free from duality, supreme, pure, and having the form of the illustrious Vajrasattva.

Having abandoned both passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*), he remains as the solid mass. The Blessed One said: "The *Sarvabuddhasamāyogadākinījālasaṃvara* abides in the secret earth element, likewise in the supreme water, in the delightful fire, in space, and in the wind—the abode of the universal self. The Śrī Devī said: "Aho! Great bliss! You are my teacher, O Great Lord. Your single form is self-arisen; it is proclaimed as the *Dharmakāya*."
The innate wisdom (*sahajā prajñā*) of this very [state] abides as the upholder of that form. The Blessed One said:

"Excellent, excellent, O Great Peaceful One, most dear to the origin of secrets! By means of which the shadow of the tree of wisdom becomes the state of perfect enlightenment—blazing in the circle of the navel, shaken by the wind of karma—that which is well-known as Vārāhī is remembered as the *Vasantatilakā*."

The goddess, whose body consists of a hundred thousand hair-tips and who is like a flash of lightning, at the times of yoga, within the pores, tips, and joints of the hairs, brings forth again the bliss of the Buddhas who have been consumed by fire. Having reached the circle of the navel, she remains as before, with equal radiance. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Narration of the Tilaka of Vajravārāhī and Śrī Heruka, known as the *Asmṛta*," in the *Vasantatilaka*, preceded by the embrace of the Great Bliss of Emanation and Enjoyment. 10.

Thus [concluded] by the illustrious Śrī Daśabalācārya from the work *Vasantatilaka-gīta*. **Appendix: The First Instruction** *Oṃ. Homage to the lotus feet of the venerable True Guru.* That which is unborn and infinite becomes, within, the form of a drop (*bindu*) at the lotus feet of the illustrious non-dual True Guru.
That lotus-drop is yours.
For that object, there is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*), the side of the thirty-seven factors of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-pakṣa*).
The syllable *ya* is said to be the lotus (*padma*); the syllable *ra* is the form of the drop (*bindu*), ending with the Lord (*īśa*).

The syllable *ja* becomes the form of sound (*nāda*); the syllable *śrī* is non-dual; the syllable *he* is the cause that is empty; the syllable *rū* is free from conceptual proliferation (*vyūha*); by the syllable *ka*, it abides nowhere. In the syllable *pa*, there is the lotus with nine drops.
The syllable *śa* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), and the syllable *va* becomes the bindu.
In its inner nature, the illustrious non-duality arises through the sequence of the four joys of the Saṃvara.

The syllable *śrī* is non-duality, and the syllable *va* becomes the bindu; the syllable *ja* is the form of the resonance (*nāda*), and the Ḍākinī, as a perfected one, is fully established within one's own body.

The letter *a* becomes the form of the *bindu*; the letter *ta* becomes the form of the *tantra*. However, for those of limited inclination, it is clearly [manifested] within the group by means of a cause.
The letter *ja* is the form of the *nāda*, and the letter *pa* is the lotus itself.
The letter *e* becomes the triangle, and the letter *vo* becomes the *bindu*.
Of what nature is that *bindu*? It has the nature of the four joys (*caturānanda*).
The syllable *yo* is the form of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the syllable *ma* is by virtue of its being the form of space (*gagana*);
the syllable *pra* is the very essence of wisdom (*prajñā*); and the syllable *kri* is likewise the kiss (*cumbana*).

The letter *ya* represents the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), endowed with the sixteen digits (*kalā*). It is not the cause; rather, the letter *ya* is the form of the machine (*yantra*), and the letter *ma* is the form of the drop (*bindu*). When the letter *ḍa*, which is the form of resonance (*nāda*), and so forth, along with the letter *lā*, causes [the elements] to dissolve (*lulute*), those of artificial disposition perform actions and the like.
The letter *śa* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), and the letter *va* becomes the form of the drop (*bindu*).
The letter *da* becomes the connection.
It is known that the scripture is composed by the sages (*ṛṣi*).

The letter *a* is in the form of a drop (*bindu*); the letter *na* is unborn; the letter *va* is by the force of the wind; the letter *ra* is devoid of form through its foremost form, like the ocean [is the source] of jewels.
The letter *va* becomes the form of the *bindu*.
The letter *sa* is said to be the letter *ka*, which is *iti*.
The letter *ta* is the supreme form of *tantra*, which is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
The letter *tri* (the syllable *tri*) is the clamor (*kolāhala*), which becomes the kiss;
because the letter *ka* is situated somewhere therein,
the first stage of the process is the embrace of the *vasantatilaka*.

The second instruction in the *Vasantatilakā*: When it is said that the syllable *a* is Nairātmyā and the syllable *tha* is Heruka, I shall explain the nature of one’s own body as established through that objective, which is the form of the deity. The syllable *bu* becomes wind;
the syllable *ddha* becomes fire.
The letter *va* becomes Varuṇa;
likewise, the letter *va* is the Earth,
and the letter *ja* is Space itself.

Therefore, the five aggregates and so forth are the Buddhas born from the body of Śrīruka. The syllable *su* is born of compassion, and the syllable *kha* is indeed emptiness (*śūnya*). The syllable *du* is the sound of the drum, and it is said that the syllable *kha* is emptiness.
The syllable *ka* is situated somewhere, and the syllable *ma* takes the form of the bindu.
It performs its activity by uttering the sound "kle," just as a lotus produces the sound "ka"; relying upon arising and dissolution, it partakes in both worldly existence and nirvana.
Having meditated upon Vasantatilaka, this is the second [chapter], the description of the form of the deity. || 2 ||
The third explanation: the syllable *a* is known as *vaṃ*; the syllable *tha* becomes *hūṃ*.
The syllable *de* is called *lalanā*, and the syllable *va* is likewise *rasanā*. The syllable *ta* is the form of *suṣumnā*; it is certain that she is *avadhūtī*.
The letter *a* is in the form of a drop (*bindu*), and the letter *pa* is the lotus;
the letter *ra* is the wind of the vajra. These fourfold gates are remembered as being situated in the center of speech and mind.
By the force of the wind of the letter *pra*, there is indeed the vigor of the letter *dhā*.
The syllable *na* is renowned as the supreme gateway, proclaimed to be both below and above;
it is the transformation of manifold forms, the form of gnosis (*jñā*), endowed with the dharma of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Na" means not born (*na jātam*).
Through the upper door, for the sake of the elements:
the letter *ā* is the triangle, and the letter *vā* is likewise the *nāda* and *bindu*.
The letter *ha* carries away the phoneme, while the letter *na* is unborn through the movements of coming and going.
The letter *sa* is declared to be *kakkola*, and the letter *ha* is indeed the *vajra*.
The letter *ha* is certainly the joy (*rati*), the stability (*sthiti*), and the delight (*prīti*).
And here, the letter *ja* is the *bindu*; therefore, it is by virtue of its innate nature (*sahajarūpa*).
Having meditated upon Vasantatilaka, this is the third [chapter], the instruction explaining the divisions of the doors of the body. || 3 ||

The fourth exposition: The letter *a* is indeed selflessness (*nairātmya*), and the letter *tha* is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). To him belongs the collection of objects; the letter *ta* is that form, and likewise the letter *tha* is the nasal sound (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*).
The letter *ga* is the sky (*gagana*), and the letter *ta* is reality itself (*tattva*).
The syllable *kā* [is] the *nāda* and *bindu*; likewise, the syllable *ya* is the form of the *yantra*.
To that object, I shall show the ground consisting of the ten seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth.
Of what nature is the seat, and what does it become?
The seat (*pīṭha*) consists of the syllable *pī*, which is four-petalled and triangular.

The syllable *ṭha* is the nature of the *bindu* of Hevajra; what is the *vajra*? The syllable *he* is the emptiness of cause, and the syllable *va* becomes the *bindu*. Having fallen, having fallen, in the middle of the triangle, the syllable *jaṃ* becomes the *nādabindu*.
From that seat arise the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Neither do the channels (*nāḍī*) proceed toward the ears, nor are they situated at the gates.
The letter *pa* becomes the lotus (*padma*), and the letter *ra* is known to become [the sun].
And all those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) are established within them;
they are joyful, for the triangle is known as "the exceedingly joyful" (pramudita).
The enclosure of the earth becomes a three-petaled lotus.
The letter *ma* becomes the *bindu*; the letter *ya* is situated somewhere within the *yantra*.
The stages (*bhūmi*) are the *ālaya* of the Bodhisattvas. What is awakening? It becomes the *bindu*.
What is the *sattva*, and of what nature is that which is called "the courageous"?
Of what is it said to be the nature—the sense faculties and so forth?
It is the abode (*ālaya*) of all Buddhas, and specifically of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the rest.
The syllable *pa* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), and the syllable *ra* becomes the drop (*bindu*) in the state of *luluta*.
When the thirty-two [drops of] bodhicitta reach fullness therein, then Buddhahood will be near for the Buddhas together with their sons.
The syllable *śa* is said to be the lotus, and the syllable *ma* becomes the drop (*bindu*).

The letter *na* is unborn; therefore, how can the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) have the nature of the four joys? The ten stages (*bhūmi*), beginning with the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), are realized when one knows fullness (*pūrṇatā*).
O Pūrṇī, does Buddhahood come together with those who have attained it? Where and how is Buddhahood situated within one's own body?
In what manner does the nectar of the Buddha’s gnosis abide?
What is considered [the sacred sites]? The *pīṭha*, the *upapīṭha*, the *kṣetra*, and likewise the *upakṣetra*;
the *chandoha* and likewise the *upachandoha*, the *melāpaka*, and likewise the *upamelāpaka*.
The cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) and the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*) are the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭha*.
Thus, according to the *Vasantatilaka*, he has entered the center of the stream of the female organ (*bhaga*).
What has he entered?
All have come together in the form of the channels (*nāḍī*). Where have they come together?
This is the fourth [chapter], the instruction on the description of the nature of the ground (*bhūmi*).

The Fifth Exposition: Now, therefore, I shall describe the nature of the channels as taught by the Blessed One. What is their nature? What is the nature of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*? What is their meaning? By what means are they differentiated through the division of the three bodies (*trikāya*)?

Having pierced what [are these]? Together with the head, they are the Malaya region and the Śikhā; likewise Jālandhara. In the four *nāḍīs*, however, the place is *smṛti* (mindfulness); in the five *nāḍīs*, the place is the *anusmṛti* (recollection) of the three Vedas, according to the *Vasantatilakā*. The fifth *nāḍī* is the place of *dharmānusmṛti* (recollection of the Dharma).

The locus of the recollection of mind consists of ten channels; likewise, together with the root, there are twelve supports (*ādhāra*). Thus it comes to be. What becomes [of them]? Through the division of the twenty-four sacred seats (*pīṭha*).
These are born from one's own body; how is it that all these triangles in one's own body are divided according to their locations?
By means of the vajra, through the piercing of the locations, is everything pierced in every location?
What would one do with the ten stages of the Buddhas, which have been cast off from the corpse?
What is the "location"? It is explained everywhere as being all the channels (*nāḍī*).
"In these places, the ḍākinīs reside in the form of the channels (nāḍī).
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Vasantatilaka*, which is the exposition on the distinctions between the ten stages (*bhūmi*) such as the sacred seats (*pīṭha*). 5.
The sixth exposition: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain and indicate the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*).
One should fashion a lotus situated in the center with eight petals and a pericarp.
The channel located in its center has the nature of a blazing fire.
What is the nature of that which resembles a *kadarī* (or *kalī*) creeper, hanging down with its face turned downward?
Within its center resides a hero, no larger than a mustard seed.
What would he do?
Śrī Heruka said: "The letter *kā* is the Unstruck (*anāhata*).
What is this Unstruck that resembles frost?
Where does that which resembles frost abide? Thus he spoke, the one who delights the hearts of embodied beings.

O Ānanda, what is the nature of the *vaḍavānala*? It is remembered as the *tilaka* of Vārāhī. Of what nature is the upward-pointing triangle (*trikoṇa*) that produces the blazing hero within the circle of the navel of action (*karmanābhi-maṇḍala*) by means of the vital wind (*māruta*), [wherein] they blaze intensely?
It is peaceful (*śānta*) in the *vasantatilaka*.
What is Priyarati?
The solitary hero Śrī Heruka is known as Vasantatilakā.
What kind of Nandana grove is the Yoginī?
What could the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, do?
Through the division of body, speech, and mind, within the three wheels, at the opening of the exit-gate, from Vajrasattva there arises the bindu;
from the half-moon, Vairocana.
The line of the mantra is Ratnasambhava;
the syllable *ha* is Amitābha;
the syllable *hūṃ* is Amoghasiddhi.
For him, the channels are form and the drop.
What is the unstruck?
The unstruck is the great elements beginning with earth.
What is the great element? It is the bodhicitta that arises from the four wheels.
What is the junction (sandhyā)? It is the nature of the four joys. What is the syllable *ca*? It is the nature of the four junctions.
The letter *tu* [is] then that letter *sa*, the lotus, the letter *dhya*, devoted to the yoga of practice.
How is the action related? What kind of agent [is it]? It has the nature of supreme bliss;
they sport in the kissing of the venerable vajra-lotus.
Where does one find the bliss of Śrī? One finds bliss where the four-petaled [lotus] exists and the four Yoginīs sport.
What is the nature of the bliss of the four wheels? It is the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the vajra-bath.
Having come together, the Yoginīs and Yogins should constantly perform worship.
When awakening is honored, what is proclaimed? The letter *e*, the triangle, the syllable *vaṃ*, and the form of the *bindu*.
When that has fallen away, the channels (*nāḍī*) are established:
*rajas* is called *lalanā*, and *tamas* is likewise *rasanā*.
The *sattva* is known as the *suṣumṇā*. What happens to you?
One becomes free from passion (*rāga-virāgī*).
The *bindu* is between the two of you (*kārakas*), O performers of action;

therefore, thirty-seven channels shall attain enlightenment. Regarding "Vasanta" and "Tilaka": what is Vasanta? It is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). The letter *pa* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), and the letter *ja* is consciousness (*saṃjñā*).
The syllable *pa* performs the function; the syllable *ra* becomes the drop (*bindu*).
The syllable *mi* arises from the nature of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth; the syllable *ta* becomes the internal resonance (*tantruta*).
This is the sixth chapter, the exposition on the description of the arrangement of the thirty-seven channel-wheels (*nāḍicakra*), in the *Vasantatilaka*.
The seventh exposition: the letter *a* is a triangle;
the letter *tha* takes the form of a bindu;
the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*) consists of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment; the letter *dha* is a triangle, and the letter *ma* becomes a bindu.
What is the purification that remains together with the machine?
It pertains to the channels.
I shall explain it.
The letter *kā* becomes the channel (*nāḍī*);
the letter *yā* becomes the form of the machine (*yantra*);
the letter *mukā* becomes the channel-drop (*nāḍabindu*).
Regarding mindfulness (*smṛti*), how is it? It is certain that the place where [the breath] arrives together with the *bindu* is the correct one.

The letter *ve* is said to be *mala*, and the letter *da* becomes the *bindu*. The letter *nā* is the *nāḍī-bindu*; thus, the place of recollection (*anusmṛti*) is wherever the *nāḍī* has arrived together [with the breath].

That is the locus. The syllable *dha* is the triangle, and the syllable *ma* is the bindu. It is the locus of recollection (*anusmṛti*), wherever that place may be, it has arrived together [with the mind].
That is the place.
Of what nature is the awakening that arises from the mind?
Of what nature is the place of recollection? That place is where and wherever the entire *nāda* and *bindu* arrive together.
What is the nature of that place? It is a triangle. What constitutes the triangle? It is the single *triyāna*.
What constitutes the triangle? Vajravārāhī and Lāmā—how are they the Mistress of Secrets (*guhyeśvarī*)? And how do Khaṇḍarohā and [the other] come to be?
How can Vārāhī, who is of the nature of selflessness (nairātmya), exist?
In whatever place the illustrious Rukmī plays, that place becomes the syllable *cha*, a triangle;
likewise, the syllable *da* is the *nāda* and *bindu*, as well as *ṛddhi*.
How have all [the elements] come into the channel and the drop?
What kind of miraculous power is at your feet? What is the kissing of the vajra-lotus at your feet?
It is *vī* (the letter *vī*) and indeed vigor (*vīrya*).
"How has the nature of the machine (yantra) come to be endowed with enlightenment through supernatural power (ṛddhi)? What are your bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda)? What are your vajra-feet?
And how do your faculties (indriya) and so forth come to be?"
How does "māṃ" become "māmakī" for you? How does "sā" become "kamalam" for you? And how does "ṛddhi" become "kamalacumbanam"?
How do the four bases of miraculous power (ṛddhipāda) arise for you? How does the mind become awakening (bodhi)?
O, how does the variously arising drop (bindu) arise as miraculous power?
How is the foot the Vajra-foot?
How does the mind become the seed of enlightenment for you? How is supernatural power the drop for you?
How is the triangle the foot?
The letter Śa is said to be the corpse, and likewise the letter Ddhe is the kiss. How is Indra the vajra? And how is Yaṃ the nature of the yantra?
How is vigor (vīrya) a lotus? How is the faculty (indriya) a thunderbolt? What is the meaning of "yaṃ"? What is water (śalila)?
How is mindfulness? It is that which conceals those desiring awakening. How is the sense faculty? It is the nature of the channel.
What is this lotus grove of yours?
How is it the lotus? How is it the drop (*bindu*)? How is it connected to wisdom (*dhī*)? How is the sense faculty the sound-drop (*nādabindu*)?
The syllable *pra* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), and the syllable *jña* is known as consciousness (*saṃjñaka*).
What sense faculty is it that has the nature of the bliss of the lotus?
The syllable *śra* is the body; how is the syllable *ddhā* the form of the drop (*bindu*)?
How is *bala*? The letter *ba*, the *bindu*, the letter *la*, and the *nāda*. How is *vī*? The triangle. How is *rthya*? The power of action (*kriyābala*). How is the *vajra*?
How is mindfulness accompanied by the sound?
How is the excellent Vajra-strength?
How is meditative concentration the power of action?
How is he the strength of the thunderbolt? How is wisdom the womb? How is the vajra the strength?
How is concentration wisdom? How is the kiss a factor of enlightenment? What is the lotus-vajra? Who are the moving asuras and non-asuras? How is vigor right desire? How is blindness?
How does one enter the end of the factors of enlightenment?
How is joy the kissing of the marks?
How is the striking [of the body] the factor of enlightenment known as pliancy?
O Saṃbodhyaṅga, why do you make this sound? O Bodhyaṅga, why do you kiss the lotus? O Dharmapravicaya, how shall the vajra-drop enter?
O Saṃbodhyaṅga, what is the body within the accumulation of the moving and the unmoving?

What is mindfulness? It is the striking of the lotus. What is the factor of enlightenment (saṃbodhyaṅga)? It is for the sake of awakening through the vajra. How is it "correct"? It is the sound and the drop (nādabindu). How is the vision? It is the falling [of the drop]. How is awakening correct? Having established the lotus upon the *samvatra*, how does one carry the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) throughout the eon? How is it "correct"? It is the attainment of the equality of the drop and the awakening of the *cādmas*.
Is right action the nature of ritual procedure? Is right livelihood the sprinkling of water upon the filaments of a lotus?
Is right effort the various oblations to be offered into the fire?
What is right mindfulness?
It consists of the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the comic, the furious, the terrifying, the compassionate, and the pacification of beings.
How does it function within right concentration to bring satisfaction to the fire through the cities of awakening?
The letter *a* is a triangle; from the letter *nu*, awakening (*bodhi*) is produced.

What is this production? Is it the drop (*bindu*), and how is it virtuous? How is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) [produced] among phenomena? For those that are unarisen, what is the nature of innate bliss? For those that have arisen, what is the nature of sound and drop (*nādabindu*)?

In the *Vasantatilaka*, this is the seventh [chapter] among the thirty-seven places where awakening is generated. **Supplement: The Eighth Instruction** The Undeveloped (*ajagdha*): I shall explain the letter *tha*, ghee itself, the letter *ho*, the triangle, and the letter *ma* as a drop (*bindu*), both in its external and internal forms. The letter *ka*—what is it? It is the place; the letter *gha* is the triangle itself. By Śrī Heruka, the enemies are incinerated.
How is the mountain [the letter *ka*]? How is the lotus with its head? How is the nectar-vessel of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)?
How is the filament of the lotus in the calyx? And how are the *vairambha* winds in the excellent vessel, respectively?
That maṇḍala has indeed arisen through the very sequence of gurus and lineage-holders.
Is the four-petaled lotus the feet? Is the skeleton the torso? Is the triangle the trident? Is the staff the vajra? Is Mount Sumeru Herukī?

How is the mountain a lotus? The thirty-two [deities] are the mind of awakening; why is it called the moon-maṇḍala situated in the center of the lotus? The glorious *Hevajra* is the lotus that creates a clamor.
What does he do? He acts as the cause for the satisfaction of the fire.
That indeed is the maṇḍala.
What is the maṇḍala? It is the triangle, the supreme essence of all things.
What is the supreme essence? That maṇḍala is indeed the wheel of the thirty-seven great channels (mahānāḍī).
Is it the all-pervading one? Is it the secret treasury of the *ḍākinī*-net, the union of all channels?
What is sound? Are the *siddhi*-deities situated within and without? Is awakening that which flows [through them]? Is *siddhi* yours, O Blessed One—is it your innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)?
By means of the arising of the meaning of the *samaya* of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
From this mandala, one attains Buddhahood in this very life; whereas for the Śrāvakas and others, it occurs only after [many] births, beginning with the state of Brahmā and so forth.
What is accomplished by the ritual substances and oblations? The fire-offering (homa) is performed in the great, blazing fire of wisdom.
What is the use of ritual worship? May it be perfected through the union of the *bīja* and the *kakkola*; how may the perfected one attain innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)?
Thus ends the eighth [chapter] in the Vasantatilaka, concerning the determination of the fire-offering ritual (homa).

The ninth instruction: It is said that the letter *a* is selflessness (*nairātmya*), and the letter *tha* is the vajra. What is the triangle? It is the womb (*bhaga*) of the woman. What is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*)? O Lord, what is the phenomenon (*dharma*) and what is awakening (*bodhi*)?
What is compassion? It is the vulva; what action is performed with that thunderbolt? It is the tongue; who is Kali? She is the woman. To him, I offer salutation, perfected through the fifty letters.

What is the syllable? It is the bearer of awakening. What is the mantra? It is the channel. What is the tantra? It is the resonance and the drop (*nādabindu*). What is the treatise? It is the drop. What is your supreme form? It is the ocean of awakening. Who is your leader? It is the nature of supreme bliss.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Instruction on the Extraction of Mantras, in the Vasantatilaka.

In the *Vasantatilakā*, the tenth instruction states: "The letter A is Vārāhī; likewise, the letter Tha is the Bhagavān. Of what nature is the letter Bha? It is indeed Bhaga. And the letter Ga is indeed the Gaganam."

Or rather, because of that formal agreement (*kriyākāra*), the Blessed One said that form is thus neither born nor dead; how then could it be that form does not exist? [It is so] because the Vajra has been established upon the Lotus.
Regarding *bhaṅga* (*bhagaṃ*): the letter *bha* is the earth and the letter *ga* is the sky;
therefore, *bhaga* is that wheel situated between the head and the navel, established in the form of the letter *e*.

What is the emanation wheel (nirmāṇacakra), and of what nature is it? It is the syllable *ni*, which is the great essence of the sense faculties and so forth; it has the form of a heart and is indeed triangular.
Furthermore, the syllable *ṇa* does not have a [conventional] form.
The letter *ca* has the nature of the four joys; the letter *kra* performs its function, and from that, the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) itself arises.
In the dharma wheel (*dharmacakra*), there is a great eight-petaled lotus where the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) proceeds. What do you think?
The syllable *dha* is said to be the lotus, *ma* (or *mai*) is the bindu,
*ca* is the nature of the four wheels, and *kre* is indeed samādhi;
therefore, it becomes the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*).
How does the wheel of Dharma become your abode? How does the syllable *ma* become the drop (*bindu*) in the wheel of great bliss, and how does the syllable *hā* become the triangle?
What is bliss? It is the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
How does the *cakre* [become] the *yonimudrā*? In such and such a manner, from that the bliss-*cakre* becomes the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*). What is awakening (*bodhi*) for you?
To him [he said]: "The letter *ha*, the *bindu*, and the *anāhata*.
What is *anāhata*? Does it go upward, or does it go downward? Does it go to the moon or the sun? Is it at rest?"
Where do *nāda* and *bindu* find rest? They find rest in Madanapura. The eightfold goal of the arising of the mind, however, abides in both sleep and waking.
Are you the awakenings situated in the twelve tones?
Are you situated as the nature of mind? Perform the relinquishment of the imperishable awakening;
where is the relinquishment?
And he has gone into the center of the *bhaga*; it is clearly a mustard seed. What is clearly manifest? It has the nature of the copper-colored morning sun. What occurs in the *nirmāṇacakra*?
O daughter of the Three, what occurs? Enmity toward the enemies is incinerated.
The pervasion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arises thereby;
what arises?
The orb of light, the awakening of the mind, known as the mind itself, which is condensed and stainless.
It was asked, "Of what nature is the body in this cycle of existence? [The reply is:
"What constitutes the path for you?
Wherever one performs an action, that becomes the path."
Is the drop of awakening severed? Is existence severed? It is auspicious, the pacification of the five [senses], free from duality, supreme, and utterly pure—the form of the illustrious Vajrasattva.
What remains? Vajrasattva; how does the "Vajra" become the form of the drop (*bindu*)?
That Vajrasattva is known as the illustrious Heruka; the Tantra is his condensed form. O Heroines, what ritual actions do you perform? The condensed state arises from the lotus of joy;
having contemplated both passion and dispassion, it remains as the condensed state.
What is expressed by the word *ghana*? It is the bliss of the *ḍākinī-jāla*, the union of all the channels. What is the secret in the element of earth? What is the element of water?
Is water the seed of enlightenment? Or is it that which resides within the Self of all in this world?

Is he who always abides truly ever-abiding? Is existence (bhava) eternal existence? Is existence born from the drop (bindu)? Is existence the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)? Is the body (piṇḍa) the drop, free from disease?

What is perfectly pure gnosis? What is the gnosis of the drop of awakening (*bodhibindu*)? It is the gnosis of reality, the Great Bliss, known as Vajrasattva, whose essential nature is all the deities; it is proclaimed as supreme bliss, the self-arisen form, the Dharma-body in the form of the drop.
O Goddess, what is Vajravārāhī? What is existence? From the tips of the pores of the body of the Yoginī, they issue forth and conquer all directions;
do you enter the gods and asuras?
Do you enter? Do you enter the Vajra?
What exists? Where is it rested? The *vasantatilakā* is the embrace of Śrī Heruka in the *Vasanta*. The *vajra* is known as Vārāhī; the *tilakā* is remembered as what has died (*mṛtā*).
This is the tenth chapter, the instruction on the narrative exposition concerning the movement and return [of breath], and the awakening of the knowledge of the mantra-tantra.

The swords, collyriums, foot-ointments, and pills; the subterranean realms, yakṣa maidens, and the alchemical elixirs (sūtaka) residing within the belly of the three worlds; all those supernatural attainments (siddhis) that follow from ritual action; and all those great powers (mahardhi) accompanied by the five sublime objects of desire in their own abodes—all these are mastered through the power arising from the Vasantatilakā yoga.

Thus, having received the guru’s instruction from the master Daśabalācārya, who observes the vow of conduct (*caryāvratida*), and having ascertained through a dream the teaching of the venerable Lord Heruka, one should contemplate clearly—according to the tradition of the glorious *Vajrasambara*—the phenomena within the *Vasantatilakā*, both externally and internally, by means of their essential nature, for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect.

"Vasantatilakā" refers to Vajravārāhī; likewise, having received the instruction of the venerable Guru Ghanācārya regarding the teaching of the glorious Heruka, this work is titled *Vasantatilakā* for the purpose of explaining its ritual procedure.

Likewise, the enlightenment of those śrāvakas who are currently being liberated and have become fixed in śrāvaka-bodhi should be described as "small" because it is not completely pure, as it primarily prioritizes only one's own welfare.

Furthermore, because perfectly complete awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) is all-pervasive, it is not something that can be diminished, for it is established by way of the actual reality (*tattva*) of phenomena. Its constituent branches are the means (*upāya*).
All the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are the very essence of the [Buddha’s] marks.
The *Vasanta-tilaka-mūla-ṭīkā*.
The hands;
the limbs,

"Direction" and "that which makes manifest" are synonyms.
As for the question, "From what do phenomena arise?",
it is that which performs the grasping.
These are the mental factors to be established for bodhisattvas abiding on the path;
they are those comprised within the side of virtue.
Because it is untainted, the truth of the path is exclusively virtuous.
Regarding the classification of the path, it is in relation to the virtuous classes of contaminated cultivation. As for the five paths:
One should understand that these are subsumed by two [paths]. Which two? The mundane path and the supramundane path.
In that regard, what are the phenomena of the mundane path?
They are the twenty-two [faculties].
What are they?
The applications of mindfulness, the right endeavors, the bases of miraculous power, and the faculties.
These are what are called the powers. In that regard, what are the supramundane path factors?
They are fifteen.
What are they? They are the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path.
In that regard, what are the four applications of mindfulness?
It is said:
the application of mindfulness to the body and the application of mindfulness to feelings.
These are the applications of mindfulness of the mind and the applications of mindfulness of phenomena.
Among them, the application of mindfulness of the body is as follows:
In this regard, for everyone and in every respect,
as long as one's own and others' bodies continue to function through the stream [of existence], whatever appears within the three realms is,
for as long as it is being thoroughly investigated, one and the same.
Abandon;

Because that which is established as a single entity is being analyzed into multiple atoms that have not arisen,

When that is clearly realized, because the various [components] fall away into subtle particles, this body is empty by virtue of being devoid of the phenomena of both [self and other]. Whatever mindfulness there is that recollects it as such, and the mental abiding that is closely and continuously focused upon it, is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Likewise, [the same applies to the others].
Furthermore, feelings characterized by pleasure and so forth are eighteenfold, because they depend upon the six collections of consciousness.

When one’s own mind remains closely established in mindfulness, thinking, "Even that pleasure is empty because it is not established when analyzed as being past and so forth," this is the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Since the objects of knowledge are of such a nature, [one likewise applies mindfulness] to the mind and...

The presence of mindfulness which recollects emptiness—the fact that [phenomena] are not established as existing prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with [their causes]—is the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Likewise, the presence of mindfulness through emptiness regarding phenomena categorized as virtuous, non-virtuous, indeterminate, and so forth, in the same manner as before, is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*);
this is the path of the bodhisattva.

Why is that? Because the three realms consist of the nature of the five [aggregates]. In that regard, through the application of mindfulness of the body, one thoroughly understands the aggregate of form.

By the middle two [links], feeling and consciousness—these two—are transcended by perception and mental formations; for the term "phenomena" (dharma) refers to... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The *Spring Drop* Root Text and Commentary:
The miraculous foot of aspiration is Pracaṇḍā;
the common diligence is the vessel-like external world.
Regarding the view of the Śrāvakas, there are [the notions of] permanence, bliss,
and purity.
As the antidotes to the four perversions involving a self— namely, permanence, pleasure, purity, and self—
the [remedies] are impermanence,
suffering, and so forth.
The distinction is that these are the applications of mindfulness characterized by impurity and selflessness; however,
in the view of Mantra, the ḍākinīs whose nature is self-awareness are the body and so forth.
One should understand them as the forms of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding their meaning, it is taught by such statements as: "In the application of mindfulness to the body, there is Ḍākinī," and so forth.
Regarding this, some who have doubts ask: "How many bases of miraculous power (ṛddhipāda) are there?
[The response is: There are four bases of miraculous power:
the basis of miraculous power of aspiration (chanda), and so forth.
The basis of miraculous power of diligence,
the basis of miraculous power of investigation, and the basis of miraculous power of the mind.
In that regard, what are the basis of miraculous power of aspiration and so forth?
They are: the basis of miraculous power associated with the formative forces of abandonment and the meditative concentration of aspiration;
and the basis of miraculous power associated with the formative forces of abandonment and the meditative concentration of diligence.
The base of miraculous power associated with the formative activities of abandonment and the meditative concentration of investigation,
and the base of miraculous power associated with the formative activities of abandonment and the meditative concentration of mind.
This is the meaning of these sūtras:
Here, all meditative concentrations (samādhi) are subject to these very six faults, which are as follows:
laziness,

Laxity, excitement,
and non-application;
The seventh detailed teaching: Caṇḍākṣī, the basis of miraculous power. By Duchen.
The foot of miraculous power of investigation is Prabhāvatī. The foot of miraculous power of mind is Mahānāsā.
She is the agent.
In this context, laxity and excitement are treated as a single fault, making five faults in total.
There are eight formative applications for abandoning these.
What are the eight?
They are faith, aspiration,
and diligence.
pliancy— these four—
and mindfulness and vigilant awareness.
Volition and equanimity— these are the eight.
Among them, the first is the antidote to laziness.
Faith causes one to thoroughly engage in virtuous actions;
aspiration abides together with that intention;
and through diligence, one abandons laziness.
That very activity of realizing abandonment through pliancy is to be called the "basis of miraculous power of aspiration.
Through mindfulness, one abandons forgetting the focal object; through wisdom...
By nature, these are sinking and agitation;
these are the bases of miraculous power consisting of diligence and investigation.
When one exerts effort to abandon [these] through the mind and equanimity, that should be called the base of miraculous power of the mind.
For that very reason, these are to be described as the four types of diligence.
This same point was taught in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
"Abiding in solitude..."
Abiding in detachment,

and completely transformed through relinquishment.
Because it is free from application to objects that have been produced, that renunciation of substantiality is called the "basis of miraculous power endowed with renunciation.
When these five branches are condensed, the four bases of miraculous power consist of twenty aspects.
What is miraculous power like?
"Expansion" refers to miraculous power (*ṛddhi*),
because it is desired [as such] from the verbal root *ṛdh* (meaning "to expand") with the suffix *yaṇ*. Regarding that, [it is explained in] the *Daśabala-vicāra-ṭīkā*.
The faculty of faith is Vīramatī; the faculty of diligence is Kharvarī;
the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī.

That which causes all the qualities of a Buddha— such as the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)— to increase and be attained is "miraculous power" (*ṛddhi*), which is perfectly complete awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Because they are like the feet of that [awakening], they are called "feet" (*pāda*).
That which brings about attainment is the basis of miraculous power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Although it is common [to all], it is specifically the method of the path; for these two bases alone are the most effective antidotes to the defects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The nature of these is Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī,
and Prabhāvatī.
Mahānāsā refers to the ḍākinīs residing in the locations of the mind wheel (*cittacakra*).
Regarding that, how many sense faculties (*indriya*) are there? There are five.
What are the five?
They are faith and diligence.
Mindfulness, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
In that regard, the four dharmas conducive to penetration on the path of preparation are: "heat," "peak," "patience," and...
These are the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharmas*).
In this regard, just as heat arises as a precursor to fire when a bodhisattva has directed themselves toward the untainted meditative absorption (*anāsravasamādhi*),
the arising of the fire of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) from the mind is described as "becoming warm" (*uṣmagata*).
That very reality abiding together with my exceedingly superior intention is the "Peak" (mūrdhan). That very reality, having the nature of being mentally endured, is "Patience" (kṣānti).
That very reality arising immediately after Patience is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Regarding their application, this [section] includes the preparatory stage.
Among them, in the first of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), those qualities such as faith and so forth are to be called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Therein, faith is [the conviction in] existence and the detailed teaching of the seven [truths].
The faculty of concentration is Śiṅdrimā;
the faculty of wisdom is Sasnyungmā;
the power of faith is Mahābhairavī.

The mental conviction regarding the supramundane path, the truths, the Three Jewels, and so forth, is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). To exert effort toward those phenomena generated by the faculty of faith is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Furthermore, there are four types:
the diligence of the preliminary stage,
the irreversible diligence, and so forth.
These are the diligence of analytical discernment and the diligence of accomplishment.
That which repeatedly directs itself toward the phenomena produced by diligence and remains without forgetfulness is the faculty of mindfulness.
To abide by focusing on the phenomena generated by the faculty of mindfulness, having completely set aside all other conventional designations, is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
To correctly discern and analytically examine the phenomena generated by the faculty of concentration is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*). Why are they called "faculties" (*indriya*)?
The faculties (*indriya*) are so called because they cause the factors conducive to virtue to emerge;
they are that which thoroughly produce the five aggregates of both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
Excluding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), [there are] Śūramati and...
Mukuta, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā— these four ḍākinīs—
Faith,
diligence,
and mindfulness.
One should understand that the meditative absorptions (samādhis) are completely pure.
In that regard, how many powers (balas) are there? There are five.
What are the five?
They are as previously explained: [the *Ṛtucaryā*] and the *Vasantatilaka-tantra-vṛtti*.
The power of effort is Vāyuvegā;
the power of mindfulness is Madyapāyinī;
the power of meditative concentration is Śyāmādevī.
The power of wisdom is Subhadrā;
the samādhi factor of enlightenment is Hayakarṇī;
the diligence factor of enlightenment is Ḍākīmukhī.
If one asks, "Is it that the functions of the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and so forth, are distinct from those of joy, faith, and the others?
It is said in reply:
That which undergoes transformation, such as faith and so forth, does so by depending on the fluctuation of the faculties; at that time,
the discordant factors, such as lack of faith, [arise].
Laziness, forgetfulness,
distraction, and mental engagement with the basis for rebirth;

The statement, "Not being crushed by impaired wisdom becomes a power," refers to their distinct functions. Together with the previously mentioned faculty of wisdom, they are the Earth-Protector of the Speech Wheel,
Mahābhairava, and [the others].
Vāyuvega,
Surābhakṣī,
and the goddess Śyāmādevī.
One should understand that these excellent factors are completely pure. In that regard, how many branches of enlightenment are there?
There are seven.
What are the seven?
They are the factor of enlightenment that is correct concentration and the factor of enlightenment that is correct diligence.
The factor of enlightenment of correct joy is Śauṇḍinī; the factor of enlightenment of correct mindfulness is Cakravarmiṇī;
the factor of enlightenment of correct equanimity is Suvīrā.
These limbs belong to awakening on the path of seeing;
for awakening is unobscured primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
That which brings the mind which sees the truths into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the limb of awakening of correct concentration.

That which exerts effort toward reality itself is the diligence factor of enlightenment (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). That which brings about a state of mind free from doubt regarding reality itself is the joy factor of enlightenment (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Because of that very joy, one gains mastery over body, speech, and mind, thereby abandoning the torment of the afflictions.

The attainment of extreme coolness is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The thorough knowledge of the nature of perfectly complete reality is the factor of enlightenment of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The non-forgetfulness of the mind regarding that very reality is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The equanimity factor of enlightenment (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the relinquishing of intolerance toward meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the absence of attachment.
Among these, the nature of the concentration and diligence factors of enlightenment should be understood as Aśvakarṇī and Ḍākāmukhī; this is the purity of the heroines of the wheel of speech.

As for the remaining five, beginning with joy (*prīti*) and so forth, they are Cakravegā; [in the Sanskrit manuscript: *theg*] Śakti; Ghoṣā; Cittā; and Vasantatilakā. Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is Mahābalā.
Right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is Cakravartinī. Right speech (*samyagvāk*) is Mahāvīryā.
Right Action is Kākāsyā;
Right Livelihood is Ulūkāsyā.
Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, and Suvīrā are their respective purities.

Having taught the path of seeing as the antidote to the afflictive obscurations, the path of meditation is now taught as the antidote to the cognitive obscurations; this consists of the eight branches of the noble path.
What are these eight? They are: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi.

In that regard, on the path of meditation, the mental state that realizes the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to be devoid of intrinsic nature is right view; this is also what constitutes the existence of the next world. Having attained that view, focusing upon selflessness is right thought.
Clearly demonstrating to sentient beings the reality that one has perceived oneself is right speech.

Exclusively virtuous conduct is the limit of physical action (*kāyakarmānta*); furthermore, causing others to feel awe in order to discipline them through miraculous powers and so forth is also right action (*samyakkarmānta*).
Seeking only the sustenance of meditative concentration and requisites such as religious robes is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
Applying oneself in all modes of conduct in accordance with one’s own mind, body, speech, and mental conventions is right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*).
Furthermore, it is said: "The seven detailed teachings are as follows: Right Effort is Śvānāsyā;
Right Mindfulness is Sūkarāsyā;
and Right Samādhi is Śrī Heruka."
To generate virtuous qualities that have not yet arisen is *yamdā*.
To [preserve] virtuous qualities that have already arisen is *pūllira* and so forth; as for the types of places, meditating in such a manner is delusion.

Through possessing inner yoga, yogins attain liberation. The certainty of the innate white [wisdom], by the mere touch of it, bestows the very fruit of buddhahood upon the world. In order to enter the wheel explained as consisting of the ten dakinis and so forth, one is eternally of the nature of the indivisible and so on.

Abiding at all times within beings, the great hero whose nature is the *dhātu*, perfectly endowed with the twenty-four [sites]: Caṇe (the crooked) and Ceṇe (the pure). This is the eighth chapter, the detailed exposition of purity.

In that regard, one should realize that the body itself is the maṇḍala; thus, it is connected with the term "the maṇḍala of the body."

If one asks how that is so, it is as follows: "Great Enlightenment" and so forth. These channels, which are the basis for the establishment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) in their purified state, are established in that very same manner as the ḍākinīs and others who abide within the wheels of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), mind, speech, body, and commitment (*samaya*). The Root Commentary on the Spring Drop:
Bodhicitta is the precious jewel;
that very essence is also the maṇḍala.
In terms of their external and internal essences,
they exist pervasively as a manifold variety:
external forms, sounds, and so forth.
The purity of the engagement of the sixth faculty is taught.
These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) are by nature associated with contact; through their complete purification,
the previously mentioned wheels of channels alone constitute the maṇḍala.
By the phrase "the mind of awakening" (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, the purity of the hero is taught.
These twenty-four elements of the nature of the flowing *bodhicitta* are themselves "jewels" because they are priceless; they are the maṇḍala of the wheel of goddesses.

That which upholds the essence of that maṇḍala is the Hero’s Maṇḍala; thus, there are two types of maṇḍalas. Externally, it consists of the four corners and so forth, while internally, the heart maṇḍala consists of the three wheels and so forth.

Here, externally, the crown of the head and so forth are Jālandhara and the other [pīṭhas], while internally they are of the nature of the channels and elements. Furthermore, these maṇḍalas do not belong to this [system] alone; [they are common to all].
These five diverse classes of beings should also be understood as being within that maṇḍala. As it was said:
"Diverse, pervasive, and abiding."
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, this is the eighth [chapter] which extensively teaches the external mandala of forms, sounds, and so forth, as well as the internal [substances] such as semen and so forth.
The substances of accomplishment abide therein; by means of the very interior together with the exterior,
it is the bodhicitta of the Vajra-holder.
With offerings characterized by both coarse and subtle natures,
which possess the nature of kinsmen for all beings—
by means of those offerings, one should worship the inner maṇḍala.
Internally, one should understand that the five nectars within the *kapāla* are for the sake of the offering of bliss.
Here, externally, the doors of the sense faculties are to be worshipped with the five qualities of desire, such as form and so forth;
internally, they abide as the substances of accomplishment—that is, the substances that naturally flow as the five spaces.
That point is taught by the passage beginning with: "Externally, forms, sounds, and so forth... and so on.
Externally, the gross and subtle [aspects] are shown to the disciples for the sake of bestowing the samaya.
Here, because the Bodhicittavajradhara— distinguished by the division into gross and subtle—
accomplishes all wandering beings as Buddhahood itself, [he acts thus].

Because the state of Buddhahood itself and even the state of a Bodhisattva are bestowed and arise through the granting of the samaya, the level [of enlightenment] will be attained from this mandala alone.
This point was taught in reliance upon the coarse and the subtle;

The Bhagavāns, the Tathāgatas, the supreme Victors, have authentically enjoyed that very speech which experiences the unchanging reality of each individual word; these are those who have attained it through exertion.
That very experience is to be seen within all the Sūtras and Tantras. It is said:
As it is said in the scriptures: "There is conviction through the scriptures,
likewise conviction through the guru,
and conviction through oneself."
This is because it is stated in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*: "Likewise, one should grasp the four reliances, which consist of faith in others," and so forth.
